“噢，我能替您说话，”他用英语回答，“因为我清楚。您的处境是这样。”他坐回摇椅，架起腿，望着我，仿佛指望我为他知道得这么多而露出惊叹的神色。“您陷在坑裡。您必须离开牙买加这岛——它确实同我亲爱的故土一样多灾多难——您又回不了家，因为缉私吏（runners）会追您。您在这儿是‘被通缉的’，在那儿也是，您无处可去。”

我望着他，被他对我案情的这一看法惊住了。他向我伸出一只胖手，声音压得更低。

“这样吧，我给您一个好差事，一个安稳的差事。而且那是个漂亮地方。”他嗓音裡调进一种慵懒的甜腻，拖长腔，“那——那位小姐的。”他换上一副公事公办的坦率神气。“您能帮我们，我们也能帮您；没有我们您过得去，没有您我们过得更好，不过如此。我们的事业——裡头有大人物，正像您熟得很的那种自由贸易，别说您不熟——从哈瓦那经营。我们需要的是一个信得过的人。我们有过一个——尼科尔斯（Nichols）。您记得您搭来的那条船上的二副。他就是尼古拉·埃尔·德莫尼奥；他不会再是了——为什么，说来话长，我不能告诉您。”

我确实清清楚楚记得泰晤士号（Thames）那个死人般脸色的新斯科舍二副，他曾气势汹汹地威吓我别在裡奥梅迪奥露脸。我记得他蜡黄发亮的脸颊，和他爪子般的双手夸张的动作。

奥布赖恩微笑。“尼科尔斯活得好好儿的，只是跟死了一样没用。这是实话。他装作胆气碎了；他一度是裁缝堆裡的魔鬼，可他如今动不动就哭。就是你们那位瞎撞的老上将的艇队不得不被打退之后，他的热劲凉了。他以为英国政府会大张旗鼓地站起来。”他话音裡含着辛酸的轻蔑，随后又恢复他平静的生意口吻。“它才不会呢。

===Original===

I’ve given them those seven poor devils that had to die today without absolution. So Nichols is done for, as far as we are concerned. I’ve got him put away to keep him from blabbing. You can have his place﻿—and better than his place. He was only a sailor, which you are not. However, you know enough of ships, and what we want is a man with courage, of course, but also a man we can trust. Any of the Creoles would bolt into the bush the moment they’d five dollars in hand. We’ll pay you well; a large share of all you take.”
I laughed outright. “You’re quite mistaken in your man,” I said. “You are, really.”
He shook his head gently, and brushed an invisible speck from his plump black knees.
“You *must* go somewhere,” he said. “Why not go with us?”
I looked at him, puzzled by his tenacity and assurance.
“Ramon here has told us you battered the admiral last night; and there’s a warrant out already against you for attempted murder. You’re hand and glove with the best of the Separationists in this island, I know, but they won’t save you from being committed﻿—for rebellion, perhaps. You know it as well as I do. You were down here to take a passage today, weren’t you, now?”
I remembered that the Island Loyalists said that the pirates and Separationists worked together to bother the admiral and raise discontent. Living in the centre of Separationist discontent with the Macdonalds, I knew it was not true. But nothing was too bad to say against the planters who clamoured for union with the United States.
O’Brien leaned forward. His voice had a note of disdain, and then took one of deeper earnestness; it sank into his chest. He extended his hand; his eyebrows twitched. He looked﻿—he was﻿—a conspirator.
“I tell you I do it for the sake of Ireland,” he said passionately. “Every ship we take, every clamour they raise here, is a stroke and is disgrace for them over there that have murdered us and ruined my own dear land.” His face worked convulsively; I was in the presence of one of the primeval passions. But he grew calm immediately after. “*You* want Separation for reasons of your own. I don’t ask what they are. No doubt you and your crony Macdonald and the rest of them will feather your own nests; I don’t ask. But help me to be a thorn in their sides﻿—just a little﻿—just a little longer. What do I put in your way? Just what you want.

===Chinese===

“我已经把他们那七个今天没领赦罪就死掉的可怜虫交了出去。所以尼科尔斯这一页，对我们算翻过去了。我把他安置起来了，免得他走漏风声。您可以顶他的位置——比他的位置还好。他只是个水手，您不是。不过您对船懂得够多，而我们要的是有胆量的人，这当然，更是信得过的人。克里奥尔人裡随便哪个，手裡一攥上五块钱就窜进树丛裡去了。我们给您的报酬优厚；你们掳来的一切，您拿大头。”

我放声笑了。“您看错人了，”我说。“真是的。”

他轻轻摇头，从黑胖的膝上掸去一粒看不见的尘屑。

“您总得去个地方，”他说。“为什么不跟我们走？”

我望着他，被他的韧性与笃定弄糊涂了。

“这儿的拉蒙告诉我们，您昨夜把上将揍了；已经有一张谋杀未遂的拘票发给您了。我知道您同这岛上最好的分离派情同手足，可他们救不了您不被起诉——罪名兴许是叛乱。这一点您跟我一样清楚。您今天下来就是打算搭船走的，是不是？”

我想起岛上的保王派说，海盗和分离派串通一气，作践上将、煽动不满。同麦克唐纳家一起住在分离派不满情绪的中心，我知道那不是真的。可是，对那些嚷着要并入合众国的种植园主，再难听的话也不算过分。

奥布赖恩俯身向前。他的声音先带一丝轻蔑，随即又换上更深的恳切；沉进胸腔裡。他伸出手；眉毛抽动。他看样子是——他本来就是——一个阴谋家。

“我告诉您，我是为了爱尔兰干这个的，”他激昂地说。“我们掳的每一条船，他们在这儿吵嚷的每一场，都是一记耳光，是他们那些人的耻辱——那边那些屠戮我们、毁了我亲爱的故土的人。”他的脸痉挛地抽动；我面对的是一种太古的激情。可他随即就平静下来。“您要分离，有您自己的理由。我不问是什么。毫无疑问，您和您的伙伴麦克唐纳还有其余那些人要自肥巢穴；我不问。可是帮我做他们肉中的刺——就一小会儿——就一小会儿。我拦了您什么路？拦的正是您想要的。

===Original===

Have your Jamaica joined to the United States. You’ll be able to come back with your pockets full, and I’ll be joyful﻿—for the sake of my own dear land.”
I said suddenly and recklessly﻿—if I had to face one race-passion, he had to look at another; we were cat and dog﻿—Celt and Saxon, as it was in the beginning: “I am not a traitor to my country.” Then I realized with sudden concern that I had probably awakened the old Don. He stirred uneasily in his chair, and lifted one hand.
“The moment I go out from here I’ll denounce you,” I said very low; “I swear I will. You’re here; you can’t get away; you’ll swing.”
O’Brien started. His eyes blazed at me. Then he frowned. “I’ve been misled,” he muttered, with a dark glance at Carlos. And recovering his jocular serenity, “Ye mean it?” he asked; “it’s not British heroics?”
The old Don stirred again and sighed. The young girl glided swiftly to his side. “Señor O’Brien,” she said, “you have so irritated my English cousin that he has awakened my father.”
O’Brien grinned gently. “ ’Tis ever the way,” he said sardonically. “The English fools do the harm and the Irish fool gets the kicking.” He rose to his feet, quite collected, a spick-and-span little man. “I suppose I’ve said too much. Well, well! You are going to denounce the senior judge of the Marine Court of Havana as a pirate. I wonder who will believe you!” He went behind the old Don’s chair with the gliding motion of a Spanish lawyer, and slipped down the open trap-hatch near the window.
It was the disappearance of a shadow. I heard some guttural mutterings come up through the hatch, a rustling, then silence. If he was afraid of me at all he carried it off very well. I apologized to the young girl for having awakened her father. Her colour was very high, and her eyes sparkled. If she had not been so very beautiful I should have gone away at once. She said angrily:
“He is odious to me, the Señor Juez. Too long my father has suffered his insolence.” She was very small, but she had an extraordinary dignity of command. “I could see, Señor, that he was annoying you. Why should you consider such a creature?” Her head drooped. “But my father is very old.”
I turned upon Carlos, who stood all black in the light of the window.
“Why did you make me meet him? He may be a judge of your Marine Court, but he’s nothing but a scoundrelly bog-trotter.”

===Chinese===

“让您的牙买加并入合众国去。到时您口袋揣满回来，我要欢喜的——为我亲爱的故土的缘故。”

我突然不顾一切地说——倘若我得面对一种种族的激情，他也得正视另一种；我们是猫和狗——凯尔特人和撒克逊，从太初起就是这样：“我不是我祖国的叛徒。”随即我忽然担心起来，我多半吵醒了老堂。他在椅子裡不安地动了动，抬起一只手。

“我一走出这儿就去告发您，”我极低地说；“我发誓。您在这儿；您跑不掉；您要上绞架。”

奥布赖恩一惊。他的眼睛朝我冒火。随后皱眉。“我被误导了，”他咕哝，阴沉地瞥了卡洛斯一眼。随即恢复他打趣的镇定，“您当真？”他问；“不是英国式的英雄做派？”

老堂又动了动，叹了口气。年轻的姑娘轻盈地滑到他身边。“奥布赖恩先生，”她说，“您把我这位英国表兄惹得这么激动，害他吵醒了我的父亲。”

奥布赖恩温和地咧嘴一笑。“向来如此，”他讥诮地说。“英国蠢货闯的祸，爱尔兰蠢货挨的踹。”他站起身，全然镇定，一个整洁利落的小个子男人。“我想我说得太多了。好吧，好吧！您要去告发哈瓦那海事法庭的资深法官是海盗。我倒想知道谁信您！”他带着西班牙律师的滑行步态绕到老堂椅后，从窗边敞开的活板口溜了下去。

那是一道影子的消失。我听见活板口下传来几声喉音的咕哝，一阵窸窣，然后寂静。倘若他果真怕我，他也掩饰得漂亮极了。我为吵醒了她父亲向年轻姑娘道歉。她的脸色绯红，眼睛发亮。若不是她美得那样出奇，我立刻就走了。她生气地说：

“我厌恶他，那位法官先生。我父亲受他的无礼太久了。”她个子很小，却有一种非凡的指挥的威严。“我看得出来，先生，他在烦扰您。何必把这样的东西放在心上？”她的头垂下去。“可我的父亲太老了。”

我转向卡洛斯，他一身黑，立在窗光裡。

“你为什么让我见他？他也许是你们海事法庭的法官，可他不过是个恶棍沼地佬。”

===Original===

Carlos said a little haughtily, “You must not denounce him. You should not leave this place if I feared you would try thus to bring dishonour on this gray head, and involve this young girl in a public scandal.” His manner became soft. “For the honour of the house you shall say nothing. And you shall come with us. I need you.”
I was full of mistrust now. If he did countenance this unlawful enterprise, whose headquarters were in Rio Medio, he was not the man for me. Though it was big enough to be made, by the papers at home, of political importance, it was, after all, neither more nor less than piracy. The idea of my turning a sort of Irish traitor was so extravagantly outrageous that now I could smile at the imbecility of that fellow O’Brien. As to turning into a sea-thief for lucre﻿—my blood boiled.
No. There was something else there. Something deep; something dangerous; some intrigue, that I could not conceive even the first notion of. But that Carlos wanted anxiously to make use of me for some purpose was clear. I was mystified to the point of forgetting how heavily I was compromised even in Jamaica, though it was worth remembering, because at that time an indictment for rebellion﻿—under the Black Act﻿—was no joking matter. I might be sent home under arrest; and even then, there was my affair with the runners.
“It is coming to pay a visit,” he was saying persuasively, “while your affair here blows over, my Juan﻿—and﻿—and﻿—making my last hours easy, perhaps.”
I looked at him; he was worn to a shadow﻿—a shadow with dark wistful eyes. “I don’t understand you,” I faltered.
The old man stirred, opened his lids, and put a gold vinaigrette to his nostrils.
“Of course I shall not denounce O’Brien,” I said. “I, too, respect the honour of your house.”
“You are even better than I thought you. And if I entreat you, for the love of your mother﻿—of your sister? Juan, it is not for myself, it is﻿—”
The young girl was pouring some drops from a green phial into a silver goblet; she passed close to us, and handed it to her father, who had leant a little forward in his chair. Every movement of hers affected me with an intimate joy; it was as if I had been waiting to see just that carriage of the neck, just that proud glance from the eyes, just that droop of eyelashes upon the cheeks, for years and years.
“No, I shall hold my tongue, and that’s enough,” I said.

===Chinese===

卡洛斯略带倨傲地说：“您不可告发他。倘若我担心您要这样给这颗白头带来耻辱、把这姑娘卷进一桩公开的丑闻，您就不该离开这地方。”他的神气软下来。“为了这个家的体面，您什么也别说。而且您要同我们一起走。我需要您。”

此刻我满腹狐疑。倘若他果真纵容这桩以裡奥梅迪奥为大本营的非法营生，他就不是配我的人。这营生虽然大得够国内的报纸把它做成政治大事，终究不比海盗行径多一分，也少一分。至于我变成某种爱尔兰式叛徒——那念头荒唐透顶，如今我可以笑话奥布赖恩那家伙的低能了。至于为财货当海上窃贼——我的血沸腾了。

不。那底下另有什么东西。某种深的；某种危险的；某种阴谋，我连最初的一点概念都无从想起。可卡洛斯急切地想把我用在什么目的上，这很清楚。我被玄虚弄到几乎忘了我在牙买加也已然陷得多深，虽然这事值得记着，因为那时一纸叛乱的起诉——按黑法令——不是闹着玩的。我可能被押解回国；况且还有我跟缉私吏的那桩事。

“就算来拜访一趟，”他正劝说着，“等您这裡的事端风头过去，我的胡安——而且——而且——或许也让我最后的日子好过些。”

我望着他；他磨损得只剩一道影子——一道带着黑亮渴念的眼睛的影子。“我不明白你，”我讷讷地说。

老人动了动，睁开眼皮，把金香盒凑到鼻端。

“我当然不会告发奥布赖恩，”我说。“我也敬重贵府的体面。”

“你比我想的还要好。倘若我恳求您，看在您母亲的份上——看在您姐姐的份上？胡安，这不是为我自己，这是——”

年轻的姑娘正把绿小瓶裡的几滴药水倒进一只银杯；她贴着我们走过，把杯子递给她微微前俯的父亲。她的每一个动作都叫我涌起一种亲密的欢喜；仿佛我等待了千百年，要看的正是这样一个颈姿，正是眼睛裡这样骄傲的一瞥，正是睫毛这样垂在颊上。

“不，我会封住嘴，这就够了，”我说。

===Original===

At that moment the old Don sat up and cleared his throat. Carlos sprang towards him with an infinite grace of tender obsequiousness. He mentioned my name and the relationship, then rehearsed the innumerable titles of his uncle, ending “and patron of the Bishopric of Pinar del Rio.”
I stood stiffly in front of the old man. He bowed his head at intervals, holding the silver cup carefully whilst his chair rocked a little. When Carlos’ mellow voice had finished the rehearsing of the sonorous styles, I mumbled something about “transcendent honour.”
He stopped me with a little, deferentially peremptory gesture of one hand, and began to speak, smiling with a contraction of the lips and a trembling of the head. His voice was very low, and quavered slightly, but every syllable was enunciated with the same beauty of clearness that there was in his features, in his hands, in his ancient gestures.
“The honour is to me,” he said, “and the pleasure. I behold my kinsman, who, with great heroism, I am told, rescued my dearly loved nephew from great dangers; it is an honour to me to be able to give him thanks. My beloved and lamented sister contracted a union with an English hidalgo, through whose house your own very honourable family is allied to my own; it is a pleasure to me to meet after many years with one who has seen the places where her later life was passed.”
He paused, and breathed with some difficulty, as if the speech had exhausted him. Afterwards he began to ask me questions about Rooksby’s aunt﻿—the lamented sister of his speech. He had loved her greatly, he said. I knew next to nothing about her, and his fine smile and courtly, aged, deferential manners made me very nervous. I felt as if I had been taken to pay a ceremonial visit to a supreme pontiff in his dotage. He spoke about Horton Priory with some animation for a little while, and then faltered, and forgot what he was speaking of. Suddenly he said:
“But where is O’Brien? Did he write to the Governor here? I should like you to know the Señor O’Brien. He is a spiritual man.”
I forbore to say that I had already seen O’Brien, and the old man sank into complete silence. It was beginning to grow dark, and the noise of suppressed voices came from the open trapdoor. Nobody said anything.

===Chinese===

正在这时，老堂坐直身子，清了清喉咙。卡洛斯带着无限的温存恭敬朝他抢步而去。他报了我的名字和亲戚关系，随后背诵起他伯父数不清的头衔，末了是“暨比纳尔德尔裡奥主教区的护法”。

我僵直地站在老人面前。他隔一阵点一次头，小心捧着银杯，椅子微微摇晃。等卡洛斯圆润的嗓音背完那一串堂皇的名号，我嗫嚅了几句“无上的荣光”之类。

他用一只手一个恭敬而专断的小手势止住我，开始说话，嘴唇收缩地微笑着，头微微颤抖。他的声音很低，微微发颤，可每一个音节都吐得同样清亮美好，正如他的五官、他的双手、他古雅的举止裡所有的那种清亮。

“荣光属于我，”他说，“欢喜也是。我见到了我的亲戚，据我所知，他以大勇救了我至爱的侄儿出大险；能向他道谢，是我的荣幸。我挚爱的、先逝的妹妹与一位英国绅士结了缡，经由他的门第，您可敬的家族与我家结了姻谊；多年之后得遇一位见过她晚年所居之地的人，是我的欢喜。”

他停了停，呼吸有些吃力，仿佛这番话耗尽了他。随后他开始问起鲁克斯比（Rooksby）的伯母——他话裡那位先逝的妹妹。他曾经非常爱她，他说。我对她几乎一无所知，而他优雅的微笑和宫廷式的、年迈的、谦和的神气叫我非常紧张。我觉得自己像被领去对一位老耄的最高祭司做礼节性拜访。他一度颇为生动地谈了几句霍顿修道院宅，随即讷讷地停住，忘了自己在说什么。忽然他说：

“可是奥布赖恩在哪裡？他给这儿的总督写信了吗？我要您认识认识奥布赖恩先生。他是个属灵的人。”

我忍住没说我已经见过奥布赖恩，老人陷入了全然的沉默。天开始黑了，敞开的活板口下传来压低的人声。谁也没有说话。

===Original===

I felt a sort of uneasiness; I could by no means understand the connection between the old Don and what had gone before, and I did not, in a purely conventional sense, know how long I ought to stop. The sky through the barred windows had grown pallid.
The old Don said suddenly, “You must visit my poor town of Rio Medio,” but he gave no specific invitation and said nothing more.
Afterwards he asked, rather querulously, “But where is O’Brien? He must write those letters for me.”
The young girl said, “He has preceded us to the ship; he will write there.”
She had gone back to her seat. Don Balthasar shrugged his shoulders to his ears, and moved his hands from his knees.
“Without doubt, he knows best,” he said, “but he should ask me.”
It grew darker still; the old Don seemed to have fallen asleep again. Save for the gleam of the silver buckle of his hat, he had disappeared into the gloom of the place. I remembered my engagement to dine with Williams on board the *Lion*, and I rose to my feet. There did not seem to be any chance of my talking to the young girl. She was once more leaning nonchalantly over the lizard, and her hair drooped right across her face like clusters of grapes. There was a gleam on a little piece of white forehead, and all around and about her there were shadows deepening. Carlos came concernedly towards me as I looked at the door.
“But you must not go yet,” he said a little suavely; “I have many things to say. Tell me﻿—”
His manner heightened my uneasiness to a fear. The expression of his eyes changed, and they became fixed over my shoulder, while on his lips the words “You must come, you must come,” trembled, hardly audible. I could only shake my head. At once he stepped back as if resigning. He was giving me up﻿—and it occurred to me that if the danger of his seduction was over, there remained the danger of arrest just outside the door.
Someone behind me said peremptorily, “It is time,” and there was a flickering diminution of the light. I had a faint instantaneous view of the old Don dozing, with his head back﻿—of the tall windows, cut up into squares by the black bars. Something hairily coarse ran harshly down my face; I grew blind; my mouth, my eyes, my nostrils were filled with dust; my breath shut in upon me became a flood of warm air. I had no time to resist.

===Chinese===

我感到一种不安；我全然无法理解老堂同方才那一切之间的关联，而且照纯粹的惯例，我不知道自己该待多久。铁栏窗外，天色已经灰白了。

老堂忽然说：“您一定要到访我寒陋的裡奥梅迪奥城。”可他没有发出具体的邀请，也没有再多说。

随后他相当聒躁地问：“可是奥布赖恩在哪裡？他得替我写那些信。”

年轻的姑娘说：“他先我们上船了；他会在船上写。”

她已回到座位上。堂·巴尔塔萨朝耳朵耸了耸肩，双手从膝上挪开。

“无疑，他最清楚，”他说，“可他应当问我一声。”

天更黑了；老堂似乎又睡着了。要不是帽子上银扣的微光，他已隐没进那屋子的昏暗裡。我想起同威廉斯约好上狮子号（Lion）吃饭，便站起身来。看样子没有同年轻姑娘说话的机会了。她又漫不经心地俯向蜥蜴，头发直垂过脸颊，像一串串葡萄。那一小块白皙的额头上有微光，她四周上下，暗影渐深。我望着门时，卡洛斯关切地走过来。

“可您还不能走，”他略带婉转地说；“我有许多话要说。告诉我——”

他的神气把我的不安抬高成了恐惧。他眼睛的表情变了，目光越过我的肩膀钉在某处，唇边颤着“您一定要来，您一定要来”，几乎听不见。我只能摇头。他立刻退后一步，像是放弃。他把我放走了——我忽然想到，倘若他诱劝的危险已经过去，门外等着的就是被捕的危险了。

背后有人专断地说：“到时候了。”光亮闪了闪，暗了下去。我瞬息间朦胧地督见打着盹、头向后仰的老堂——督见被黑铁栏切成方格的高窗。一样毛糙粗粝的东西粗暴地从我脸上抹下来；我瞎了；我的嘴、我的眼、我的鼻孔塞满了尘土；我屏住的呼吸变成一股热浪。我来不及反抗。

===Original===

I kicked my legs convulsively; my elbows were drawn tight against my sides. Someone grunted under my weight; then I was carried﻿—down, along, up, down again; my feet were knocking along a wall, and the top of my head rubbed occasionally against what must have been the roof of a low stone passage, issuing from under the back room of Ramon’s store. Finally, I was dropped upon something that felt like a heap of wood-shavings. My surprise, rage, and horror had been so great that, after the first stifled cry, I had made no sound. I heard the footsteps of several men going away.

===Chinese===

我痉挛地踢着双腿；臂肘被紧紧按在体侧。有谁在我身子底下哼了一声；随后我被抬走——向下，向前，向上，又向下；我的脚一路磕着墙，头顶时而蹭着什么，想必是一条低矮石通道的顶，从拉蒙铺子后屋底下通出来。最后，我被撂在一堆摸着像刨花的东西上。我的惊愕、狂怒和恐怖那样剧烈，以致第一声闷喊之后，我再没有出声。我听见几个男人的脚步走远了。

### IV / 四
===Original===

I remained lying there, bound hand and foot, for a long time; for quite long enough to allow me to collect my senses and see that I had been a fool to threaten O’Brien. I had been nobly indignant, and behold! I had a sack thrown over my head for my pains, and was put away safely somewhere or other. It seemed to be a cellar.
I was in search of romance, and here were all the elements; Spaniards, a conspirator, and a kidnapping; but I couldn’t feel a fool and romantic as well. True romance, I suppose, needs a whirl of emotions to extinguish all the senses except that of sight, which it dims. Except for sight, which I hadn’t at all, I had the use of them all, and all reported unpleasant things.
I ached and smarted with my head in a sack, with my mouth full of flour that had gone mouldy and offended my nostrils; I had a sense of ignominy, and I was extremely angry; I could see that the old Don was in his dotage﻿—but Carlos I was bitter against.
I was not really afraid; I could not suppose that the Riegos would allow me to be murdered or seriously maltreated. But I was incensed against Fate or Chance or whatever it is﻿—on account of the ignominious details, the coarse sack, the mouldy flour, the stones of the tunnel that had barked my shins, the tightness of the ropes that bound my ankles together, and seemed to cut into my wrists behind my back.
I waited, and my fury grew in a dead silence. How would it end﻿—with what outrage? I would show my contempt and preserve my dignity by submitting without a struggle﻿—I despised this odious plot. At last there were voices, footsteps; I found it very hard to carry out my resolution and refrain from stifled cries and kicks. I was lifted up and carried, like a corpse, with many stumbles, by men who sometimes growled as they hastened along. From time to time somebody murmured, “Take care.” Then I was deposited into a boat. The world seemed to be swaying, splashing, jarring﻿—and it became obvious to me that I was being taken to some ship. The Spanish ship, of course. Suddenly I broke into cold perspiration at the thought that, after all, their purpose might be to drop me quickly overboard. “Carlos!” I cried. I felt the point of a knife on my breast. “Silence, Señor!” said a gruff voice.

===Chinese===

我手脚被捆，在那裡躺了很久；久得足以叫我定下神来，看清自己威胁奥布赖恩是干了件蠢事。我义愤填膺得高尚，结果呢！脑袋上换了一只麻袋，还被妥妥地藏到了什么所在。看样子是间地窖。

我寻的是罗曼斯，而要素样样齐全：西班牙人、一个阴谋家、一场绑架；可我没法同时觉得自己又蠢又罗曼斯。真正的罗曼斯，我想，需要一场情绪的旋风，熄掉全部感官，只留视觉，还叫它半瞎。除了视觉——我一点没有——我的感官样样都在，而且个个报告不痛快的事。

脑袋套在麻袋裡，我又痛又辣，满嘴发霉的面粉，呛着鼻孔；我有一种受辱之感，又气得不行；我看得出老堂已经老糊涂了——可卡洛斯，我对他怨得深。

我倒不是真怕；我不能设想列戈家会容人谋杀我或认真虐待我。可我怒的是命运，或者机缘，或者随便它叫什么——为那些丢脸的细节：粗麻袋、霉面粉、蹭破我胫骨的地道石棱、捆脚踝的绳子勒得那样紧、背后勒进手腕。

我等着，火气在死寂裡越烧越旺。这将如何收场——以何等暴行？我要以不挣扎的顺从表示我的轻蔑、保住我的体面——我鄙夷这可憎的阴谋。终于有了人声、脚步；我发现要贯彻决心、摃住闷喊和踢蹬，实在艰难。我被抬起来，像一具尸首，磕磕绊绊地，抬的人一路疾走，时时低吼。不时有人咕哝：“小心。”随后我被放进一条小船。世界仿佛在摇晃、泼溅、颠震——我明白了，我正被送上某条船。西班牙船，自然。想到他们终究可能把我迅速丢进海裡，我忽然出了一身冷汗。“卡洛斯！”我喊。我感到刀尖抵上胸口。“安静，先生！”一个粗嗓音说。

===Original===

This fear vanished when we came alongside a ship evidently already under way; but I was handled so roughly and clumsily that I was thoroughly exhausted and out of breath, by the time I was got on board. All was still around me; I was left alone on a settee in the main cabin, as I imagined. For a long time I made no movement; then a door opened and shut. There was a murmured conversation between two voices. This went on in animated whispers for a time. At last I felt as if someone were trying, rather ineffectually, to remove the sack itself. Finally, that actually did rub its way over my head, and something soft and silken began to wipe my eyes with a surprising care, and even tenderness. “This was stupidly done,” came a discontented remark; “you do not handle a caballero like this.”
“And how else was it to be done, to that kind of caballero?” was the curt retort.
By that time I had blinked my eyes into a condition for remaining open for minute stretches. Two men were bending over me﻿—Carlos and O’Brien himself. The latter said:
“Believe me, your mistake made this necessary. This young gentleman was about to become singularly inconvenient, and he is in no way harmed.”
He spoke in a velvety voice, and walked away gently through the darkness. Carlos followed with the lantern dangling at arm’s length; strangely enough he had not even looked at me. I suppose he was ashamed, and I was too proud to speak to him, with my hands and feet tied fast. The door closed, and I remained sitting in the darkness. Long small windows grew into light at one end of the place, curved into an outline that suggested a deep recess. The figure of a crowned woman, that moved rigidly up and down, was silhouetted over my body. Groaning creaks of wood and the faint swish of water made themselves heard continuously.
I turned my head to a click, I saw a door open a little way, and the small blue flame of a taper floated into the room. Then the door closed with a definite sound of shutting in. The light shone redly through protecting fingers, and upwards on to a small face. It came to a halt, and I made out the figure of a girl leaning across a table and looking upwards. There was a click of glass, and then a great blaze of light created a host of shining things; a glitter of gilded carvings, red velvet couches, a shining table, a low ceiling, painted white, on carved rafters.

===Chinese===

等我们靠上一条显然已经启航的船，这恐惧才消散；可我被摆弄得那样粗暴笨拙，上得船来，我已筋疲力尽，气喘吁吁。四周一片寂静；我被独自撂在——我想是——主舱的一张沙发上。很久我没有动；随后一扇门开了又关。两个声音在低语交谈。这样活跃地窃窃私语了一阵。最后我觉得有人试着摘掉麻袋，摘得相当笨拙。终于它当真从我头上蹭了过去，一样柔软丝滑的东西开始擦我的眼睛，带着惊人的细致，甚至是温柔。“这事办得蠢透了，”一句不满的话传来；“对一位绅士不能这样摆弄。”

“对那种绅士，还能怎样办？”是生硬的反唇相讥。

到那时我已把眼睛眨到能睁开片刻的地步。两个人俯身在我上方——卡洛斯和奥布赖恩本人。后者说：

“请相信我，是您的错才不得已出此下策。这位年轻先生眼看要变得格外碍事，而他毫发无伤。”

他用天鹅绒般的嗓音说着，轻轻穿过黑暗走开。卡洛斯跟在后面，灯笼垂在伸直的臂端；说来奇怪，他连看都没看我一眼。我想他是慚愧，而我也骄傲得不肯同他说话，手脚还被死死捆着。门关上了，我留在黑暗裡坐着。狭长的窗在一端渐渐亮起来，弯出一道轮廓，像深深的凹龛。一个戴冠女人的身影，僵直地上下移动，投影在我身上。木头的呻吟声和水微弱的拍溅声连绵入耳。

我朝一声咔哒转过头，看见一扇门开了条缝，一小朵蓝色的烛火飘进屋来。随后门关上，一声明确的关禁之声。烛光从护着的手指间红红地透出，向上照亮一张小小的脸。它停住了，我辨认出一个姑娘的身影，俯在一张桌子上向上张望。玻璃一响，随即一大片光亮造出一屋子灿然的东西：镀金雕饰的闪光，红丝绒的卧榻，一张亮堂的桌子，低低的天花板，漆成白色，架在雕花的梁上。

===Original===

A large silver lamp she had lighted kept on swinging to the gentle motion of the ship.
She stood just in front of me; the girl that I had seen through the door; the girl I had seen play with the melon seeds. She was breathing fast﻿—it agitated me to be alone with her﻿—and she had a little shining dagger in her hand.
She cut the rope round my ankles, and motioned me imperiously to turn round. “Your hands﻿—your hands!”
I turned my back awkwardly to her, and felt the grip of small, cool, very firm fingers upon my wrists. My arms fell apart, numb and perfectly useless; I was half aware of pain in them, but it passed unnoticed among a cloud of other emotions. I didn’t feel my fingertips because I had the agitation, the flutter, the tantalization of looking at her.
I was all the while conscious of the﻿—say, the irregularity of my position, but I felt very little fear. There were the old Don, an ineffectual, silver-haired old gentleman, who obviously was not a pirate; the sleek O’Brien, and Carlos, who seemed to cough on the edge of a grave﻿—and this young girl. There was not any future that I could conceive, and the past seemed to be cut off from me by a narrow, very dark tunnel through which I could see nothing at all.
The young girl was, for the moment, what counted most on the whole, the only thing the eye could rest on. She affected me as an apparition familiar, yet absolutely new in her charm. I had seen her gray eyes; I had seen her red lips; her dark hair, her lithe gestures; the carriage of her head; her throat, her hands. I knew her; I seemed to have known her for years. A rush of strange, sweet feeling made me dumb. She was looking at me, her lips set, her eyes wide and still; and suddenly she said:
“Ask nothing. The land is not far yet. You can escape, Carlos thought.﻿ ﻿… But no! You would only perish for nothing. Go with God.” She pointed imperiously towards the square stern-ports of the cabin.
Following the direction of her hand, my eyes fell upon the image of a Madonna; rather large﻿—perhaps a third life-size; with a gilt crown, a pink serious face bent a little forward over a pink naked child that perched on her left arm and raised one hand. It stood on a bracket, against the rudder casing, with fat cherubs’ heads carved on the supports. The young girl crossed herself with a swift motion of the hand.

===Chinese===

她点亮的那盏大银灯，随着船的轻轻摇动一直晃着。

她就站在我面前；那扇门后见过的姑娘；那摆弄瓜子的姑娘。她呼吸急促——同她独处叫我心旌摇荡——她手裡握着一把亮闪闪的小匕首。

她割断我脚踝上的绳，专断地示意我转身。“你的手——你的手！”

我笨拙地把背转向她，感到小而凉、非常有力的手指扣住了我的手腕。我的两条胳膊散开，麻木得全无用处；我也半觉出胳膊裡的痛，可它淹没在别的一片情绪裡，无从理会。我感觉不到指尖，因为我正受着看她一眼的激动、颤栗、煎熬。

我始终意识到我的处境的——就算它离奇吧——不合规矩，可我几乎没有恐惧。想想都有谁：老堂，一个全然无用的银发老绅士，明摆着不是海盗；油光的奥布赖恩；卡洛斯，像是站在坟墓边沿上咳嗽——还有这位年轻姑娘。我想象不出任何未来，而过去仿佛被一条狭窄的、极暗的地道从我身上截断，裡面什么也望不见。

这位年轻姑娘，眼下是全局中最要紧的，是眼睛唯一能停驻的东西。她给我的感受像一道熟悉的幻影，可她的魅力又是全新的。我见过她的灰眼睛；见过她的红唇；她的黑发，她轻盈的举止；她头颈的姿势；她的喉咙，她的手。我认识她；我仿佛已认识她多年。一阵奇异而甜蜜的情感涌来，叫我哑了。她望着我，唇抿着，眼睛睁大而安静；忽然她说：

“什么也别问。陆地还不远。你逃得掉，卡洛斯想。……可是不！你只会白白送死。愿上帝与你同行。”她专断地指向舱室方形的海天窗。

顺着她的手，我的目光落在一尊圣母像上；相当大——约莫真人的三分之一；金冠，粉红的严肃的脸微微前俯，罩着伏在她左臂上的粉红裸体圣婴，婴孩举着一只手。它供在舵机罩旁的壁架上，托架上雕着胖乎乎的小天使头。年轻姑娘手一挥，飞快画了个十字。

===Original===

The stern-ports, glazed in small panes, were black, and gleaming in a white framework.
“Go﻿—go﻿—go with God,” the girl whispered urgently. “There is a boat﻿—”
I made a motion to rise; I wanted to go. The idea of having my liberty, of its being again a possibility, made her seem of less importance; other things began to have their share. But I could not stand, though the blood was returning, warm and tingling, in my legs and hands. She looked at me with a sharp frown puckering her brows a little; beat a hasty tattoo with one of her feet, and cast a startled glance towards the forward door that led on deck. Then she walked to the other side of the table, and sat looking at me in the glow of the lamp.
“Your life hangs on a thread,” she murmured.
I answered, “You have given it to me. Shall I never﻿—?” I was acutely conscious of the imperfection of my language.
She looked at me sharply; then lowered her lids. Afterwards she raised them again. “Think of yourself. Every moment is﻿—”
“I will be as quick as I can,” I said.
I was chafing my ankles and looking up at her. I wanted, very badly, to thank her for taking an interest in me, only I found it very difficult to speak to her. Suddenly she sprang to her feet:
“That man thinks he can destroy you. I hate him﻿—I detest him! You have seen how he treats my father.”
It struck me, like a blow, that she was merely avenging O’Brien’s insolence to her father. I had been kidnapped against Don Balthasar Riego’s will. It gave me very well the measure of the old man’s powerlessness in face of his intendant﻿—who was obviously confident of afterwards soothing the resentment.
I was glad I had not thanked her for taking an interest in me. I was distressed, too, because once more I had missed Romance by an inch.
Someone kicked at the locked door. A voice cried﻿—I could not help thinking﻿—warningly, “Seraphina, Seraphina,” and another voice said with excessive softness, “*Señorita!* *Voyons! quelle folie.*”
She sprang at me. Her hand hurt my wrist as she dragged me aft. I scrambled clumsily into the recess of the counter, and put my head out. The night air was very chilly and full of brine; a little boat towing by a long painter was sheering about in the phosphorescent wake of the ship. The sea itself was pallid in the light of the moon, invisible to me.

===Chinese===

海天窗嵌着小格玻璃，黑沉沉的，在白色的窗框裡闪着光。

“走——走——愿上帝与你同行，”姑娘急切地低语。“有一条小船——”

我做了个起身的动作；我想走。重新获得自由、自由重新成为可能，这念头使她显得不那么重要了；别的东西开始各占其份。可我站不起来，尽管血正带着暖意和麻刺涌回我的腿和手。她望着我，眉头微微蹙起一道凌厉的皱纹；一只脚急促地嗒嗒点地，朝通甲板的前门惊惶地督了一眼。随后她走到桌子另一边，坐下，在灯光裡望着我。

“你的命悬在一根线上，”她喃喃说。

我答：“是您把它交还给我的。难道我永远不能——？”我痛感到自己语言的不完备。

她锐利地看我一眼；随后垂下眼帘。之后又抬起来。“想想你自己。每一刻都是——”

“我尽量快，”我说。

我搓着脚踝，抬眼望她。我非常想谢谢她对我的关切，只是发觉同她说话非常艰难。她忽然跳起来：

“那人以为他能毁掉你。我恨他——我憎恶他！你见了他怎样对待我父亲。”

像一个打击，我猛然想到：她不过是在报奥布赖恩对她父亲无礼之仇。我是在违背堂·巴尔塔萨·列戈（Don Balthasar Riego）意愿的情况下被绑架的。这再好不过地量出了老人在他那位总管面前的无能为力——那总管显然笃定事后能安抚这怨懤。

我庆幸自己没有谢她对我的关切。我也难过，因为我又差一寸错过了罗曼斯。

有人踢那扇锁着的门。一个声音喊着——我不由想——是警告：“塞拉菲娜，塞拉菲娜，”另一个声音过分柔和地说：“小姐！得了（*Voyons! quelle folie*）！多荒唐。”

她扑向我。她拽我向船尾时，手捏痛了我的手腕。我笨拙地爬上船尾凹龛，探出头去。夜风冷冽，饱含咸腥；一条用长缆拖着的小船，在船身磷光的尾流裡左右摆荡。月亮照着苍白的海，我看不见月亮本身。

===Original===

A little astern of us, on our port quarter, a vessel under a press of canvas seemed to stand still; looming up like an immense pale ghost. She might have been coming up with us, or else we had just passed her﻿—I couldn’t tell. I had no time to find out, and I didn’t care. The great thing was to get hold of the painter. The whispers of the girl urged me, but the thing was not easy; the rope, fastened higher up, streamed away out of reach of my hand. At last, by watching the moment when it slacked, and throwing myself half out of the stern window, I managed to hook it with my fingertips. Next moment it was nearly jerked away from me, but I didn’t lose it, and the boat taking a run just then under the counter, I got a good hold. The sound of another kick at the door made me swing myself out, head first, without reflection. I got soused to the waist before I had reached the bows of the boat. With a frantic effort I clambered up and rolled in. When I got on my legs, the jerky motion of tossing had ceased, the boat was floating still, and the light of the stern windows was far away already. The girl had managed to cut the painter.
The other vessel was heading straight for me, rather high on the water, broad-beamed, squat, and making her way quietly, like a shadow. The land might have been four or five miles away﻿—I had no means of knowing exactly. It looked like a high black cloud, and purple-gray mists here and there among the peaks hung like scarves.
I got an oar over the stern to scull, but I was not fit for much exertion. I stared at the ship I had left. Her stern windows glimmered with a slight up-and-down motion; her sails seemed to fall into black confusion against the blaze of the moon; faint cries came to me out of her, and by the alteration of her shape I understood that she was being brought to, preparatory to lowering a boat. She might have been half a mile distant when the gleam of her stern windows swung slowly round and went out. I had no mind to be recaptured, and began to scull frantically towards the other vessel. By that time she was quite near﻿—near enough for me to hear the lazy sound of the water at her bows, and the occasional flutter of a sail. The land breeze was dying away, and in the wake of the moon I perceived the boat of my pursuers coming over, black and distinct; but the other vessel was nearly upon me.

===Chinese===

在我们后方偏左一点，一条满帆的船仿佛站定不动；像一具巨大的苍白幽灵隐现。它也许正赶上来，也许我们刚超过它——我说不清。我没工夫弄清，也不在乎。要紧的是抓住那条拖缆。姑娘的低声催促着我，可事情不容易：缆绳系在更高处，飘在我够不着的地方。终于，瞅准它松弛的一瞬，半个身子探出海天窗，我用指尖勾住了它。下一刻它险些被拽脱，可我没撒手，恰好小船一荡荡到船尾底下，我一把抓牢。又一声踢门传来，我不假思索头朝前翻出窗去。还没摸到船头，我已半身没进水裡。一阵拼命，我攀上去滚进船裡。等我站起腿来，小船不再颠抛，浮着不动，海天窗的灯光已经远了。姑娘设法割断了拖缆。

那条船正朝我笔直驶来，吃水较高，船幅宽，矮墩墩的，悄悄行进，像一道影子。陆地也许在四五英里外——我无从确切知道。它像一朵高高的黑云，峰间这儿那儿挂着紫灰的雾，像披巾。

我把一支桨从船尾放下去摇，可我使不出大力。我盯着那条离开的船。它的海天窗随着轻微的起伏闪着微光；它的帆在月亮的炽白前仿佛塌成一团黑乱；微弱的喊声从它那裡传来，凭它形状的变化，我明白它正在停船，预备放小艇。当它海天窗的微光缓缓转过去、熄掉时，它离我约有半英裡。我不想被捉回去，开始朝另一条船拼命摇去。到那时它已很近——近得我听得见它船头慵懒的水声，和船帆偶尔的拍动。陆风正在消歇，月光裡我望见追我的人的小船划过来，黑而分明；可那条船几乎已压到我头顶。

===Original===

I sheered under her starboard bow and yelled, “Ship ahoy! Ship ahoy!”
There was a lot of noise on board, and no one seemed to hear my shouts. Several voices yelled. “That cursed Spanish ship ahead is heaving-to athwart our hawse.” The crew and the officers seemed all to be forward shouting abuse at the “lubberly Dago,” and it looked as though I were abandoned to my fate. The ship forged ahead in the light air; I failed in my grab at her fore chains, and my boat slipped astern, bumping against the side. I missed the main chain, too, and yelled all the time with desperation, “For God’s sake! Ship ahoy! For God’s sake throw me a rope, somebody, before it’s too late!”
I was giving up all hope when a heavy coil﻿—of a brace, I suppose﻿—fell upon my head, nearly knocking me over. Half stunned as I was, desperation lent me strength to scramble up her side hand over hand, while the boat floated away from under my feet. I was done up when I got on the poop. A yell came from forward, “Hard aport.” Then the same voice addressed itself to abusing the Spanish ship very close to us now. “What do you mean by coming-to right across my bows like this?” it yelled in a fury.
I stood still in the shadows on the poop. We were drawing slowly past the stern of the Spaniard, and O’Brien’s voice answered in English:
“We are picking up a boat of ours that’s gone adrift with a man. Have you seen anything of her?” “No﻿—confound you and your boat.” Of course those forward knew nothing of my being on board. The man who had thrown me the rope﻿—a passenger, a certain Major Cowper, going home with his wife and child﻿—had walked away proudly, without deigning as much as to look at me twice, as if to see a man clamber on board a ship ten miles from the land was the most usual occurrence. He was, I found afterwards, an absurd, pompous person, as stiff as a ramrod, and so full of his own importance that he imagined he had almost demeaned himself by his condescension in throwing down the rope in answer to my despairing cries. On the other hand, the helmsman, the only other person aft, was so astounded as to become quite speechless. I could see, in the light of the binnacle thrown upon his face, his staring eyes and his open mouth.

===Chinese===

我转到它右船头下，高喊：“船上的！船上的！”

船上一片喧哗，似乎没人听见我的喊。几条嗓子叫道：“前头那条该死的西班牙船顶在我们的锚链上停船了。”船员和军官似乎全涌到船头，臭骂那“笨手笨脚的西班牙佬”，看来我注定被弃给命运了。船在微风裡前行；我抓它的前链索没抓住，小船滑向船尾，磕着船壳。主链我又没够着，一路绝望地喊：“看在上帝份上！船上的！看在上帝份上扔我一条绳吧，哪位，趁还来得及！”

我正要放弃一切指望，一捆重绳——我想是根操帆索——砸在我头上，险些把我打翻。我半晕着，绝望借给我力气，手换手攀上船侧，小船从脚下漂走了。爬上尾楼时我已瘫了。船头传来一声喊：“左满舵。”随后还是那个嗓音，转而痛骂此刻已离得很近的西班牙船。“你这是什么意思，这样横在我的船头收帆？”它狂怒地喊。

我站在尾楼的阴影裡一动不动。我们正缓缓驶过那条西班牙船的船尾，奥布赖恩的声音用英语答道：

“我们在捞我们的一条小船，连人带船漂走了。你们见过吗？”“没见过——叫你和你的船见鬼去。”当然，船头那些人全然不知我在船上。扔绳给我的那人——一位乘客，某位考珀少校（Major Cowper），带着妻儿回国——已骄傲地走开了，连第二次看我都不屑，仿佛离岸十英裡看见一个人攀上船，是天下最平常的事。我后来发现，他是个荒唐自负的人物，挺得像根通条，自我满得以为回应我绝望的呼救、扔下那条绳，已经是屈尊得几乎有失身份了。另一面，舵工——船尾仅有的另一个人——惊得说不出话来。罗经灯照着他的脸，我看得见他瞪圆的眼和张开的嘴。

===Original===

The voice forward had subsided by then, and as the stern of the Spanish ship came abreast of the poop, I stepped out of the shadow of the sails, and going close to the rail I said, not very loud﻿—there was no need to shout﻿—but very distinctly:
“I am out of your clutches, Mr. O’Brien, after all. I promise you that you shall hear of me yet.”
Meanwhile, another man had come up from forward on the poop, growling like a bear, a short, rotund little man, the captain of the ship. The Spanish vessel was dropping astern, silent, with her sails all black, hiding the low moon. Suddenly a hurried hail came out of her.
“What ship is this?”
“What’s that to you, blank your eyes? The *Breeze*, if you want to know. What are you going to do about it?” the little skipper shouted fiercely. In the light wind the ships were separating slowly.
“Where are you bound to?” hailed O’Brien’s voice again.
The little skipper laughed with exasperation. “Dash your blanked impudence. To Havana, and be hanged to you. Anything more you want to know? And my name’s Lumsden, and I am sixty years old, and if I had you here, I would put a head on you for getting in my way, you﻿—”
He stopped, out of breath. Then, addressing himself to his passenger:
“That’s the Spanish chartered ship that brought these sanguinary pirates that were hanged this morning, major. She’s taking the Spanish commissioner back. I suppose they had no man-of-war handy for the service in Cuba. Did you ever﻿—”
He had caught sight of me for the first time, and positively jumped a foot high with astonishment.
“Who on earth’s that there?”
His astonishment was comprehensible. The major, without deigning to enlighten him, walked proudly away. He was too dignified a person to explain.
It was left to me. Frequenting, as I had been doing, Ramon’s store, which was a great gossiping centre of the maritime world in Kingston, I knew the faces and the names of most of the merchant captains who used to gather there to drink and swap yarns. I was not myself quite unknown to little Lumsden. I told him all my story, and all the time he kept on scratching his bald head, full of incredulous perplexity. Old Señor Ramon! Such a respectable man. And I had been kidnapped? From his store!
“If I didn’t see you here in my cuddy before my eyes, I wouldn’t believe a word you say,” he declared absurdly.
But he was ready enough to take me to Havana.

===Chinese===

船头的声音那时已低下去，西班牙船的船尾与尾楼并齐时，我从帆影裡跨出，走近栏杆，不太响——无须喊——但极清晰地说：

“我终究逃出你的掌心了，奥布赖恩先生。我向你担保，你还有我的消息。”

这时另一人从船头上了尾楼，像熊一样咆哮，一个矮胖的小个子，本船船长。西班牙船渐渐落在后面，悄然无声，帆全黑了，遮着低低的月亮。忽然它传来一声急促的招呼：

“这是什么船？”

“关你什么事，瞎了你的眼？微风号（*Breeze*），你想知道的话。你待怎样？”小个子船长凶狠地喊。微风裡两条船缓缓分开。

“你们去哪儿？”又是奥布赖恩的声音喊道。

小个子船长气得笑出声。“让你这无礼的混账见鬼去。去哈瓦那（Havana），你自己吊死吧。还想知道什么？我叫拉姆斯登，六十岁，你要在我眼前，我要给你安个脑袋，谁叫你挡我的道，你——”

他停住，气喘。随后转向他的乘客：

“那就是送今早绞死的那伙杀人海盗来的西班牙包船，少校。它送西班牙专员回去。大概是古巴（Cuba）一时抽不出军舰来办这差。你见过——”

他头一回看见了我，惊得实实在在跳起一尺高。

“那到底是谁？”

他的惊愕可以理解。少校不屑于替他解惑，骄傲地走开了。他是太体面的人物，不肯解释。

这就留给了我。由于我常去拉蒙的铺子——金斯敦（Kingston）海事圈的一大闲话中心——来往聚在那儿喝酒吹牛的商船船长，脸孔名字我大多认得。小个子拉姆斯登对我也不算全然陌生。我把事情原原本本告诉了他，他一路直挠他的秃头，满腹狐疑。老拉蒙先生！那样一位体面人。而我竟被绑架了？就从他铺子裡！

“要不是亲眼看见你在我舱裡坐在我眼前，你一个字我也不会信，”他荒唐地宣称。

可他倒是愿意带我到哈瓦那。

===Original===

However, he insisted upon calling down his mate, a gingery fellow, short, too, but wizened, and as stupid as himself.
“Here’s that Kemp, you know. The young fellow that Macdonald of the Horton Pen picked up somewhere two years ago. The Spaniards in that ship kidnapped him﻿—so he says. He says they are pirates. But that’s a government chartered ship, and all the pirates that have ever been in her were hanged this morning in Kingston. But here he is, anyhow. And he says that at home he had throttled a Bow Street runner before he went off with the smugglers. Did you ever hear the likes of it, Mercer? I shouldn’t think he was telling us a parcel of lies; hey, Mercer?”
And the two grotesque little chaps stood nodding their heads at me sagaciously.
“He’s a desperate character, then,” said Mercer at last, cautiously. “This morning, the very last thing I heard ashore, as I went to fetch the fresh beef off, is that he had been assaulting a justice of the peace on the highroad, and had been trying to knock down the admiral, who was coming down to town in a chaise with Mr. Topnambo. There’s a warrant out against him under the Black Act, sir.”
Then he brightened up considerably. “So he must have been kidnapped or something after all, sir, or he would be in chokey now.”
It was true, after all. Romance reserved me for another fate, for another sort of captivity, for more than one sort. And my imagination had been captured, enslaved already by the image of that young girl who had called me her English cousin, the girl with the lizard, the girl with the dagger! And with every word she uttered romance itself, if I had only known it, the romance of persecuted lovers, spoke to me through her lips.
That night the Spanish ship had the advantage of us in a freshening wind, and overtook the *Breeze*. Before morning dawned she passed us, and before the close of the next day she was gone out of sight ahead, steering, apparently, the same course with ourselves.
Her superior sailing had an enormous influence upon my fortunes; and I was more adrift in the world than ever before, more in the dark as to what awaited me than when I was lugged along with my head in a sack. I gave her but little thought. A sort of numbness had come over me.

===Chinese===

不过他坚持要把大副叫下来，一个姜黄色头发的家伙，也矮，可是干瘪，跟他一样蠢。

“这就是那个肯普，你知道。两年前霍顿垦殖园的麦克唐纳不知从哪儿捡来的小伙子。那条船上的西班牙人绑架了他——他自己说的。他说他们是海盗。可那是条政府包船，上头有过的海盗今早全在金斯敦绞死了。可他到底是上来了。他还说他在国内跟走私贩子跑之前掐死过一个弓街缉私吏。你听过这样的怪事吗，默瑟（Mercer）？我看他不至于给我们编一包谎；嗯，默瑟？”

两个古怪的小个子站在那儿，睿智地朝我点头。

“那他是个亡命角色了，”默瑟末了谨慎地说。“今早上岸取鲜肉时我听到的最后一件事，就是他在大路上殴打了一位治安官，还想撂倒上将——上将正同托普南博先生坐马车进城。有一张按黑法令发的拘票在通缉他，船长。”

随后他豁然开朗。“这么说，他到底还是被绑架了还是怎么的，船长，不然这会儿他早蹲班房了。”

到底还是真的。罗曼斯把我留给了另一种命运，另一种囚禁，不止一种。而我的想象力已被捕获、已被奴役，被那称我为英国表兄的年轻姑娘的形象，携蜥蜴的姑娘，持匕首的姑娘！而她吐出的每一个字，倘若我当时懂得，罗曼斯本身——受迫害的恋人们的罗曼斯——正通过她的唇对我说话。

当夜，风渐紧，西班牙船占了我们的上风，赶过了微风号。天亮之前它越过我们，第二天日暮之前，它已在前方望不见了，走的显然同我们一条航路。

它那更胜一筹的帆力对我的命运影响巨大；我比以往任何时候都更漂泊无定，比脑袋套在麻袋裡被拖走时更不知等着我的究竟是什么。我几乎不去想它。一种麻木罩住了我。

===Original===

I could think of the girl who had cut me free, and for all my resentment at the indignity of my treatment, I had hardly a thought to spare for the man who had me bound. I was pleased to remember that she hated him; that she had said so herself. For the rest, I had a vague notion of going to the English Consul in Havana. After all, I was not a complete nobody. I was John Kemp, a gentleman, well connected; I could prove it. The Bow Street runner had not been dead as I had thought. The last letter from Veronica informed me that the man had given up thief-catching, and was keeping, now, a little inn in the neighbourhood. Ralph, my brother-in-law, had helped him to it, no doubt. I could come home safely now.
And I had discovered I was no longer anxious to return home.

===Chinese===

我想得起的只有那割开我绳索的姑娘，尽管我对所受屈辱满腹怨懤，对那捆我的人，我却几乎匀不出一个念头。想起她恨他，我很高兴；她自己说过的。至于其余，我模模糊糊打算去找哈瓦那的英国领事。说到底，我不是全然的无名之辈。我是约翰·肯普（John Kemp），一位绅士，有体面的关系；我拿得出证明。那个弓街缉私吏并没有死，不像我原先以为的那样。维罗妮卡（Veronica）最近的信告诉我，那人已改行不当捕贼的了，如今在附近开着一家小客栈。我姐夫拉尔夫多半帮了他这个忙。我现在可以安然回家了。

而我发现自己已不再急于回家了。

### V / 五
===Original===

There wasn’t any weirdness about the ship when I woke in the sunlight. She was old and slow and rather small. She carried Lumsden (master), Mercer (mate), a crew that seemed no better and no worse than any other crew, and the old gentleman who had thrown me the rope the night before, and who seemed to think that he had derogated from his dignity in doing it. He was a Major Cowper, retiring from a West Indian regiment, and had with him his wife and a disagreeable little girl, with a yellow pigtail and a bony little chest and arms.
On the whole, they weren’t the sort of people that one would have chosen for companions on a pleasure-trip. Major Cowper’s wife lay all day in a deck chair, alternately drawing to her and repulsing the whining little girl. The major talked to me about the scandals with which the world was filled, and kept a suspicious eye upon his wife. He spent the morning in shaving what part of his face his white whiskers did not cover, the afternoon in enumerating to me the subjects on which he intended to write to the Horse Guards. He had grown entirely amiable, perhaps for the reason that his wife ignored my existence.
Meantime I let the days slip by idly, only wondering how I could manage to remain in Havana and breathe the air of the same island with the girl who had delivered me. Perhaps some day we might meet﻿—who knows? I was not afraid of that Irishman.
It never occurred to me to bother about the course we were taking, till one day we sighted the Cuban coast, and I heard Lumsden and Mercer pronounce the name of Rio Medio. The two ridiculous old chaps talked of Mexican privateers, which seemed to rendezvous off that place. They pointed out to me the headland near the bay. There was no sign of privateer or pirate, as far as the eye could reach. In the course of beating up to windward we closed in with the coast, and then the wind fell.
I remained motionless against the rail for half the night, looking at the land. Not a single light was visible. A wistful, dreamy longing, a quiet longing pervaded me, as though I had been drugged. I dreamed, as young men dream, of a girl’s face. She was sleeping there within this dim vision of land. Perhaps this was as near as I should ever be able to approach her. I felt a sorrow without much suffering. A great stillness reigned around the ship, over the whole earth. At last I went below and fell asleep.

===Chinese===

我在阳光裡醒来时，这条船毫无诡异之处。它又老又慢，也相当小。船上载着拉姆斯登（船长）、默瑟（Mercer，大副）、一伙看上去不好也不坏的水手，还有那位头天夜裡扔绳给我的老绅士——他似乎觉得那样做有失他的尊严。他是考珀少校（Major Cowper），从西印度团退役，带着妻子和一个讨人嫌的小姑娘，黄黄的辫子，瘦骨嶙峋的小胸脯小胳膊。

总的说来，他们不是谁会挑来作逍遥旅行同伴的那路人。考珀少校的妻子整日躺在躺椅上，一会儿把哭哭啼啼的小姑娘拉到身边，一会儿又推开她。少校同我谈论世风日下的种种丑闻，又用猜疑的眼睛盯着自己的妻子。他上午用来刮白色颊须盖不着的那部分脸，下午用来向我数说他打算写信给陆军部的种种题目。他变得完全和蔼了，也许因为他妻子不理睬我的存在。

其间我任凭日子懒懒滑过，只是盘算怎样设法留在哈瓦那（Havana），同那救过我的姑娘呼吸同一座岛的空气。也许哪天我们能相遇——谁知道呢？我不怕那个爱尔兰人。

我从没想过操心我们的航路，直到有一天我们望见了古巴海岸，听见拉姆斯登和默瑟念出裡奥梅迪奥（Rio Medio）的名字。这两个可笑的老家伙谈着墨西哥私掠船，说它们似乎常在那地方外海集结。他们指给我看海湾附近的海岬。目力所及，没有半点私掠船或海盗的影子。迎风抢行的过程中我们渐渐贴近海岸，随后风停了。

后半夜我倚着栏杆一动不动，望着陆地。看不见一盏灯。一种怅惘的、梦一般的渴念，一种安静的渴望浸透了我，仿佛被下了药。我像年轻人那样梦想着一张姑娘的脸。她正睡在这片朦胧陆地的暗影裡。也许我这辈子能靠近她的，就近到这样了。我感到一种没有多少痛楚的哀伤。巨大的寂静笼罩着船的四周，笼罩着整个大地。终于我下舱去睡了。

===Original===

I was awakened by the idea that I had heard an extraordinary row﻿—shouting and stamping. But there was a dead silence, to which I was listening with all my ears. Suddenly there was a little pop, as if someone had spat rather vigorously; then a succession of shouts, then another little pop, and more shouts, and the stamping overhead. A woman began to shriek on the other side of the bulkhead, then another woman somewhere else, then the little girl. I hurried on deck, but it was some minutes before I could make things fit together. I saw Major Cowper on the poop; he was brandishing a little pistol and apostrophizing Lumsden, who was waving ineffectual arms towards the sky; and there was a great deal of shouting, forward and overhead. Cowper rushed at me, and explained that something was an abominable scandal, and that there were women on board. He waved his pistol towards the side; I noticed that the butt was inlaid with mother-of-pearl. Lumsden rushed at him and clawed at his clothes, imploring him not to be rash.
We were so close in with the coast that the surf along the shore gleamed and sparkled in full view.
Someone shouted aloft, “Look out! They are firing again.”
Then only I noticed, a quarter of a mile astern and between the land and us, a little schooner, rather low in the water, curtseying under a cloud of white canvas﻿—a wonderful thing to look at. It was as if I had never seen anything so instinct with life and the joy of it. A snowy streak spattered away from her bows at each plunge. She came at a great speed, and a row of faces looking our way became plain, like a beady decoration above her bulwarks. She swerved a little out of her course, and a sort of mushroom of smoke grew out of her side; there was a little gleam of smouldering light hidden in its heart. The spitting bang followed again, and something skipped along the wave-tops beside us, raising little pillars of spray that drifted away on the wind. The schooner came back on her course, heading straight for us; a shout like groaned applause went up from on board us. Lumsden hid his face in his hands.
I could hear little Mercer shrieking out orders forwards. We were shortening sail. The schooner, luffing a little, ranged abreast. A hail like a metal blare came out of her.
“If you donn’d heef-to we seenk you! We seenk you! By God!”
Major Cowper was using abominable language beside me.

===Chinese===

我被一个念头惊醒：我听见了一场异乎寻常的大闹——喊叫加跺脚。可四下死寂，我竖着耳朵听。忽然噗的一小响，像谁狠狠啐了一口；接着一连串喊叫，又噗一小响，更多的喊叫，头顶的跺脚。一个女人在舱壁那头尖叫起来，随后别处又一个，随后是小姑娘。我急忙上了甲板，可过了好几分钟我才把事情拼拢。我看见考珀少校在尾楼上；他挥着一支小手枪，慷慨陈词地数落拉姆斯登，后者朝天上挥着全然无用的双臂；船头和桅顶一片大喊大叫。考珀冲向我，宣称某事是可憎的丑闻，船上有妇女。他朝舷侧挥枪；我注意到枪柄镶着珠母。拉姆斯登冲向他，抓住他的衣裳，求他别鲁莽。

我们离海岸那么近，沿岸的浪花在眼前明晃晃地闪烁。

桅上有人喊：“小心！他们又开火了。”

这时我才注意到，船尾四分之一英裡处，陆地与我们之间，一条小纵帆船，吃水颇低，在一团白帆下连连屈膝——一件好看得惊人的东西。仿佛我从没见过这样浑身活气、浑身活乐的东西。它每一次俯冲，船头就溅起一道雪白。它以高速扑来，一排朝我们张望的脸渐渐分明，像它舷墙上沿一串珠子似的装饰。它稍稍偏离航向，一丛蘑菇似的烟从它侧面冒出；烟心裡藏着一小点焖着的火光。噗的一声爆响又到，有什么贴着我们船边的浪尖一路跳过去，激起一根根小小的水柱，随风飘散。纵帆船回到航路上，笔直朝我们来；我们船上响起一声像呻吟的喝彩。拉姆斯登把脸埋进手裡。

我听得见小个子默瑟在船头尖着嗓子下令。我们在收帆。纵帆船微微迎风，靠了上来并排。一声金属炸响似的呼喊从它那边传来。

“你们要是不停船，俺们就打沉你们！打沉你们！老天作证！”

考珀少校在我旁边骂着不堪入耳的话。

===Original===

Suddenly he began to call out to someone:
“Go down﻿ ﻿… go down, I say.”
A woman’s face disappeared into the hood of the companion like a rabbit’s tail into its burrow. There was a great volley of cracks from the loose sails, and the ship came to. At the same time the schooner, now on our beam and stripped of her light kites, put in stays and remained on the other tack, with her foresheet to windward.
Major Cowper said it was a scandal. The country was going to the dogs because merchantmen were not compelled by law to carry guns. He spluttered into my ears that there wasn’t so much as a twopenny signal mortar on board, and no more powder than enough to load one of his duelling pistols. He was going to write to the Horse Guards.
A blue-and-white ensign fluttered up to the main gaff of the schooner; a boat dropped into the water. It all went breathlessly﻿—I hadn’t time to think. I saw old Cowper run to the side and aim his pistol overboard; there was an ineffectual click; he made a gesture of disgust, and tossed it on deck. His head hung dejectedly down upon his chest.
Lumsden said, “Thank God, oh, thank God!” and the old man turned on him like a snarling dog.
“You infernal coward,” he said. “Haven’t you got a spark of courage?”
A moment after, our decks were invaded by men, brown and ragged, leaping down from the bulwarks one after the other.
They had come out at break of day (we must have been observed the evening before), a big schooner﻿—full of as ill-favoured, ragged rascals as the most vivid imagination could conceive. Of course, there had been no resistance on our part. We were outsailed, and at the first ferocious hail the halyards had been let go by the run, and all our crew had bolted aloft. A few bronzed bandits posted abreast of each mast kept them there by the menace of bell-mouthed blunderbusses pointed upwards. Lumsden and Mercer had been each tied flat down to a spare spar. They presented an appearance too ridiculous to awaken genuine compassion. Major Cowper was made to sit on a hen-coop, and a bearded pirate, with a red handkerchief tied round his head and a cutlass in his hand, stood guard over him. The major looked angry and crestfallen. The rest of that infamous crew, without losing a moment, rushed into the cuddy to loot the cabins for wearing apparel, jewellery, and money.

===Chinese===

忽然他开始朝什么人喊：

“下去……下去，我说。”

一张女人的脸缩进升降口的罩子裡，像兔子尾巴缩回洞去。松帆噼裡啪啦响成一片，船停了下来。同时，那条已到我们正横、卸了轻帆的纵帆船，转舵换舷，停在了另一舷上，前帆迎风。

考珀少校说这是丑闻。国家要完蛋了，就因为法律不强制商船装炮。他朝我耳朵裡唾沫横飞地说，船上连一门两便士的信号迫击炮都没有，火药也只够装他一支决斗手枪。他要写信给陆军部。

一面蓝白二色的军旗升上纵帆船的主斜桁；一条小船落进水裡。一切都快得叫人喘不过气——我没工夫想。我看见老考珀奔向舷侧，把手枪朝舷外瞄；咔哒一声空响；他做个厌恶的手势，把枪扔在甲板上。他的头垂头丧气地耷拉到胸前。

拉姆斯登说：“感谢上帝，噢，感谢上帝！”老头像条龇牙的狗一样朝他转过身。

“你这该死的胆小鬼，”他说。“你就没有一星半点的勇气吗？”

片刻之后，我们甲板被一群棕色皮肤、衣衫褴褛的人侵占了，一个个从舷墙跳下来。

他们是天破晓时出来的（头天傍晚我们必定被发现了），一条大纵帆船——装满了想象力再活跃也想得出的最面目可憎的褴褛恶棍。当然，我们这边没有抵抗。他们帆比我们快，第一声凶恶的呼喝一起，升降索就被一把放到底，我们全体水手都窜上了桅顶。几个古铜色的强盗分守各桅旁，用朝天指着的喇叭口大铳吓着，不让他们下来。拉姆斯登和默瑟各自被脸朝下捆在一根备用桅木上。他们那样子可笑得叫人发不出真正的怜悯。考珀少校被按坐在一只鸡笼上，一个头缠红手巾、手持弯刀的海盗看守着他。少校看上去又怒又丧气。那伙无耻的贼众，一刻也不耽搁，冲进舱裡洗劫客舱的衣服、首饰和钱。

===Original===

They squabbled amongst themselves, throwing the things on deck into a great heap of booty.
The schooner flying the Mexican flag remained hove to abeam. But in the man in command of the boarding party I recognized Tomas Castro!
He *was* a pirate. My surmises were correct. He looked the part to the life, in a plumed hat, cloaked to the chin, and standing apart in a saturnine dignity.
“Are you going to have us all murdered, Castro?” I asked, with indignation. To my surprise he did not seem to recognize me; indeed, he pretended not to see me at all. I might have been thin air for any sign he gave of being aware of my presence; but, turning his back on me, he addressed himself to the ignobly captive Lumsden, telling him that he, Castro, was the commander of that Mexican schooner, and menacing him with dreadful threats of vengeance for what he called the resistance we had offered to a privateer of the Republic. I suppose he was pleased to qualify with the name of armed resistance the miserable little pop of the major’s pocket pistol. To punish that audacity he announced that no private property would be respected.
“You shall have to give up all the money on board,” he yelled at the wretched man lying there like a sheep ready for slaughter. The other could only gasp and blink. Castro’s ferocity was so remarkable that for a moment it struck me as put on. There was no necessity for it. We were meek and silent enough, only poor Major Cowper muttered:
“My wife and child.﻿ ﻿…”
The ragged brown men were pouring on deck from below; their arms full of bundles. Half a dozen of them started to pull off the main hatch tarpaulin. Up aloft the crew looked down with scared eyes. I began to say excitedly, in my indignation, almost into his very ear:
“I know you, Tomas Castro﻿—I know you﻿—Tomas Castro.”
Even then he seemed not to hear; but at last he looked into my face balefully, as if he wished to convey the plague to me.
“Hold your tongue,” he said very quickly in Spanish. “This is folly!” His little hawk’s beak of a nose nestled in his moustache. He waved his arm and declared forcibly, “I don’t know you. I am Nicola el Demonio, the Mexican.”
Poor old Cowper groaned. The reputation of Nicola el Demonio, if rumours were to be trusted, was a horrible thing for a man with women depending on him.

===Chinese===

他们自己人吵吵嚷嚷，把东西扔上甲板，堆成一大堆赃物。

那条挂着墨西哥旗的纵帆船停在正横处。而指挥登船队的那个人，我认出了——托马斯·卡斯特罗（Tomas Castro）！

他果真是海盗。我的猜测没错。他扮这角色扮得惟妙惟肖：插羽毛的帽子，斗篷裹到下巴，独自站在一边，阴沉而威严。

“你要把我们全杀了吗，卡斯特罗？”我愤慨地问。出乎意料，他似乎不认得我；确实，他干脆装作根本没看见我。就他理会的任何迹象而言，我仿佛是稀薄的空气；他背过我去，对受尽屈辱的阶下囚拉姆斯登训起话来，说他卡斯特罗是那条墨西哥纵帆船的指挥官，并以骇人的报复相威胁，罪名是我们所谓的对共和国私掠船的抵抗。我想，他很乐意把少校那支袖珍手枪可怜的一小响命名为武装抵抗。为惩罚这胆大妄为，他宣布私有财产一概不予尊重。

“你们得交出船上所有的钱，”他朝那个像待宰羔羊般瘫在那裡的可怜人吼道。对方只会喘气和眨眼。卡斯特罗的凶恶那样夸张，一时叫我觉得是装出来的。毫无必要嘛。我们驯顺安静得很，只有可怜的考珀少校喃喃着：

“我的妻子和孩子。……”

褴褛的棕色人众从下面涌上甲板；怀裡抱满了包袱。半打人动手去揭主舱口的帆布。上头桅顶，水手们惊惶地朝下望。我开始激动地说，愤慨得几乎是凑在他耳边：

“我认得你，托马斯·卡斯特罗——我认得你——托马斯·卡斯特罗。”

即便那时他也似乎听不见；可终于他凶狠地直视我的脸，仿佛想把瘟疫传给我。

“闭嘴，”他用西班牙语飞快地说。“这是蠢事！”他那小小的鹰喙鼻藏进髭须裡。他挥挥胳膊，斩钉截铁地宣称：“我不认得你。我是尼古拉·埃尔·德莫尼奥，墨西哥人。”

可怜的老考珀呻吟起来。倘若传闻可信，尼古拉·埃尔·德莫尼奥的名声，对一个有妻小依靠的男人，是件可怕的东西。

===Original===

Five or six of these bandits were standing about Lumsden, the major, and myself, fingering the locks of their guns. Poor old Cowper, breaking away from his guard, was raging up and down the poop; and the big pirate kept him off the companion truculently. The major wanted to get below; the little girl was screaming in the cuddy, and we could hear her very plainly. It was rather horrible. Castro had gone forward into the crowd of scoundrels round the hatchway. It was only then that I realized that Major Cowper was in a state of delirious apprehension and fury; I seemed to remember at last that for a long time he had been groaning somewhere near me. He kept on saying:
“Oh, for God’s sake﻿—for God’s sake﻿—my poor wife.”
I understood that he must have been asking me to do something.
It came as a shock to me. I had a vague sensation of his fears. Up till then I hadn’t realized that anyone could be much interested in Mrs. Cowper.
He caught hold of my arm, as if he wanted support, and stuttered:
“Couldn’t you﻿—couldn’t you speak to﻿—” He nodded in the direction of Tomas Castro, who was bent and shouting down the hatch. “Try to﻿—” the old man gasped. “Didn’t you hear the child scream?” His face was pallid and wrinkled, like a piece of crumpled paper; his mouth was drawn on one side, and his lips quivered one against the other.
I went to Castro and caught him by the arm. He spun round and smiled discreetly.
“We shall be using force upon you directly. Pray resist, Señor; but not too much. What? His wife? Tell that stupid *Inglez* with whispers that she is safe.” He whispered with an air of profound intelligence, “We shall be ready to go as soon as these foul swine have finished their stealing. I cannot stop them,” he added.
I could not pause to think what he might mean. The child’s shrieks resounding louder and louder, I ran below. There were a couple of men in the cabin with the women. Mrs. Cowper was lying back upon a sofa, her face very white and drawn, her eyes wide open. Her useless hands twitched at her dress; otherwise she was absolutely motionless, like a frozen woman. The black nurse was panting convulsively in a corner﻿—a palpitating bundle of orange and purple and white clothes. The child was rushing round and round, shrieking. The two men did nothing at all. One of them kept saying in Spanish:
“But﻿—we only want your rings. But﻿—we only want your rings.”

===Chinese===

五六个强盗围在拉姆斯登、少校和我四周，手指拨弄着枪机。可怜的老考珀挣脱看守，在尾楼上暴怒地走来走去；那高大的海盗凶横地拦着他不许靠近升降口。少校要下舱去；小姑娘在舱裡尖叫，我们听得分明。相当骇人。卡斯特罗已到船头，扎进舱口边那群恶棍当中。直到那时我才明白，考珀少校正处于谵妄般的惊惧与狂怒之中；我仿佛终于记起，好久以来他一直在近旁某处呻吟。他不停地说：

“噢，看在上帝份上——看在上帝份上——我可怜的妻子。”

我明白了，他必定一直在求我做什么。

这对我像一记震击。我模模糊糊感到了他的恐惧。直到那时我还不明白，世上竟有人会这样牵挂考珀太太。

他抓住我的胳膊，像要人搀扶，结结巴巴地说：

“你能不能——你能不能同——说一说——”他朝托马斯·卡斯特罗的方向点头，那人正弯着腰朝舱口下喊。“想办法——”老头喘着气。“你没听见孩子尖叫吗？”他的脸苍白起皱，像一张揉皱的纸；嘴歪向一边，两片嘴唇彼此打着颤。

我走到卡斯特罗跟前，抓住他的胳膊。他霍地转身，谨慎地一笑。

“我们马上就要对你们动粗了。请您务必抵抗，先生；但别太用力。什么？他的妻子？小声告诉那个蠢英国人（*Inglez*），说她平安无事。”他带着高深莫测的神气耳语，“等这些臭猪偷完了，我们就走。我拦不住他们，”他补充道。

我无暇琢磨他这话什么意思。孩子的尖叫越响越厉，我奔下舱去。舱裡有两个男人同女人们在一起。考珀太太仰躺在沙发上，脸煞白抽紧，眼睛睁得老大。她那双无用的手抽搐着扯自己的衣裳；除此之外一动不动，像冻住了的女人。黑保姆在一个角落裡抽搐地喘气——一包颤动的橙、紫、白。孩子绕着圈狂奔，尖声叫。那两个男人什么也不干。一个不停地用西班牙语说：

“可是——我们只要你们的戒指。可是——我们只要你们的戒指。”

===Original===

The other made feeble efforts to catch the child as it rushed past him. He wanted its earrings﻿—they were contraband of war, I suppose.
Mrs. Cowper was petrified with terror. Explaining the desires of the two men was like shouting things into the ear of a very deaf woman. She kept on saying:
“Will they go away then? Will they go away then?” All the while she was drawing the rings off her thin fingers, and handing them to me. I gave them to the ruffians whose presence seemed to terrify her out of her senses. I had no option. I could do nothing else. Then I asked her whether she wished me to remain with her and the child. She said:
“Yes. No. Go away. Yes. No﻿—let me think.”
Finally it came into my head that in the captain’s cabin she would be able to talk to her husband through the deck ventilator, and, after a time, the idea filtered through to her brain. She could hardly walk at all. The child and the nurse ran in front of us, and, practically, I carried her there in my arms. Once in the stateroom she struggled loose from me, and, rushing in, slammed the door violently in my face. She seemed to hate me.

===Chinese===

另一个作着微弱的努力，想抓住跑过身边的孩子。他要她的耳环——那想必是战争的违禁品。

考珀太太吓僵了。向她解释那两个人的愿望，就像朝一个极聋的女人耳朵裡喊话。她不停地说：

“那他们会走吗？那他们会走吗？”一面说，一面把戒指从瘦手指上褪下来，递给我。我把它们交给那两个恶棍，他们的在场似乎把她吓得魂不附体。我没有别的办法。我什么都做不了。随后我问她，要不要我和孩子留下来陪她。她说：

“要。不要。走开。要。不——让我想想。”

最后我想到，在船长舱裡，她可以通过甲板通风筒同丈夫说话，过了一阵，这念头才渗进她的脑子。她几乎全然走不动路。孩子和保姆跑在前头，实际上，是我把她抱过去的。一进特等舱她就挣脱我，冲进去，砰地朝我脸上把门狠狠摔上。她似乎恨我。

### VI / 六
===Original===

I went on deck again. On the poop about twenty men had surrounded Major Cowper; his white head was being jerked backwards and forwards above their bending backs; they had got his old uniform coat off, and were fighting for the buttons. I had just time to shout to him, “Your wife’s down there, she’s all right!” when very suddenly I became aware that Tomas Castro was swearing horribly at these thieves. He drove them away, and we were left quite alone on the poop, I holding the major’s coat over my arm. Major Cowper stooped down to call through the skylight. I could hear faint answers coming up to him.
Meantime, some of the rascals left on board the schooner had filled on her in a light wind, and, sailing round our stern, had brought their vessel alongside. Ropes were thrown on board and we lay close together, but the schooner with her dirty decks looked to me, now, very sinister and very sordid.
Then I remembered Castro’s extraordinary words; they suggested infinite possibilities of a disastrous nature, I could not tell just what. The explanation seemed to be struggling to bring itself to light, like a name that one has had for hours on the tip of a tongue without being able to formulate it. Major Cowper rose stiffly, and limped to my side. He looked at me askance, then shifted his eyes away. Afterwards, he took his coat from my arm. I tried to help him, but he refused my aid, and jerked himself painfully into it. It was too tight for him. Suddenly, he said:
“You seem to be deuced intimate with that man﻿—deuced intimate.”
His tone caused me more misgiving than I should have thought possible. He took a turn on the deserted deck; went to the skylight; called down, “All well, still?” waited, listening with his head on one side, and then came back to me.
“You drop into the ship,” he said, “out of the clouds. Out of the clouds, I say. You tell us some sort of cock-and-bull story. I say it looks deuced suspicious.” He took another turn and came back. “My wife says that you took her rings and﻿—and﻿—gave them to﻿—”
He had an ashamed air. It came into my head that that hateful woman had been egging him on to this through the skylight, instead of saying her prayers.
“Your wife!” I said. “Why, she might have been murdered﻿—if I hadn’t made her give them up. I believe I saved her life.”
He said suddenly, “Tut, tut!” and shrugged his shoulders.

===Chinese===

我又上了甲板。尾楼上约莫二十个人围住了考珀少校（Major Cowper）；他白发的头在他们俯下的脊背之间被扯得前仰后合；他们剥了他的旧军官外套，正为纽扣打作一团。我刚来得及朝他喊一句“你妻子在那下面，她平安无事！”就非常突然地发觉，托马斯·卡斯特罗（Tomas Castro）正朝这些窃贼破口大骂。他把他们赶开了，尾楼上只剩我们两个，我臂上搭着少校的外套。考珀少校俯下身，隔着天窗朝下喊。我听得见微弱的应答升上来。

其间，留在纵帆船上的几个无赖乘着微风掉转了船头，绕过我们的船尾，把他们的船靠了上来。缆绳抛上船来，我们紧靠在一起，可那条甲板肮脏的纵帆船，此刻在我看来，非常阴险、非常龌龊。

这时我想起卡斯特罗那些离奇的话；它们暗示着无限种灾难性的可能，我说不清究竟是什么。解释仿佛正挣扎着要见天日，像一个名字在舌尖上挂了几个钟头却吐不出来。考珀少校僵硬地起身，一瘸一拐走到我身边。他斜眼看我，随即又把目光挪开。随后，他从我臂上取过外套。我想帮他，可他拒绝了，忍着疼自己一挣一挣地穿上。那外套他穿着太紧了。忽然他说：

“你同那人好像熟得邪门——熟得邪门。”

他的腔调引起的不安，超出我原先以为可能的程度。他在空荡荡的甲板上踱了一圈；走到天窗边；朝下喊：“还好吧，还好吗？”侧着头等了等，听了听，然后回到我这裡。

“你从天上掉进这条船，”他说，“从天上掉下来的，我说。你给我们讲了个荒诞不经的故事。我说，这看上去邪门得很。”他又踱一圈，回来。“我妻子说你拿走了她的戒指，还——还——交给了——”

他一副羞惭的神气。我忽然想到，那个可恨的女人方才一直在隔着天窗撺掇他，而不是祷告。

“你的妻子！”我说。“嘻，要是我不逼她交出来，她没准已经被杀了。我相信我救了她的命。”

他忽然“啧、啧”两声，耸了耸肩。

===Original===

He hung his head for a minute, then he added, “Mind, I don’t say﻿—I don’t say that it mayn’t be as you say. You’re a very nice young fellow.﻿ ﻿… But what I say is﻿—I am a public man﻿—you ought to clear yourself.” He was beginning to recover his military bearing.
“Oh! don’t be absurd,” I said.
One of the Spaniards came up to me and whispered, “You must come now. We are going to cast off.” At the same time Tomas Castro prowled to the other side of the ship, within five yards of us. I called out, “Tomas Castro! Tomas Castro! I will not go with you.” The man beside me said, “Come, señor! *Vamos!*”
Suddenly Castro, stretching his arm out at me, cried, “Come, hombres. This is the caballero; seize him.” And to me in his broken English he shouted, “You may resist, if you like.”
This was what I meant to do with all my might. The ragged crowd surrounded me; they chattered like monkeys. One man irritated me beyond conception. He looked like an innkeeper in knee-breeches, had a broken nose that pointed to the left, and a double chin. More of them came running up every minute. I made a sort of blind rush at the fellow with the broken nose; my elbow caught him on the soft folds of flesh and he skipped backwards; the rest scattered in all directions, and then stood at a distance, chattering and waving their hands. And beyond them I saw old Cowper gesticulating approval. The man with the double chin drew a knife from his sleeve, crouched instantly, and sprang at me. I hadn’t fought anybody since I had been at school; raising my fists was like trying a dubious experiment in an emergency. I caught him rather hard on the end of his broken nose; I felt the contact on my right, and a small pain in my left hand. His arms went up to the sky; his face, too. But I had started forward to meet him, and half a dozen of them flung their arms round me from behind.
I seemed to have an exaggerated clearness of vision; I saw each brown dirty paw reach out to clutch some part of me. I was not angry any more; it wasn’t any good being angry, but I made a fight for it. There were dozens of them; they clutched my wrists, my elbows, and in between my wrists and my elbows, and my shoulders. One pair of arms was round my neck, another round my waist, and they kept on trying to catch my legs with ropes.

===Chinese===

他垂着头站了一分钟，然后加上一句：“记住，我不是说——不是说事情不见得如你所说。你是个很好的小伙子。……可我要说的是——我是个公众人物——你应当把自己的嫌疑洗清。”他开始恢复他的军人气概了。

“噢！别荒唐了，”我说。

一个西班牙人走上前来对我耳语：“您现在得走了。我们要解缆了。”同时托马斯·卡斯特罗踱到船的另一舷，离我们不到五码。我叫起来：“托马斯·卡斯特罗！托马斯·卡斯特罗！我不跟你们走。”我身边的人说：“来吧，先生！走吧（*Vamos*）！”

忽然卡斯特罗朝我伸直了胳膊，喊道：“来，伙计们。这就是那位绅士；抓住他。”又用他的破英语朝我喊：“你可以抵抗，要是你乐意。”

这正是我打算全力以赴的。褴褛的人群围住我；他们像猴子一样聒噪。有一个人叫我恼火得无以复加。他像个穿及膝短裤的客栈老板，塌鼻梁偏向左边，双层下巴。他们每分钟都有更多跑过来的。我朝那塌鼻子家伙瞎冲了一阵；我的臂肘撞在他肉褶的软处，他蹦了回去；其余人四散逃开，随即又站到远处，摆着手聒噪。在他们的外围，我看见老考珀打着手势叫好。双层下巴那家伙从袖子裡抽出一把刀，随即蹲下，朝我扑来。自从离了学堂我没跟人打过架；举起双拳，像在紧急关头试一个没把握的实验。我相当结实地打中他塌鼻子的末端；我感到右手接触了他，左手一小阵痛。他的双臂朝了天；他的脸也是。可我已迎着他抢步向前，半打人从背后抡臂抱住了我。

我仿佛有一种夸张的目明；我看见每一只肮脏的棕爪伸出来抓我身上的某个部位。我不再愤怒了；愤怒也无用，可我搏了一场。他们有几十个；他们抓住我的手腕、臂肘、手腕和臂肘之间，还有肩膀。一双胳膊箍着我的脖子，另一双箍着我的腰，他们还不时想用绳子套我的腿。

===Original===

We seemed to stagger all over the deck; I expect they got in each other’s way; they would have made a better job of it if they hadn’t been such a multitude. I must then have got a crack on the head, for everything grew dark; the night seemed to fall on us, as we fought.
Afterwards I found myself lying gasping on my back on the deck of the schooner; four or five men were holding me down. Castro was putting a pistol into his belt. He stamped his foot violently, and then went and shouted in Spanish:
“Come you all on board. You have done mischief enough, fools of *Lugareños*. Now we go.”
I saw, as in a dream of stress and violence, some men making ready to cast off the schooner, and then, in a supreme effort, an effort of lusty youth and strength, which I remember to this day, I scattered men like chaff, and stood free.
For the fraction of a second I stood, ready to fall myself, and looking at prostrate men. It was a flash of vision, and then I made a bolt for the rail. I clambered furiously; I saw the deck of the old barque; I had just one exulting sight of it, and then Major Cowper uprose before my eyes and knocked me back on board the schooner, tumbling after me himself.
Twenty men flung themselves upon my body. I made no movement. The end had come. I hadn’t the strength to shake off a fly, my heart was bursting my ribs. I lay on my back and managed to say, “Give me air.” I thought I should die.
Castro, draped in his cloak, stood over me, but Major Cowper fell on his knees near my head, almost sobbing: “My papers! My papers! I tell you I shall starve. Make them give me back my papers. They ain’t any use to them﻿—my pension﻿—mortgages﻿—not worth a penny piece to you.”
He crouched over my face, and the Spaniards stood around, wondering. He begged me to intercede, to save him those papers of the greatest importance.
Castro preserved his attitude of a conspirator. I was touched by the major’s distress, and at last I condescended to address Castro on his behalf, though it cost me an effort, for I was angry, indignant, and humiliated.
“Whart﻿—whart? What do I know of his papers? Let him find them.” He waved his hand loftily.
The deck was hillocked with heaps of clothing, of bedding, casks of rum, old hats, and tarpaulins. Cowper ran in and out among the plunder, like a pointer in a turnip field. He was groaning.

===Chinese===

我们仿佛在整个甲板上踉跄；我想是他们自己人碍了自己人的事；要是没有这么一大群，他们本会干得更利落。那时我必定是头上挨了一下，因为眼前全黑了；我们厮打时，夜幕仿佛整个压了下来。

之后我发现自己仰面躺在纵帆船甲板上喘气；四五个人按着我。卡斯特罗正往腰带上插一支手枪。他狠狠跺了跺脚，然后走开，用西班牙语喊：

“你们全都上船来。你们闯的祸够了，乡下蠢货（*Lugareños*）。现在我们走。”

我像在一场暴烈的梦裡，看见一些人准备解开纵帆船的缆；随后，凭着一次超凡的发力——一次青春血气的发力，我至今记得——我把人像糠秕一样抖散，站直了。

有一瞬的刹那我站着，自己也几乎倒下，望着四仰八叉的人们。那是目力的一闪，随即我朝栏杆狂奔。我拼命攀爬；我看见那条老船的甲板；我刚得意地望了一眼，考珀少校就崛起在我眼前，一拳把我打回纵帆船上，他自己也跟着栽了进来。

二十个人扑到我身上。我一动不动。末日到了。我连抖掉一只苍蝇的力气都没有，我的心撞得肋骨欲裂。我仰面躺着，勉强说：“给我空气。”我以为我要死了。

卡斯特罗裹着斗篷，立在我上方，考珀少校却在我头边跪下，几乎在呜咽：“我的文件！我的文件！告诉你，我会饿死的。叫他们把文件还我。那些对他们没用——我的抚恤金——抵押契据——对你们一文不值。”

他俯在我脸上，西班牙人围在四周，啧啧称奇。他求我说项，替他保住那些至关紧要的文件。

卡斯特罗保持着他的阴谋家风度。少校的苦楚打动了我，我终于屈尊为他向卡斯特罗开口，虽然颇费力气，因为我又气、又愤、又受辱。

“什——什么？他的文件我知道什么？叫他自己找去。”他高傲地挥挥手。

甲板上堆起一座座小丘：衣裳、铺盖、一桶桶朗姆酒、旧帽子、帆布。考珀在赃物间进进出出，像萝卜地裡的猎犬。他呻吟着。

===Original===

Beside one of the pumps was a small pile of shiny cases; ship’s instruments, a chronometer in its case, a medicine chest.
Cowper tottered at a black dispatch-box. “There, there!” he said; “I tell you I shall starve if I don’t have it. Ask him﻿—ask him﻿—” He was clutching me like a drowning man.
Castro raised the inevitable arm towards heaven, letting his round black cloak fall into folds like those of an umbrella. Cowper gathered that he might take his japanned dispatch-box; he seized the brass handles and rushed towards the side, but at the last moment he had the good impulse to return to me, holding out his hand, and spluttering distractedly, “God bless you, God bless you.” After a time he remembered that I had rescued his wife and child, and he asked God to bless me for that too. “If it is ever necessary,” he said, “on my honour, if you escape, I will come a thousand miles to testify. On my honour﻿—remember.” He said he was going to live in Clapham. That is as much as I remember. I was held pinned down to the deck, and he disappeared from my sight. Before the ships had separated, I was carried below in the cabin of the schooner.
They left me alone there, and I sat with my head on my arms for a long time, I did not think of anything at all; I was too utterly done up with my struggles, and there was nothing to be thought about. I had grown to accept the meanness of things as if I had aged a great deal. I had seen men scratch each other’s faces over coat buttons, old shoes﻿—over Mercer’s trousers. My own future did not interest me at this stage. I sat up and looked round me.
I was in a small, bare cabin, roughly wainscotted and exceedingly filthy. There were the grease-marks from the backs of heads all along a bulkhead above a wooden bench; the rough table, on which my arms rested, was covered with layers of tallow spots. Bright light shone through a porthole. Two or three ill-assorted muskets slanted about round the foot of the mast﻿—a long old piece, of the time of Pizarro, all red velvet and silver’ chasing, on a swivelled stand, three English fowling-pieces, and a coachman’s blunderbuss. A man was rising from a mattress stretched on the floor; he placed a mandolin, decorated with red favours, on the greasy table. He was shockingly thin, and so tall that his head disturbed the candle-soot on the ceiling.

===Chinese===

一部泵旁边堆着一小堆亮闪闪的匣子；航海仪器、装在匣子裡的天文钟、一只药箱。

考珀朝一只黑色公文箱摇晃过去。“那儿，那儿！”他说；“告诉你，没有它我会饿死的。求求他——求求他——”他抓住我，像溺水的人。

卡斯特罗把那条免不了的手臂举向天空，让黑斗篷像伞一样垂出褶子。考珀领会到他可以拿走他的黑漆公文箱；他抓住铜把手冲向舷侧，可最后一刻他生出一个好念头，回到我这裡，伸出手来，语无伦次地喷着唾沫：“上帝保佑你，上帝保佑你。”过了一阵他想起我救过他的妻女，又为此请上帝保佑我一遍。“万一有需要，”他说，“以我的名誉，要是你逃出去，我愿意走一千英裡来作证。以我的名誉——记住。”他说他要去克拉彭住。我记得的就是这么多。我被按在甲板上，他从我眼前消失了。两条船分开之前，我被抬下去，进了纵帆船的舱。

他们留我一个人在那儿，我头枕着胳膊坐了很久，什么也不想；我被挣扎折腾得太彻底，也没有什么可想。我已经惯于接受事情的卑污，仿佛老了许多。我见过人们为外套纽扣互相抓脸，为旧鞋——为默瑟（Mercer）的裤子。我自己的前途，在这个阶段引不起我的兴致。我坐直了，环顾四周。

我在一间狭小、光秃的舱裡，粗陋地装着壁板，脏得出奇。一条木凳上方的舱壁上，齐齐一排后脑勺蹭出的油渍；我臂肘撑着的粗桌子上，覆着一层层牛油斑点。明亮的光从一个舷窗照进来。两三支不成套的火枪斜倚在桅杆脚下——一支又长又老的家伙，皮萨罗时代的货色，红丝绒镶银雕，架在旋转枪架上；三支英国猎枪；一支马车夫用的大口径短铳。一个人正从铺在地上的床垫上起身；他把一把缀着红饰带的曼陀林放上油腻的桌子。他瘦得吓人，又高得头顶蹭着天花板上的烛烟。

===Original===

He said: “Ah, I was waiting for the cavalier to awake.”
He stalked round the end of the table, slid between it and the side, and grasped my arm with wrapt earnestness as he settled himself slowly beside me. He wore a red shirt that had become rather black where his long brown ringlets fell on his shoulders; it had tarnished gilt buttons ciphered “G.R.,” stolen, I suppose, from some English ship.
“I beg the Señor Caballero to listen to what I have to record,” he said, with intense gravity. “I cannot bear this much longer﻿—no, I cannot bear my sufferings much longer.”
His face was of a large, classical type; a close-featured, rather long face, with an immense nose that from the front resembled the section of a bell; eyebrows like horseshoes, and very large-pupilled eyes that had the purplish-brown lustre of a horse’s. His air was mournful in the extreme, and he began to speak resonantly as if his chest were a sounding-board. He used immensely long sentences, of which I only understood one-half.
“What, then, is the difference between me, Manuel-del-Popolo Isturiz, and this Tomas Castro? The Señor Caballero can tell at once. Look at me. I am the finer man. I would have you ask the ladies of Rio Medio, and leave the verdict to them. This Castro is an Andalou﻿—a foreigner. And we, the braves of Rio Medio, will suffer no foreigner to make headway with our ladies. Yet this Andalusian is preferred because he is a humble friend of the great Don, and because he is for a few days given the command. I ask you, Señor, what is the radical difference between me, the sailing captain of this vessel, and him, the fighting captain for a few days? Is it not I that am, as it were, the brains of it, and he only its knife? I ask the Señor Caballero.”
I didn’t in the least know what to answer. His great eyes wistfully explored my face. I expect I looked bewildered.
“I lay my case at your feet,” he continued. “You are to be our chief leader, and, on account of your illustrious birth and renowned intelligence, will occupy a superior position in the council of the notables. Is it not so? Has not the Señor Juez O’Brien so ordained? You will give ear to me, you will alleviate my indignant sufferings?” He implored me with his eyes for a long time.
Manuel-del-Popolo, as he called himself, pushed the hair back from his forehead.

===Chinese===

他说：“啊，我正等着骑士老爷醒来。”

他大步绕过桌子一头，从桌子和船壁之间侧身挤过，慢慢在我身边坐下时，用一种全然的恳切抓住我的胳膊。他穿一件红衬衫，棕色长鬈发垂肩的地方已经磨得相当黑；纽扣是发乌的镀金，錾着“G.R.”字样，想必是从哪条英国船上偷的。

“我求骑士先生听听我要申诉的事，”他说，无比庄重。“我再也受不了啦——不，我的苦楚我再也受不了啦。”

他的脸是大型古典式的；五官挤紧的长脸，一只大鼻子，正面看像一口钟的剖面；眉毛像马蹄铁，瞳孔极大的眼睛泛着马眼那种紫褐的光泽。他的神气哀伤到极点，开口时铿然作响，仿佛胸腔是一面共鸣板。他用极其长的句子，我只听得懂一半。

“那么，我，曼努埃尔（Manuel-del-Popolo Isturiz），同这个托马斯·卡斯特罗，差别何在？骑士先生一看便知。看看我。我是更出色的人。请您去问问裡奥梅迪奥（Rio Medio）的太太小姐们，把裁决留给她们。这个卡斯特罗是安达卢人——一个外乡人。而我们，裡奥梅迪奥的好汉们，容不得任何外乡人在我们的太太小姐那裡得势。可这安达卢西亚人偏受偏爱，因为他是大堂的卑微朋友，又因为给了他几天的指挥权。我问您，先生，我，这条船的航行船长，同他，那几天的作战船长，根本的差别何在？难道我不正是这桩事业的脑子，而他不过是它的刀子？我请问骑士先生。”

我全然不知怎样回答。他的大眼睛渴念地探着我的脸。我想我一脸茫然。

“我把我的案子放在您脚下，”他接着说。“您要做我们的首领，由于您高贵的出身和闻名的智慧，将在名流的议事会裡占据超然的地位。不是这样吗？奥布赖恩法官先生（Señor Juez O’Brien）不是这样裁定的吗？您会听我说话，您会减轻我愤懑的苦楚吧？”他用眼睛恳求了我很久。

曼努埃尔，如他自称的，把额发向后一掠。

===Original===

I had noticed that the love-locks were plaited with black braid, and that he wore large dirty silk ruffles.
“The caballero” he continued, marking his words with a long, white finger a-tap on the table, “will represent my views to the notables. My position at present, as I have had the honour to observe, is become unbearable. Consider, too, how your worship and I would work together. What lightness for you and me. You will find this Castro unbearably gross. But I﻿—I assure you I am a man of taste﻿—an *improvisador*﻿—an artist. My songs are celebrated. And yet!﻿ ﻿…”
He folded his arms again, and waited; then he said, employing his most impressive voice:
“I have influence with the men of Rio. I could raise a riot. We Cubans are a jealous people; we do not love that foreigners should take our best from us. We do not love it; we will not suffer it. Let this Castro bethink himself and go in peace, leaving us and our ladies. As the proverb says, ‘It is well to build a bridge for a departing enemy.’ ”
He began to peer at me more wistfully, and his eyes grew more luminous than ever. This man, in spite of his grotesqueness, was quite in earnest, there was no doubting that.
“I have a gentle spirit,” he began again, “a gentle spirit. I am submissive to the legitimate authorities. What the Señor Juez O’Brien asks me to do, I do. I would put a knife into anyone who inconvenienced the Señor Juez O’Brien, who is a good Catholic; we would all do that, as is right and fitting. But this Castro﻿—this Andalou, who is nearly as bad as a heretic! When my day comes, I will have his arms flayed and the soles of his feet, and I will rub red pepper into them; and all the men of Rio who do not love foreigners will applaud. And I will stick little thorns under his tongue, and I will cut off his eyelids with little scissors, and set him facing the sun. Caballero, you would love me; I have a gentle spirit. I am a pleasant companion.” He rose and squeezed round the table. “Listen”﻿—his eyes lit up with rapture﻿—“you shall hear me. It is divine﻿—ah, it is very pleasant, you will say.”
He seized his mandolin, slung it round his neck, and leant against the bulkhead. The bright light from the porthole gilded the outlines of his body, as he swayed about and moved his long fingers across the strings; they tinkled metallically. He sang in a nasal voice:

===Chinese===

我早已注意到，他那几绺情鬓编着黑辫带，戴着又大又脏的丝绒褶边。

“骑士先生，”他接着说，一根长白手指在桌上一下一下点着，加重他的话，“要向名流们转达我的见解。我眼下的地位，如我曾有幸陈述的，已变得无法忍受。也请想想，老爷您同我会怎样共事。您和我该多么轻盈。您会发现这卡斯特罗粗俗得难以忍受。可我——我向您保证，我是个有品味的人——一位即兴诗人（*improvisador*）——一位艺术家。我的歌是有名的。然而！……”

他又交抱起双臂，等着；然后他动用他最有感染力的嗓音说：

“我在裡奥的人裡有影响。我能掀起一场暴动。我们古巴人是个妒忌的民族；我们不爱外乡人夺走我们最好的东西。我们不爱；我们不容。叫这卡斯特罗自己想一想，体面地走掉，留下我们和我们的太太小姐。俗话说了：‘给退走的敌人搭一座桥，是好事。’”

他开始更渴念地端详我，他的眼睛比先前更亮了。这个人，尽管滑稽，却是全然认真的，这无可怀疑。

“我有一个温柔的性子，”他又开始，“一个温柔的性子。我顺服正当的权威。奥布赖恩法官先生叫我做什么，我就做什么。谁要给奥布赖恩法官先生添不便，我就把刀子捅进他身体，他是好天主教徒；我们都会那样做，这是理所应当。可这个卡斯特罗——这个安达卢人，差不多跟异端一样坏！等我的日子来了，我要剥他的胳膊、剥他的脚底，把红辣椒揉进去；裡奥所有不爱外乡人的人都会鼓掌。我还要在他舌头底下扎小刺，用小剪子剪掉他的眼皮，叫他对着太阳。骑士先生，您会爱我的；我有温柔的性子。我是个愉快的同伴。”他起身，侧身挤过桌子那边。“听好”——他的眼睛狂喜地发亮——“您要听我唱了。美极了——啊，非常悦耳，您会说的。”

他抓起曼陀林，套上脖颈，斜倚着舱壁。舷窗透进的亮光给他身体的轮廓镀了金，他一面摇摆，长长的手指在弦上抹过；琴弦铮铮地响。他用鼻音唱起来：
