And then, with an ejaculation of impatience, Tomas Castro caught at my hand, and whirled me round.
The great doors had swung noiselessly open, and the black night, bespangled with little flames, was framed in front of me. He suddenly unsheathed his portentous sword, and, hanging his great hat upon his maimed arm, stalked, a pathetic and sinister figure of grief, down the great steps. I followed him in the vivid and extraordinary compulsion of the sinister body that, like one fabulous and enormous monster, swayed impenetrably after me.
My heart beat till my head was in a tumultuous whirl, when thus, at last, I stepped out of that house﻿—but I suppose my grim robes cloaked my emotions﻿—though, seeing very clearly through the eyeholes, it was almost incredible to me that I was not myself seen. But these Brothers of Pity were a secret society, known to no man except their spiritual head, who chose them in turn, and not knowing even each other. Their good deeds of charity were, in that way, done by pure stealth. And it happened that their spiritual director was the Father Antonio himself. At that foot of the palace steps, drawn back out of our way, stood the great glass coach of state, containing, even then, the woman who was all the world to me, invisible to me, unattainable to me, not to be comforted by me, even as her great griefs were to me invisible and unassuageable. And there between us, in the great coffin, held on high by the grim, shadowy beings, was all that she loved, invisible, unattainable, too, and beyond all human comfort. Standing there, in the midst of the whispering, bareheaded, kneeling, and villainous crowd, I had a vivid vision of her pale, dim, pitiful face. Ah, poor thing!

===Chinese===

“如今，地上再没有我的地方了。”

一阵阵闪光忽然照亮那座巨大哀伤的府邸的高柱，许久之后，全然无声——只有巨火炬的毕剥——一批难以置信地如鬼似魅的人影，从头到脚裹着黑袍，眼洞奇幻地窥视着，摇摇晃晃进了大厅的大拱门。他们头顶上方是那具巨大的黑棺。那景象骇人而意外，我站在那裡呆望着，全然动弹不得，直到想起我自己也是这样一身。随后托马斯·卡斯特罗不耐地低喝一声，抓住我的手，把我一旋。

大门无声地敞开，缀着点点火焰的黑夜在我面前框出。他忽然拔出他那柄骇人的剑，把大帽子挂上残臂，迈下大台阶——一个悲怆而阴森的哀伤身影。我跟着他，身后那具阴森的机体像一头神话中的庞然巨怪，莫测地摇曳随行，带着一种鲜活而非凡的强制力。

当我终于这样走出那座宅子时，我的心跳得脑袋裡一片翻腾——不过我想我那阴森的袍子罩住了我的情绪——虽然透过眼洞看得分明，我自己竟不被看见，于我几乎难以置信。可这慈悲兄弟会是个秘密结社，除他们的神长外无人知晓，会员由神长轮流选任，彼此也互不相识。他们的慈善善举便这样以纯粹的隐秘完成。而碰巧，他们的神师正是安东尼奥神父本人。府邸台阶脚下，退让在道旁的，是那辆巨大的国事玻璃车，裡面坐着——即便在那时——那个就是我整个世界、于我不可见、于我不可及、不可由我安慰的女人，正如她的巨大悲伤于我不可见、不可抚。而在我与她之间，在那具被阴森幢幢的身影高高抬着的大棺裡，是她所爱的一切，也同样不可见、不可及，超出一切人间的安慰。站在那耳语纷纷的、光头跪地的刁民人丛中央，我鲜活地望见她苍白、朦胧、可怜的脸。啊，可怜的人！

===Original===

she was going away for good from all that state, from all that seclusion, from all that peace, mutely, and with a noble pride of quietness, into a world of dangers, with no head but mine to think for her, no arm but mine to ward off all the great terrors, the immense and dangerous weight of a new world.
In the twinkle of innumerable candles, the priceless harness of the white mules, waiting to draw the great coach after us, shone like streaks of ore in an infinitely rich silver mine. A double line of tapers kept the road to the cathedral, and a crowd of our negroes, the bell muzzles of their guns suggested in the twinkling light, massed themselves round the coach. Outside the lines were the crowd of rapscallions in red jackets, their women and children﻿—all the population of the Aldea Bajo, groaning. The whole crowd got into motion round us, the white mules plunging frantically, the coach swaying. Ahead of me marched the sardonic, gallantly grotesque figure of true Tomas, his sword point up, his motions always jaunty. Ahead of him, again, were the white robes of many priests, a cluster of tall candles, a great jewelled cross, and a tall saint’s figure swaying, more than shoulder high, and disappearing up above into the darkness. For me, under my cowl, it was suffocatingly hot; but I seemed to move forward, following, swept along without any volition of my own. It appeared an immensely long journey; and then, as we went at last up the cathedral steps, a voice cried harshly, “Death to the heretic!” My heart stood still. I clutched frantically at the handle of a pistol that I could not disengage from folds of black cloth. But, as a matter of fact, the cry was purely a general one; I was supposed to be shut up in the palace still.
The sudden glow, the hush, the warm breath of incense, and the blaze of light turned me suddenly faint; my ears buzzed, and I heard strange sounds.
The cathedral was a mass of heads. Everyone in Rio Medio was present, or came trooping in behind us. The better class was clustered near the blaze of gilding, mottled marble, wax flowers, and black and purple drapery that vaulted over the two black coffins in the choir. Down in the unlit body of the church the riffraff of O’Brien kept the doors.

===Chinese===

她要永远离开那一切威仪、那一切深闺、那一切安宁了，默默的，怀着一种安静的贵族骄傲，进到一个危险的世界，除我的头颅再没有别的头颅替她思想，除我的臂膀再没有别的臂膀替她挡开一切巨大的恐怖、一个新世界的浩大而危险的分量。

无数烛光的闪烁中，白骡子那无价的挽具——等着拖那辆大车随我们而行——像一座无限富饶的银矿裡的一道道矿脉发亮。两行烛台守着通向大教堂的路，我们的一群黑人，枪的铃口在闪烁的光裡若隐若现，聚拢在车周。行列之外是红短褂的暴徒、他们的女人孩子——下村的全体人口，一片呜咽。整个人群围着我们动起来，白骡狂跳，大车摇晃。我前面走着讥诮的、英武而怪诞的真正的托马斯，剑尖朝上，步子始终轻快。再前面，是许多神父的白袍、一簇高烛、一座嵌宝的大十字架，还有一尊高过肩头的圣像摇曳着，向上没入黑暗。至于我，风帽底下热得窒息；可我仿佛不由自主地被裹挟着向前。那是一段极其漫长的路；随后，当我们终于踏上大教堂的台阶时，一个声音狠狠地喊：“异端该死！”我的心停了。我狂乱地去抓一柄手枪的柄，它却缠在黑布裡抽不出。可事实上那喊声纯然是一句泛泛的口号；人们还当我被关在府邸裡呢。

骤然而至的亮光、肃静、馨香的暖息和光的炽烈忽然使我发晕；耳朵嗡嗡响，我听见奇异的声音。

大教堂是一片人头的海。裡奥梅迪奥的人全到了，或正跟在我们后面涌进来。体面的人们聚在诗班席那两具黑棺上方镀金、斑岩、蜡花和黑紫帏幔交织的辉煌近旁。教堂未点灯的深处，奥布赖恩的渣滓把着各处门。

===Original===

I followed the silent figure of Tomas Castro to the bishop’s own stall, right up in the choir, and we became hidden from the rest by the forest of candles round the catafalque. Up the centre of the great church, and high over the heads of the kneeling people, came the great coffin, swaying, its bearers robbed of half their grimness by the blaze of lights. Tomas Castro suddenly caught at my sleeve whilst they were letting the coffin down on to the bier. He drew me unnoticed into the shadow behind the bishop’s stall. In the swift transit, I had a momentary glance of a small, black figure, infinitely tiny in that quiet place, and infinitely solitary, veiled in black from head to foot, coming alone up the centre of the nave.
I stood hidden there beside the bishop’s stall for a long time, and then suddenly I saw the black figure alone in the gallery, looking down upon me﻿—from the loggia of the Riegos. I felt suddenly an immense calm; she was looking at me with unseeing eyes, but I knew and felt that she would follow me now to the end of the world. I had no more any doubts as to the issue of our enterprise; it was open to no unsuccess with a figure so steadfast engaged in it; it was impossible that blind fate should be insensible to her charm, impossible that any man could strike at or thwart her.
Monks began to sing; a great brass instrument grunted lamentably; in the body of the building there was silence. The bishop and his supporters moved about, as if aimlessly, in front of the altar; the chains of the gold censors clicked ceaselessly. Seraphina’s head had sunk forward out of my sight. All the heads of the cathedral bowed down, and suddenly, from round the side of the stall, a hand touched mine, and a voice said, “It is time.” Very softly, as if it were part of the rite, I was drawn round the stall through a door in the side of the screen. As we went out, in his turnings, the old bishop gave us the benediction. Then the door closed on the glory of his robes, and in a minute, in the darkness we were rustling down a circular narrow staircase into the dimness of a crypt, lit by the little blue flame of an oil lamp. From above came sounds like thunder, immense, vibrating; we were immediately under the choir. Through the cracks round a large stone showed a parallelogram of light.

===Chinese===

我跟着托马斯·卡斯特罗无言的身影走到主教自己的席位，一直上到诗班席，我们被灵台四周的烛林遮住，别人望不见了。大教堂正中，跪着的人头顶上方高处，那具大棺摇摇而来，杠夫们被炽亮的光夺去了一半狰狞。棺木放上台架时，托马斯·卡斯特罗忽然抓住我的袖子。他把我神不知鬼不觉地拽进主教席位后面的阴影。急促的一瞥间，我督见一个小小的黑影，在那清寂之地无限纤小、无限孤独，从头到脚罩着黑纱，独自沿正厅正中走来。

我在主教席位旁的阴影裡藏了很久，随后忽然看见那黑影独自在楼上廊座裡，俯望着我——从列戈家的廊台上。我忽然感到一种巨大的平静；她用看不见万物的眼睛望着我，可我知道、也感到她如今会随我到天涯海角。我对我们的事业再无怀疑；有这样一个坚毅的身影参与，它不容失败；盲目的命运不可能对她的魅力无动于衷，不可能有人能打击她、阻挠她。

修士们开始歌唱；一件巨大的铜器哀哀地呜咽；教堂正身一片寂静。主教和他的辅祭们在祭坛前无目的地走动；金香炉的链子咔哒不停。塞拉菲娜的头前俯，出了我的视线。全教堂的头都低下去，忽然，从席位一侧，一只手碰到我的手，一个声音说：“到时候了。”极轻地，仿佛仪式的一部分，我被引着绕过席位，穿过诗班屏侧的一扇门。我们出去时，老主教在转身之间给了我们祝福。随后门关上，隔断了他法衣的辉煌，一分钟后，我们在黑暗裡窸窣着走下一道圆形窄楼梯，进了地下墓室的幽暗，一盏油灯的小蓝火照着。头顶传来雷鸣般的声音，浩大，震动；我们就在诗班席正下方。一块大石四周的缝隙裡透出一个平行四边形的光。

===Original===

In the dimness I had a glimpse of the face of my conductor﻿—a thin, wonderfully hollow-cheeked lay brother. He began, with great gentleness, to assist me out of my black robes, and then he said:
“The señorita will be here very soon with the Señor Tomas,” and then added, with an infinitely sad and tender, dim smile:
“Will not the Señor Caballero, if it is not repugnant, say a prayer for the repose of﻿ ﻿…” He pointed gently upwards to the great flagstone above which was the coffin of Don Balthasar and Carlos. The priest himself was one of those very holy, very touching﻿—perhaps, very stupid﻿—men that one finds in such places. With his dim, wistful face he is very present in my memory. He added: “And that the good God of us all may keep it in the Señor Caballero’s heart to care well for the soul of the dear señorita.”
“I am a very old man,” he whispered, after a pause. He was indeed an old man, quite worn out, quite without hope on earth. “I have loved the señorita since she was a child. The Señor Caballero takes her from us. I would have him pray﻿—to be made worthy.”
Whilst I was doing it, the place began to be alive with whispers of garments, of hushed footsteps, a small exclamation in a gruff voice. Then the stone above moved out of its place, and a blaze of light fell down from the choir above.
I saw beside me Seraphina’s face, brilliantly lit, looking upwards. Tomas Castro said:
“Come quickly﻿ ﻿… come quickly﻿ ﻿… the prayers are ending; there will be people in the street.” And from above an enormous voice intoned:
“*Tu﻿ ﻿… u﻿ ﻿… ba mi﻿ ﻿… i﻿ ﻿… i﻿ ﻿… irum﻿ ﻿…*” And the serpent groaned discordantly. The end of a great box covered with black velvet glided forward above our heads; ropes were fastened round it. The priest had opened a door in the shadowy distance, beside a white marble tablet in the thick walls. The coffin up above moved forward a little again; the ropes were readjusted with a rattling, wooden sound. A dry, formal voice intoned from above:
“*Èrit﻿ ﻿… justus﻿ ﻿… Ab﻿ ﻿… auditione﻿ ﻿…*”
From the open door the priest rattled his keys, and said, “Come, come,” impatiently.
I was horribly afraid that Seraphina would shriek or faint, or refuse to move. There was very little time. The pirates might stream out of the front of the cathedral as we came from the back; the bishop had promised to accentuate the length of the service.

===Chinese===

幽暗裡我看清了引路人的脸——一个瘦削、双颊深陷得出奇的在俗修士。他极其温和地帮我脱下黑袍，随后说：

“小姐很快就到，同托马斯先生一起，”随后带着一个无限哀伤而温柔的、朦胧的微笑加一句：

“骑士先生若不嫌忌讳，可愿为……的安息诵一篇祈祷文？”他轻轻朝上方那块大石板一指，堂·巴尔塔萨和卡洛斯的棺就在它上面。这神父本人正是人们在那类地方见到的那种极圣洁、极动人——也许，极愚拙——的人。他那张朦胧渴念的脸，至今活在我记忆裡。他补了一句：“愿我们大家的好上帝，使骑士先生心中记住，好好照拂亲爱的小姐的灵魂。”

“我很老了，”停了停他低语。他确实老了，全然衰竭，在人世全然无望。“她还是个孩子时我就爱她。骑士先生要把她从我们身边带走了。我愿他祈祷——求得相配。”

我正照办，那地方开始窸窣地活了：衣裾的低语、放轻的脚步、一个粗嗓子裡的小小惊呼。随后头顶的石板挪开，一道光焰从上面的诗班席直泻下来。

我看见塞拉菲娜的脸在我旁边，被照得通亮，仰着。托马斯·卡斯特罗说：

“快……快……祈祷快完了；街上要有人了。”头顶上一个洪大的声音起腔：

“号……角……奇迹……（*Tu…u…ba mi…i…i…irum…*）”那铜蛇不谐和地呜咽着。一只黑天鹅绒包面的大箱子的一端，在我们头顶上方滑移向前；绳子绕它系好。神父已在幽暗的远处、厚墙裡一方白色大理石板旁打开了一扇门。上面的棺又向前挪了挪；绳子重新调整，发出木质声响。一个干巴巴、照本宣科的声音从上面起腔：

“义人……必因……听闻……而活（*Èrit…justus…Ab…auditione…*）”

神父从敞开的门裡把钥匙摇得哗啦响，不耐烦地说：“来，来。”

我怕极了塞拉菲娜会尖叫或晕倒，或拒不动弹。时间很少。我们从后门出来时，海盗们可能正从前门涌出大教堂；主教答应过把仪式拖长。

===Original===

But Seraphina glided towards the open door; a breath of fresh air reached us. She looked back once. The coffin was swinging right over the hole, shutting out the light. Tomas Castro took her hand and said, “Come﻿ ﻿… come,” with infinite tenderness.
He had been sobbing convulsedly. We went up some steps, and the door shut behind us with a sound like a sigh of relief.
We walked fast, in perfect blackness and solitude, on the deserted beach between the old town and the village. Every soul was near the cathedral. A boat lay half afloat. To the left in the distance the light of the schooner opposite the Casa Riego wavered on the still water.
Suddenly Tomas Castro said:
“The señorita never before set foot to the open ground.”
At once I lifted her into the boat. “Shove off, Tomas,” I said, with a beating heart.

===Chinese===

可塞拉菲娜朝敞开的门滑去；一缕新鲜空气拂到我们。她回头看了一眼。棺正正悬在洞口上方，遮断了光。托马斯·卡斯特罗握住她的手，带着无限的温柔说：“来……来。”

他一直在痉挛地呜咽。我们上了几级台阶，门在我们身后关上，那一声像一声如释重负的叹息。

我们在纯粹的黑与荒寂裡快步走，走在旧城与村子之间无人的沙滩上。每一个灵魂都在大教堂近旁。一条小船半浮在水裡。左边远处，列戈宅对面那条纵帆船的灯火在静水上摇曳。

忽然托马斯·卡斯特罗说：

“小姐从没有把脚踏上过露天的地。”

我立刻把她抱进船裡。“推开，托马斯，”我说，心跳如鼓。

## Part IV. Blade and Guitar / 第四部 剑与吉他
===Original===



===Chinese===

第四部 剑与吉他

### I / 一
===Original===

There was a slight, almost imperceptible jar, a faint grating noise, a whispering sound of sand﻿—and the boat, without a splash, floated.
The earth, slipping as it were away from under the keel, left us borne upon the waters of the bay, which were as still as the windless night itself. The pushing off of that boat was like a launching into space, as a bird opens its wings on the brow of a cliff, and remains poised in the air. A sense of freedom came to me, the unreasonable feeling of exultation﻿—as if I had been really a bird essaying its flight for the first time. Everything, sudden and evil and most fortunate, had been arranged for me, as though I had been a lay figure on which Romance had been wreaking its bewildering unexpectedness; but with the floating clear of the boat, I felt somehow that this escape I had to manage myself.
It was dark. Dipping cautiously the blade of the oar, I gave another push against the shelving shore. Seraphina sat, cloaked and motionless, and Tomas Castro, in the bows, made no sound. I didn’t even hear him breathe. Everything was left to me. The boat, impelled afresh, made a slight ripple, and my elation was replaced in a moment by all the torments of the most acute anxiety.
I gave another push, and then lost the bottom. Success depended upon my resource, readiness, and courage. And what was this success? Immediately, it meant getting out of the bay, and into the open sea in a twelve-foot dinghy looted from some ship years ago by the Rio Medio pirates, if that miserable population of sordid and ragged outcasts of the Antilles deserved such a romantic name. They were sea-thieves.
Already the wooded shoulder of a mountain was thrown out intensely black by the glow in the sky behind. The moon was about to rise. A great anguish took my heart as if in a vice. The stillness of the dark shore struck me as unnatural. I imagined the yell of the discovery breaking it, and the fancy caused me a greater emotion than the thing itself, I flatter myself, could possibly have done. The unusual silence in which, through the open portals, the altar of the cathedral alone blazed with many flames upon the bay, seemed to enter my very heart violently, like a sudden access of anguish. The two in the boat with me were silent, too. I could not bear it.
“Seraphina,” I murmured, and heard a stifled sob.

===Chinese===

轻轻一震，几乎觉察不到，一阵微弱的刮擦，一阵沙的窸窣——小船没有溅起一点水花，浮起来了。

大地仿佛从龙骨底下滑走，撇下我们浮在湾水上，水同无风的夜一样静。那小船的推离像一次升空，像一只鸟在崖沿张开翅膀，悬定在空中。一种自由之感来到我身上，那种无由的飞扬——仿佛我真是一只初试飞行的鸟。一切，突然的、凶险的、大幸的，都替我安排好了，仿佛我是一具衣架，任罗曼斯在我身上施展它令人迷乱的突兀；可小船一旦漂离，我却隐隐觉得，这场逃亡必须由我自己来操持。

天黑。我小心地探下桨叶，朝浅滩又推了一把。塞拉菲娜坐着，裹着斗篷，一动不动；托马斯·卡斯特罗（Tomas Castro）在船头，不作一点声息。我甚至听不见他呼吸。一切都交给了我。小船再被推动，漾起微澜，我的得意顷刻换成了最尖锐的焦虑的全部煎熬。

我又推了一把，随后够不着底了。成败系于我的机智、敏捷和勇气。而这成就是什么？眼下，它意味着驶出湾去，进入外海，乘一条十二英尺的小艇——多年前裡奥梅迪奥（Rio Medio）海盗们从某条船上劫来的；倘若安的列斯那些褴褛邋遢的被弃者当得起那样一个罗曼斯名字的话。他们是海上的贼。

林木的山肩已被天边的余照衬得漆黑。月亮就要升了。一阵大痛苦像铁钳般攫住我的心。黑暗海岸的寂静，打击我似属反常。我想像发觉的呐喊将它撕破，这想象给我的激动，我敢自诩，比事情本身所能给的还大。不寻常的寂静裡，敞着的大门间唯有大教堂的祭坛烛焰齐明，照在湾上，仿佛猛然撞进我的心，像一阵骤发的剧痛。同船的两人也沉默。我受不住了。

“塞拉菲娜，”我喃喃，听见一声压抑的呜咽。

===Original===

“It is time to take the oars, Señor,” whispered Castro suddenly, as though he had fallen asleep as soon as he had scrambled into the bows, and only had awaked that instant. “The mists in the middle of the bay will hide us when the moon rises.”
It was time﻿—if we were to escape. Escape where? Into the open sea? With that silent, sorrowing girl by my side! In this miserable cockleshell, and without any refuge open to us? It was not really a hesitation; she could not be left at the mercy of O’Brien. It was as though I had for the first time perceived how vast the world was; how dangerous; how unsafe. And there was no alternative. There could be no going back.
Perhaps, if I had known what was before us, my heart would have failed me utterly out of sheer pity. Suddenly my eyes caught sight of the moon making like the glow of a bush fire on the black slope of the mountain. In a moment it would flood the bay with light, and the schooner anchored off the beach before the Casa Riego was not eighty yards away. I dipped my oar without a splash. Castro pulled with his one hand.
The mists rising on the lowlands never filled the bay, and I could see them lying in moonlight across the outlet like a silvery white ghost of a wall. We penetrated it, and instantly became lost to view from the shore.
Castro, pulling quickly, turned his head, and grunted at a red blur very low in the mist. A fire was burning on the low point of land where Nichols﻿—the Nova Scotian﻿—had planted the battery which had worked such havoc with Admiral Rowley’s boats. It was a mere earthwork and some of the guns had been removed. The fire, however, warned us that there were some people on the point. We ceased rowing for a moment, and Castro explained to me that a fire was always lit when any of these thieves’ boats were stirring. There would be three or four men to keep it up. On this very night Manuel-del-Popolo was outside with a good many rowboats, waiting on the Indiaman. The ship had been seen nearing the shore since noon. She was becalmed now. Perhaps they were looting her already.
This fact had so far favoured our escape. There had been no strollers on the beach that night. Since the investment of the Casa Riego, Castro had lived amongst the besiegers on his prestige of a superior person, of a caballero skilled in war and diplomacy.

===Chinese===

“该换您拿桨了，先生，”卡斯特罗忽然低语，仿佛他一爬进船头就睡着了，此刻方醒。“湾心的雾会在月亮升起时藏住我们。”

是该了——倘若我们还要逃。逃去哪儿？进外海？身边是那沉默哀伤的姑娘！乘这只可怜的蛋壳，没有任何庇护向我们敞开？其实算不上犹豫；她不能被丢给奥布赖恩摆布。这仿佛是我头一回看清世界有多大；多危险；多不安全。而没有别的路。回不了头了。

也许，我若知道前路有什么，我的心会纯粹出于怜悯而彻底垮掉。忽然我看见月亮像山坡上林火的光，在那黑色的坡上亮起来。转眼它就要把湾照成白昼，而泊在列戈宅（Casa Riego）前滩外的那条纵帆船不到八十码。我无声地探下桨。卡斯特罗用他的一只手划。

低地上升起的雾从不满湾，我望得见它卧在月光裡，横过湾口，像一道银白的、墙的幽灵。我们钻了进去，立时从岸上望不见了。

卡斯特罗急划着，回头朝雾裡一团很低的红影哼了一声。一炉火燃在低低的岬角上，尼科尔斯（Nichols）——那个新斯科舍人——就是在那裡设了炮阵，把罗利海军上将（Admiral Rowley）的艇队打得那样惨。如今不过一座土工事，几门炮也挪走了。可那火警告我们，岬上有人。我们停桨片刻，卡斯特罗向我解释，这帮贼的船只要有动静，就总点起火。守火的会有三四个。就在今夜，曼努埃尔·德尔·波波洛正带着许多划艇在外面，守着那条印度商船。中午以来那船就被望见朝岸边靠近。此刻它被困住了无风。说不定他们已经在洗劫它了。

这件事至今都在帮我们的逃亡。那夜沙滩上没有游荡的人。自列戈宅被围以来，卡斯特罗一直住在围困者中间，凭他上等人的威望，凭一个娴于兵事与外交的绅士身份。

===Original===

No one knew how much the tubby, saturnine little man was in the confidence of the Juez O’Brien; and there was no doubt that he was a good Catholic. He was a very grave, a very silent caballero. In reality his heart had been broken by the death of Carlos, and he did not care what happened to him. His action was actuated by his scorn and hate of the Rio Medio population, rather than by any friendly feeling towards myself.
On that night Domingo’s partisans were watching the Casa Riego, while Manuel (who was more of a seaman) had taken most of his personal friends, and all the larger boats that would float, to do a bit of “outside work,” as they called it, upon the becalmed West Indiaman.
This had facilitated Castro’s plan, and it also accounted for the smallness of the boat, which was the only one of the refuse lot left on the beach that did not gape at every seam. She was not tight by any means, though. I could hear the water washing above the bottom-boards, and I remember how concern about keeping Seraphina’s feet dry mingled with the grave apprehensions of our enterprise.
We had been paddling an easy stroke. The red blur of the fire on the point was growing larger, while the diminished blaze of lights on the high altar of the cathedral pierced the mist with an orange ray.
“The boat should be baled out,” I remarked in a whisper.
Castro laid his oar in and made his way to the thwart. It shows how well we were prepared for our flight, that there was not even a half-coconut shell in the boat. A gallon earthenware jar, stoppered with a bunch of grass, contained all our provision of fresh water. Castro displaced it, and, bending low, tried to bale with his big, soft hat. I should imagine that he found it impracticable, because, suddenly, he tore off one of his square-toed shoes with a steel buckle. He used it as a scoop, blaspheming at the necessity, but in a very low mutter, out of respect for Seraphina.
Standing up in the stern-sheets by her side, I kept on sculling gently. Once before I had gone desperately to sea﻿—escaping the gallows, perhaps﻿—in a very small boat, with the drunken song of Rangsley’s uncle heralding the fascination of the unknown to a very callow youth. That night had been as dark, but the danger had been less great.

===Chinese===

谁也不知道这矮胖阴沉的小个子在多大程度上参与着奥布赖恩法官（Juez O’Brien）的机密；而无疑他是个好天主教徒。他是个非常庄重、非常沉默的绅士。实际上，他的心已被卡洛斯之死砸碎，他不在乎自己会落个什么。他的行动是出于对裡奥梅迪奥民众的轻蔑和恨，而非对我的任何好感。

那夜，多明戈（Domingo）的党羽守着列戈宅，而曼努埃尔（他更算个水手）带着他大部分私党，和所有浮得起来的大船，去对那条被困的西印度商船做一点他们所谓的“外活”。

这就便利了卡斯特罗的计划，也解释了这条船为什么小——它是滩上那一堆破烂裡唯一一条不处处开缝的。但它也绝不严实。我听得见水在底板上面荡，我记得，怎样对保持塞拉菲娜的双脚干燥的操心，同我们此行的重大忧惧交缠在一起。

我们缓缓地划着。岬上火的红团越来越大，大教堂高坛减暗的灯焰则以一道橙光刺透雾。

“该把船裡的水舀出去，”我低声说。

卡斯特罗收桨挪到座板上。这表明我们对出逃准备得何等周全：船上连半只椰子壳都没有。一只陶罐，草团塞着口，装着我们全部的淡水。卡斯特罗把它挪开，俯下身，试着用他那顶大软帽舀水。我想他发现行不通，因为他忽然脱下一只缀钢扣的方头鞋。他拿它当勺用，为这必要低声咒骂着神明，但声音压得极低，出于对塞拉菲娜的敬意。

我立在她身边的船尾座上，轻轻摇着橹桨。从前我也有过一次拼死出海——逃的也许是绞架——乘一条很小的船，朗兹利伯父醉醺醺的歌为一个乳臭未开的少年预告着未知的迷人。那夜一样黑，但危险较小。

===Original===

The boat, it is true, had actually sunk under us, but then it was only the sea that might have swallowed me who knew nothing of life, and was as much a stranger to fate as the animals on our farm. But now the world of men stood ready to devour us, and the Gulf of Mexico was of no more account than a puddle on a road infested by robbers. What were the dangers of the sea to the passions amongst which I was launched﻿—with my high fortunes in my hand, and, like all those who live and love, with a sword suspended above my head?
The danger had been less great on that old night, when I had heard behind me the soft crash of the smugglers’ feet on the shingle. It had been less great, and, if it had had a touch of the sordid, it had led me to this second and more desperate escape﻿—in a cockleshell, carrying off a silent and cloaked figure, which quickened my heartbeats at each look. I was carrying her off from the evil spells of the Casa Riego, as a knight a princess from an enchanted castle. But she was more to me than any princess to any knight.
There was never anything like that in the world. Lovers might have gone, in their passion, to a certain death; but never, it seemed to me, in the history of youth, had they gone in such an atmosphere of cautious stillness upon such a reckless adventure. Everything depended upon slipping out through the gullet of the bay without a sound. The men on the point had no means of pursuit, but, if they heard or saw anything, they could shout a warning to the boats outside. These were the real dangers﻿—my first concern. Afterwards﻿ ﻿… I did not want to think of afterwards. There were only the open sea and the perilous coast. Perhaps, if I thought of them, I should give up.
I thought only of gaining each successive moment and concentrated all my faculties into an effort of stealthiness. I handled the boat with a deliberation full of tense prudence, as if the oar had been a stalk of straw, as if the water of the bay had been the film of a glass bubble an unguarded movement could have shivered to atoms. I hardly breathed, for the feeling that a deeper breath would have blown away the mist that was our sole protection now.
It was not blown away. On the contrary, it clung closer to us, with the enveloping chill of a cloud wreathing a mountain crag.

===Chinese===

那回，船确实当真在我们脚下沉了，可那时只有海能吞掉我，一个对生活一无所知、同命运素不相识的人，一如我们农场上的牲畜。而现在，人的世界张口等着吞我们，墨西哥湾不过是大盗出没的路上一个泥洼。海的险，比之于我投身其中的种种激情，算得了什么——我高攀的姻缘握在手裡，又像所有活着爱着的人一样，一柄剑悬在头顶？

那旧一夜的危险较小，那时我听见身后走私贩子的脚在卵石滩上软软的轰响。危险较小，而倘若它带一点肮脏的气昧，它也引我到了这第二场、更绝望的出逃——乘一只蛋壳，载走一个沉默的裹斗篷的身影，每看一眼都催快我的心跳。我把她从列戈宅的邪祟裡夺出来，像骑士从魔堡裡夺公主。可她于我，胜过任何公主之于任何骑士。

世上从没有过这样的事。恋人们尽可以在激情裡赴一场必死；可在青春的历史上，我想，从没有人这样、在这样屏息的寂静裡，去赴这样一场不顾一切的冒险。一切系于不出一声地溜过湾的咽喉。岬上的人没法追，可他们若听见或看见什么，就能朝外面的船喊警。这些才是真危险——我的头一桩心事。往后……我不愿想往后。只有外海和凶险的海岸。也许，一想它们，我就会放弃。

我只想赢得接续而来的每一刻，把全部官能凝成一阵隐秘的努力。我操纵小船，怀着紧绷的审慎的从容，仿佛桨是一根麦秆，仿佛湾水是一只玻璃泡的薄膜，一个不慎的动作就会把它震成齑粉。我几乎不呼吸，因为觉得一口深气就会吹散那雾——我们此刻唯一的护佑。

雾没有被吹散。相反，它贴我们更近了，带着裹住山岩的云那种包围的寒意。

===Original===

The vague shadows and dim outlines that had hung around us began, at last, to vanish utterly in an impenetrable and luminous whiteness. And through the jumble of my thoughts darted the sudden knowledge that there was a sea-fog outside﻿—a thing quite different from the nightly mists of the bay. It was rolling into the passage inexplicably, for no stir of air reached us. It was possible to watch its endless drift by the glow of the fire on the point, now much nearer us. Its edges seemed to melt away in the flight of the water-dust. It was a sea-fog coming in. Was it disastrous to us, or favourable? It, at least, answered our immediate need for concealment, and this was enough for me, when all our future hung upon every passing minute.
The Rio picaroons, when engaged in thieving from some ship becalmed on the coast, began by towing one of their schooners as far as the entrance. They left her there as a rallying point for the boats, and to receive the booty.
One of these schooners, as I knew, was moored opposite the Casa Riego. The other might be lying at anchor somewhere right in the fairway ahead, within a few yards. I strained my ears for some revealing sound from her, if she were there﻿—a cough, a voice, the creak of a block, or the fall of something on her deck. Nothing came. I began to fear lest I should run stem on into her side without a moment’s warning. I could see no further than the length of our twelve-foot boat.
To make certain of avoiding that danger, I decided to shave close the spit of sand that tipped the narrow strip of lowland to the south. I set my teeth, and sheered in resolutely.
Castro remained on the after-thwart, with his elbows on his knees. His head nearly touched my leg. I could distinguish the woeful, bent back, the broken swaying of the plume in his hat. Seraphina’s perfect immobility gave me the measure of her courage, and the silence was so profoundly pellucid that the flutter of the flames that we were nearing began to come loud out of the blur of the glow. Then I heard the very crackling of the wood, like a fusillade from a great distance. Even then Castro did not deign to turn his head.

===Chinese===

悬在我们四周的朦胧影子和模糊轮廓，终于开始在一片不透光的、发亮的白裡彻底消失。我纷乱的思绪中忽然闪过一个认识：外面有海雾——同湾裡夜夜起的雾全然是两回事。它正不可解地涌进口门，因为一丝风也没有到我们这裡。凭着岬上火的光——它此刻离我们近多了——望得见它无尽的漂移。它的边缘仿佛在飞行的水尘裡融化。是海雾进来了。它于我们是祸是福？至少，它应了我们眼下藏身的急需，这就够了，当我们的全部未来都悬在逝去的每一分钟上。

裡奥的海寇（picaroons）劫掠岸边被困的船时，总是先拖一条纵帆船到湾口。他们把它留在那儿，作小艇的集合点和赃物的收容所。

其中一条，我知道，系泊在列戈宅对面。另一条说不定正锚在前面航道正中的什么地方，几码之内。我竖起耳朵捕捉它可能发出的任何声响——一声咳嗽，一句话，滑车的吱呀，或什么东西落在甲板上。什么也没有。我开始怕会毫无预警地一头撞上它的船侧。我看不见十二英尺小船长度以外的东西。

为稳妥避开那危险，我决定紧贴南边低狭沙洲的尖梢擦过。我咬紧牙，果断地压了过去。

卡斯特罗留在后座板上，双肘支在膝上。他的头几乎碰到我的腿。我分辨得出那哀伤的弓背，他帽上羽翎断折的摇曳。塞拉菲娜全然的沉静，给了我丈量她勇气的尺度；寂静澄澈到这般地步，我们渐渐驶近的那炉火的焰闪，开始从光晕裡大声传出。随后我听见木头的毕剥本身，像一阵极远处的排枪。即便那时，卡斯特罗也不屑回头。

===Original===

Such as he was﻿—a born vagabond, *contrabandista*, spy in armed camps, sutler at the tail of the *Grande Armée* (escaped, God only knows how, from the snows of Russia), beggar, *guerrillero*, bandit, sceptically murderous, draping his rags in saturnine dignity﻿—he had ended by becoming the sinister and grotesque squire of our quixotic Carlos. There was something romantically sombre in his devotion. He disdained to turn round at the danger, because he had left his heart on the coffin as a lesser affection would have laid a wreath. I looked down at Seraphina. She too, had left a heart in the vaults of the cathedral. The edge of the heavy cloak drawn over her head concealed her face from me, and, with her face, her ignorance, her great doubts, her great fears.
I heard, above the crackling of dry wood, a husky exclamation of surprise, and then a startled voice exclaiming:
“Look! *Santissima Madre!* What is this?”
Sheer instinct altered at once the motion of my hand so as to incline the bows of the dinghy away from the shore; but a sort of stupefying amazement seized upon my soul. We had been seen. It was all over. Was it possible? All over, already?
In my anxiety to keep clear of the schooner which, for all I know to this day, may not have been there at all, I had come too close to the sand, so close that I heard soft, rapid footfalls stop short in the fog. A voice seemed to be asking me in a whisper:
“Where, oh, where?”
Another cried out irresistibly, “I see it.”
It was a subdued cry, as if hushed in sudden awe.
My arm swung to and fro; the turn of my wrist went on imparting the propelling motion of the oar. All the rest of my body was gripped helplessly in the dead expectation of the end, as if in the benumbing seconds of a fall from a towering height. And it was swift, too. I felt a draught at the back of my neck﻿—a breath of wind. And instantly, as if a battering-ram had been let swing past me at many layers of stretched gauze, I beheld, through a tattered deep hole in the fog, a roaring vision of flames, borne down and springing up again; a dance of purple gleams on the strip of unveiled water, and three coal-black figures in the light.
One of them stood high on lank black legs, with long black arms thrown up stiffly above the black shape of a hat. The two others crouched low on the very edge of the water, peering as if from an ambush.

===Chinese===

就是这样一个人——天生的流浪汉，私贩子，武营裡的探子，大军团（*Grande Armée*）尾巴上的随军小贩（天知道怎么从俄国的雪原逃出来的），乞丐，游击队员，强盗，怀疑一切又杀伐果决，把他的破烂披上阴沉的尊严——到头来成了我们那位堂吉诃德式的卡洛斯的阴森而怪诞的侍从。他的忠诚裡有某种罗曼斯的幽暗。他不屑于朝危险回头，因为他已把心留在了棺上，正如一段较轻的感情会献上花圈。我俯看塞拉菲娜。她也一样，把一颗心留在了大教堂的地下墓室。罩在她头上那件厚斗篷的边遮住了她的脸，连同她的脸，她的懵懂，她的大疑，她的大惧。

我听见，在干柴的毕剥之上，一声嘶哑的惊呼，随后一个吃惊的声音喊：

“看！至圣之母（*Santissima Madre*）！这是什么？”

纯粹的本能立刻改变了我的手的动作，把小艇的船头压离海岸；可一种令人麻木的惊愕攫住了我的灵魂。我们被看见了。全完了。可能吗？全完了，就这样完了？

由于一心避开那条纵帆船——至今我也说不清它到底在不在那儿——我贴沙洲贴得太近，近得我听见软而急的脚步在雾裡蓦地停住。一个声音仿佛在对我耳语：

“哪儿，哦，哪儿？”

另一个忍不住喊：“我看见了。”

那是一声压低的喊，像忽然被敬畏噤住。

我的手臂来回摆动；手腕的转动继续把桨的推力传给船。我身体的其余部分无助地僵在死的预期裡，仿佛从高处坠落的使人麻木的几秒钟。而事情也快。我觉出后颈上的一阵流——一口风。随即，仿佛一具攻城槌从我身旁荡过层层绷紧的纱幕，我透过雾上一个撕破的深洞，望见一片咆哮的火的幻象，压低又蹿起；一片揭开水面上的紫色光舞，和光裡的三个煤黑的人影。

其中一个高高立在细长的黑腿上，长长的黑臂僵直地扬过帽子的黑形。另两个蹲伏在贴水的边上，窥探着，仿佛从埋伏裡。

===Original===

The clearness of this vision was contained by a thick and fiery atmosphere, into which a soft white rush and swirl of fog fell like a sudden whirl of snow. It closed down and overwhelmed at once the tall flutter of the flames, the black figures, the purple gleams playing round my oar. The hot glare had struck my eyeballs once, and had melted away again into the old, fiery stain on the mended fabric of the fog. But the attitudes of the crouching men left no room for doubt that we had been seen. I expected a sudden uplifting of voices on the shore, answered by cries from the sea, and I screamed excitedly at Castro to lay hold of his oar.
He did not stir, and after my shout, which must have fallen on the scared ears with a weird and unearthly note, a profound silence attended us﻿—the silence of a superstitious fear. And, instead of howls, I heard, before the boat had travelled its own short length, a voice that seemed to be the voice of fear itself asking, “Did you hear that?” and a trembling mutter of an invocation to all the saints. Then a strangled throat trying to pronounce firmly, “The souls of the dead *Inglez*. Crying from pain.”
Admiral Rowley’s seamen, so miserably thrown away in the ill-conceived attack on the bay, were making a ghostly escort for our escape. Those dead boats’-crews were supposed to haunt the fatal spot, after the manner of spectres that linger in remorse, regret, or revenge, about the gates of departure. I had blundered; the fog, breaking apart, had betrayed us. But my obscure and vanquished countrymen held possession of the outlet by the memory of their courage. In this critical moment it was they, I may say, who stood by us.
We, on our part, must have been disclosed, dark, indistinct, utterly inexplicable; completely unexpected; an apparition of stealthy shades. The painful voice in the fog said:
“Let them be. Answer not. They shall pass on, for none of them died on the shore﻿—all in the water. Yes, all in the water.”
I suppose the man was trying to reassure himself and his companions. His meaning, no doubt, was that, being on shore, they were safe from the ghosts of those *Inglez* who had never achieved a landing. From the enlarging and sudden deepening of the glow, I knew that they were throwing more brushwood on the fire.

===Chinese===

这幻象的清晰被一层炽热的厚气氛框着，一阵柔软的白雾的急涌卷旋落进去，像一阵突起的雪旋。它合拢下来，立时淹没了火焰高高的摇曳、黑影、绕我船桨的紫光。灼热的强光打击了我的眼球一次，随即又融回雾那张补过的织品上旧有的火渍。可那两个蹲伏者的姿势不容置疑：我们被看见了。我等着一阵骤然的高声从岸上扬起，海上的呼喊应和；我激动地朝卡斯特罗尖喊，叫他把住他的桨。

他没有动，而我那一声喊——落在那些受惊的耳朵裡必像一种怪异非人间的音调——之后，一片深深的寂静伴随我们——迷信的恐惧的寂静。而代替嚎叫的，小船还没驶出自身一船之长，我听见一个仿佛是恐惧本身的声音问：“你听见了吗？”和一阵颤抖的、对诸圣的呼求的咕哝。随后一条被扼住的喉咙努力咬定：“是死去的英国人的魂灵。痛得在哭。”

罗利海军上将的水兵们，在那场失策的攻湾之战裡可悲地抛掷了性命，此刻正为我们的逃亡作一支幽灵的护卫。人们说那些死去的艇员在该处出没，一如萦绕在离逝之门畔的悔恨、遗恨或复仇的幽灵。我失着了；雾的破散出卖了我们。可我那些湮没无闻的败亡的同胞，凭他们勇气的记忆，占据着湾口。在这危急的时刻，可以说，是他们守护了我们。

而我们这一边，显露出来必定是黑的、模糊的、全然不可解的；全然出乎意料的；一伙潜行阴影的显形。雾裡那个痛苦的声音说：

“由它们去。别应声。它们自会过去，因为没有一个是死在岸上的——全在水裡。是的，全在水裡。”

我想那人是在给自己和同伴壮胆。他的意思无疑是：他们在岸上，就安全，不怕那些从未得以上岸的英国人的鬼魂。从火光的扩大和骤然加亮，我知道他们正往火裡添柴。

===Original===

I kept on sculling, and gradually the sharp fusillade of dry twigs grew more distant, more muffled in the fog. At last it ceased altogether. Then a weakness came over me, and, hauling my oar in, I sat down by Seraphina’s side. I longed for the sound of her voice, for some tender word, for the caress of a murmur upon my perplexed soul. I was sure of her, as of a conquered and rare treasure, whose possession simplifies life into a sort of adoring guardianship﻿—and I felt so much at her mercy that an overwhelming sense of guilt made me afraid to speak to her. The slight heave of the open sea swung the boat up and down.
Suddenly Castro let out a sort of lugubrious chuckle, and, in low tones, I began to upbraid him with his apathy. Even with his one arm he should have obeyed my call to the oar. It was incomprehensible to me that we had not been fired at. Castro enlightened me, in a few moody and scornful words. The Rio Medio people, he commented upon the incident, were fools, of bestial nature, afraid of they knew not what.
“Castro, the valour of these dead countrymen of mine was not wasted; they have stood by us like true friends,” I whispered in the excitement of our escape.
“These insensate English,” he grumbled.﻿ ﻿…
“A dead enemy would have served the turn better. If the caballero had none other than dead friends.﻿ ﻿…”
His harsh, bitter mumble stopped. Then Seraphina’s voice said softly:
“It is you who are the friend, Tomas Castro. To you shall come a friend’s reward.”
“Alas, Señorita!” he sighed. “What remains for me in this world﻿—for me who have given for two masses for the souls of that illustrious man, and of your cousin Don Carlos, my last piece of silver?”
“We shall make you very rich, Tomas Castro,” she said with decision, as if there had been bags of gold in the boat.
He returned a high-flown phrase of thanks in a bitter, absent whisper. I knew well enough that the help he had given me was not for money, not for love﻿—not even for loyalty to the Riegos. It was obedience to the last recommendation of Carlos. He ran risks for my safety, but gave me none of his allegiance.
He was still the same tubby, murderous little man, with a steel blade screwed to the wooden stump of his forearm, as when, swelling his breast, he had stepped on his toes before me like a bloodthirsty pigeon, in the steerage of the ship that had brought us from home.

===Chinese===

我继续摇桨，干枝尖锐的爆响渐渐远了，在雾裡闷了下去。末了完全停了。随后一阵虚弱涌上我，我收进桨，在塞拉菲娜身边坐下。我渴望她声音的声响，一句温存的话，一声低语对我纷乱灵魂的爱抚。我确信她，像确信一件征服来的稀世珍宝，它的占有把生活简化为一种崇敬的守护——而我又那样任她摆布，一种压倒的负罪感使我不敢同她说话。外海轻微的涌把小船荡上荡下。

忽然卡斯特罗发出一声惨淡的低笑，我低声数落他的麻木。哪怕只有一条胳膊，他也该应我那声唤拿起桨。我们竟没有挨枪，这于我不可解。卡斯特罗用几句阴郁轻蔑的话点醒了我。裡奥梅迪奥这帮人，他就这事件评论道，是蠢货，畜生的天性，连自己怕什么也不知道。

“卡斯特罗，我这些死去的同胞的勇武没有白费；他们像真正的朋友一样守护了我们，”我在出逃的兴奋裡低语。

“这些没头脑的英国人，”他咕哝。……

“一个死掉的仇人倒更顶用。要是这位绅士除了死掉的朋友之外一无所有。……”

他尖刻辛酸的咕哝停了。随后塞拉菲娜的声音柔柔地说：

“你才是朋友，托马斯·卡斯特罗。朋友的报答会轮到你。”

“唉，小姐！”他叹道。“这世上还给我剩下什么——给我这个把最后一块银钱拿去为那位显贵者和您表兄堂卡洛斯做了两台弥撒的人？”

“我们会叫你非常富有，托马斯·卡斯特罗，”她决然地说，仿佛船裡就放着几袋金子。

他用一句高扬的谢辞作答，声音辛酸而恍惚。我很清楚，他给我的相助不为钱，不为爱——甚至不为对列戈家的忠。那是对卡洛斯最后嘱托的服从。他为我的安全冒险，却不给我半点他的忠心。

他还是那同一个矮胖的、杀气的小个子，前臂的木桩上拧着一条钢刃，一如当年在载我们离开家乡的那条船上，在统舱裡，挺着胸，踮着脚尖在我面前踱步，像一只嗜血的鸽子。

===Original===

I heard him mumble, with almost incredible, sardonic contempt, that, indeed, the señor would soon have none but dead friends if he refrained from striking at his enemies. Had the señor taken the very excellent opportunity afforded by Providence, and that any sane Christian man would have taken﻿—to let him stab the Juez O’Brien﻿—we should not then be wandering in a little boat. What folly! What folly! One little thrust of a knife, and we should all have been now safe in our beds.﻿ ﻿…
His tone was one of weary superiority, and I remained appalled by that truth, stripped of all chivalrous pretence. It was clear, in sparing that defenceless life, I had been guilty of cruelty for the sake of my conscience. There was Seraphina by my side; it was she who had to suffer. I had let her enemy go free, because he had happened to be near me, disarmed. Had I acted like an Englishman and a gentleman, or only like a fool satisfying his sentiment at other people’s expense? Innocent people, too, like the Riego servants, Castro himself; like Seraphina, on whom my high-minded forbearance had brought all these dangers, these hardships, and this uncertain fate.
She gave no sign of having heard Castro’s words. The silence of women is very impenetrable, and it was as if my hold upon the world﻿—since she was the whole world for me﻿—had been weakened by that shade of decency of feeling which makes a distinction between killing and murder. But suddenly I felt, without her cloaked figure having stirred, her small hand slip into mine. Its soft warmth seemed to go straight to my heart soothing, invigorating﻿—as it she had slipped into my palm a weapon of extraordinary and inspiring potency.
“Ah, you are generous,” I whispered close to the edge of the cloak overshadowing her face.
“You must now think of yourself, Juan,” she said.
“Of myself,” I echoed sadly. “I have only you to think of, and you are so far away﻿—out of my reach. There are your dead﻿—all your loss, between you and me.”
She touched my arm.
“It is I who must think of my dead,” she whispered. “But you, you must think of yourself, because I have nothing of mine in this world now.”
Her words affected me like the whisper of remorse. It was true. There were her wealth, her lands, her palaces; but her only refuge was that little boat.

===Chinese===

我听见他咕哝，带着几乎不可思议的讥诮的轻蔑：说真的，先生若再不朝他的敌人们下手，很快就只剩死掉的朋友了。先生若抓住天意送上的那个绝好机会——任何一个神志清楚的基督徒都会抓住的——让一刀捅进奥布赖恩法官——我们现在就不会在一条小船裡漂流了。多蠢！多蠢！一刀小小的捅刺，我们此刻就都安然睡在自己的床上了。……

他的语调是疲惫的居高临下，我为那剥去一切骑士饰词的真相所震骇。显然，在饶恕那条不设防的性命时，我为了自己的良心犯了残忍之罪。塞拉菲娜就在我身边；受苦的是她。我放走了她的仇人，只因他碰巧在我近旁，缴了械。我行事像了英国人和绅士呢，还是只像一个拿别人付费来满足自己感伤的傻瓜？而且是无辜的人，像列戈家的仆人，像卡斯特罗自己；像塞拉菲娜，我高尚的宽容给她带来了这一切危险、这一切苦难、这未定的命运。

她没有显出听见卡斯特罗话的样子。女人的沉默深不可测，而仿佛我对世界的把握——她就是我的整个世界——被那一点体面的情感的微影削弱了，那情感在杀戮与谋杀之间作出区分。可忽然，她裹斗篷的身影并没有动，我感到她的小手滑进我的手裡。那柔软的暖意仿佛径直抚进我的心，安神，提气——仿佛她往我掌心放了一件异乎寻常、鼓舞人心的兵器。

“啊，你慷慨，”我凑着她罩脸的斗篷边缘低语。

“你现在必须想想你自己，胡安，”她说。

“想想我自己，”我哀哀地应。“我只有你可想，而你这样远——够不着。隔在你我之间的，是你的死者们——你全部的丧失。”

她碰碰我的臂。

“想我的死者，是我自己的事，”她低语。“可你，你必须想想你自己，因为这世上我已没有一样属于我的东西。”

她的话像悔恨的低语一样打动我。这是真的。她有财富，有田地，有府邸；可她唯一的避难所是这条小船。

===Original===

Her father’s long aloofness from life had created such an isolation round his closing years that his daughter had no one but me to turn to for protection against the plots of her own Intendente. And, at the thought of our desperate plight, of the suffering awaiting us in that small boat, with the possibility of a lingering death for an end, I wavered for a moment. Was it not my duty to return to the bay and give myself up? In that case, as Castro expressed it, our throats would be cut for love of the Juez.
But Seraphina, the rabble would carry to the Casa on the palms of their hands﻿—out of veneration for the family, and for fear of O’Brien.
“So, Señor,” he mumbled, “if to you tomorrow’s sun is as little as to me, let us pull the boat’s head round.”
“Let us set our hands to the side and overturn it, rather,” Seraphina said, with an indignation of high command.
I said no more. If I could have taken O’Brien with me into the other world, I would have died to save her the pain of so much as a pinprick. But because I could not, she must even go with me; must suffer because I clung to her as men cling to their hope of highest good﻿—with an exalted and selfish devotion.
Castro had moved forward, as if to show his readiness to pull round. Meantime I heard a click. A feeble gleam fell on his misty hands under the black halo of the hat rim. Again the flint and blade clicked, and a large red spark winked rapidly in the bows. He had lighted a cigarette.

===Chinese===

她父亲长年的离群索居，给他的暮年围出了这样的孤绝，以致他的女儿除了我没有别人可以投靠，来抵御她自己总管的阴谋。而一想到我们绝望的处境，想到这条小船裡等着我们的苦楚，想到可能以一场拖延的死收场，我动摇了一阵。回到湾裡去自首，难道不是我的本分？那样的话，用卡斯特罗的说法，我们的喉咙会为着对法官的爱被割掉。

而塞拉菲娜，暴民会把她捧在掌心裡送回列戈宅——出于对这家族的崇敬，也出于对奥布赖恩的畏惧。

“所以，先生，”他咕哝，“要是明天的太阳于您同于我一样无关紧要，那咱们就把船头转回去吧。”

“不如让我们把手按在船舷上，把它掀翻，”塞拉菲娜说，带着一种高贵的命令的义懤。

我没有再说话。倘若我能拉着奥布赖恩一起进另一个世界，为使她免遭针扎之痛我也甘愿去死。可我不能，她就只得随我走；就得受苦，因为我抓住她，像人们抓住他们至善的希望——以一种崇高的、自私的忠诚。

卡斯特罗已挪向船头，仿佛表示他随时准备掉头。这时我听见一声咔哒。一线微光落在他雾蒙蒙的双手上，在帽檐的黑晕底下。火石与钢刃又咔哒一响，一大粒红火星在船头急速眨眼。他点着了一支烟。

### II / 二
===Original===

Silence, stillness, breathless caution were the absolute conditions of our existence. But I hadn’t the heart to remonstrate with him for the danger he caused Seraphina and myself. The fog was so thick now that I could not make out his outline, but I could smell the tobacco very plainly.
The acrid odour of *picadura* seemed to knit the events of three years into one uninterrupted adventure. I remembered the shingle beach; the deck of the old *Thames*. It brought to my mind my first vision of Seraphina, and the emblazoned magnificence of Carlos’ sick bed. It all came and went in a whiff of smoke; for of all the power and charm that had made Carlos so seductive there remained no such deep trace in the world as in the heart of the little grizzled bandit who, like a philosopher, or a desperado, puffed his cigarette in the face of the very spirit of murder hovering round us, under the mask and cloak of the fog. And by the serene heaven of my life’s evening, the spirit of murder became actually audible to us in hasty and rhythmical knocks, accompanied by a cheerful tinkling.
These sounds, growing swiftly louder, at last induced Castro to throw away his cigarette. Seraphina clutched my arm. The noise of oars rowing fast, to the precipitated jingling of a guitar, swooped down upon us with a gallant ferocity.
“*Caramba*,” Castro muttered; “it is the fool Manuel himself!”
I said, then: “We have eight shots between us two, Tomas.”
He thrust his brace of pistols upon my knees.
“Dispose of them as your worship pleases,” he muttered.
“You mustn’t give up, yet,” I whispered.
“What is it that I give up?” he mumbled wearily. “Besides, there grows from my forearm a blade. If I shall find myself indisposed to quit this world alone.﻿ ﻿… Listen to the singing of that imbecile.”
A carolling falsetto seemed to hang muffled in upper space, above the fog that settled low on the water, like a dense and milky sediment of the air. The moonlight fell into it strangely. We seemed to breathe at the bottom of a shallow sea, white as snow, shining like silver, and impenetrably opaque everywhere, except overhead, where the yellow disc of the moon glittered through a thin cloud of steam. The gay truculence of the hollow knocking, the metallic jingle, the shrill trolling, went on crescendo to a burst of babbling voices, a mad speed of tinkling, a thundering shout, “*Altro, Amigos!

===Chinese===

寂静、静止、屏息的谨慎，是我们存在的绝对条件。可我没有心肠去责备他给塞拉菲娜和我带来的危险。雾这样浓，我认不出他的轮廓，可烟草味我闻得清清楚楚。

雪茄烟的辛辣气味，仿佛把三年的事件织成了一场不间断的冒险。我想起卵石滩；想起老泰晤士号（Thames）的甲板。它唤回我对塞拉菲娜的第一瞥，和卡洛斯病榻那纹章的华丽。这一切随一口烟来去；因为曾使卡洛斯那样迷人的全部威力与魅力，在这世上留下的最深的痕迹，莫过于这小个子灰白强盗心裡的了——他像个哲学家，或亡命徒，当着以雾为面具和斗篷、盘旋在我们四周的凶杀之灵的面，喷着他的烟。而凭我生命晚晴的澄净天空作证，那凶杀之灵竟当真让我们听见了，一串急促而有节奏的敲击，伴着欢快的叮当。

这些声音迅速大起来，终于促使卡斯特罗丢掉烟卷。塞拉菲娜攥住我的臂。急划的桨声，和着仓促的吉他叮咚，带着一股豪勇的凶悍朝我们压下来。

“该死（*Caramba*），”卡斯特罗咕哝；“正是那个傻瓜曼努埃尔本人！”

我说：“我们两个手里有八发子弹，托马斯。”

他把那一对手枪塞到我膝上。

“随老爷处置，”他咕哝。

“你还不许放弃，”我低声说。

“我放弃什么？”他倦倦地嘟哝。“再说，我前臂上长着一条刃呢。倘若我发觉自己不愿独自离开这世界。……听听那低能儿的歌。”

一支欢唱的假声，仿佛闷悬在上空，在低低沉在水面、像空气的浓稠乳浆的雾上方。月光落进去，奇异地。我们仿佛在一片浅海的底上呼吸，雪白，银亮，处处不透光，唯独头顶上方，月亮的黄盘透过一层薄薄的水汽闪闪发光。空壳般的敲击那快意的横暴、金属的叮当、尖利的吟唱，一路渐强，爆成一团嘈杂的人声、一阵疯狂的急响、一声雷鸣般的大喊：“划呀，伙伴们（*Altro, Amigos*）！

===Original===

*” followed by a great clatter of oars flung in. The sudden silence pulsated with the ponderous strokes of my heart.
To escape now seemed impossible. At least it seemed impossible while they talked. A dark spot in the shining expanse of fog swam into view. It shifted its place after I had first made it out, and then remained motionless, astern of the dinghy. It was the shadow of a big boat full of men, but when they were silent, I was not sure that I saw anything at all. I made no doubt, had they been aware of our nearness, there were amongst them eyes that could have detected us in the same elusive way. But how could they even dream of anything of the kind? They talked noisily, and there must have been a round dozen of them, at the least.
Sometimes they would fall a-shouting all together, and then keep quiet as if listening. By-and-by I began to hear answering yells, that seemed to converge upon us from all directions.
We were in the thick of it. It was Manuel’s boat, as Castro had guessed, and the other boats were rallying upon it gropingly, keeping up a succession of yells:
“*Ohe! Ohe!* Where, where?”
And the people in Manuel’s boat howled back at them, “*Ohe! Ohe﻿ ﻿… e!* This way; here!”
Suddenly he struck the guitar a mighty blow, and chanted in an inspired and grandiose strain:
“Steer﻿—for﻿—the﻿—song.”
His fingers ran riot among the strings, and above the jingling his voice, forced to the highest pitch, declaimed, as in the midst of a tempest:

> “I adore the saints in the glory of heaven

And, on the dust of the earth,

The print of her footsteps.”

===Chinese===

”随后是收桨入舱的一大阵乱响。骤然的寂静裡，只有我沉重的心跳在搏动。

此刻逃跑似乎不可能了。至少，在他们说话时不可能。发亮的雾海裡，一个黑点游进视野。我初初认出它之后它挪了挪位，随后停住不动，在艇尾后面。那是一条载满人的大船的影子，可他们一静下来，我连自己是否看见了什么也不能确信。我毫不怀疑，他们若知道我们就在近旁，他们中间有的是眼睛，能以同样飘忽的方式发现我们。可他们怎能梦想到这一类事？他们大声谈笑，起码有一打人，只多不少。

有时他们齐声大喊，随后又静下来，像在听。渐渐我听见应答的喊声，仿佛从四面八方向我们汇聚。

我们正在风口浪尖的中央。那是曼努埃尔的船，卡斯特罗猜对了，其余的船正摸索着朝它聚拢，连声喊着：

“喂！喂（*Ohe! Ohe!*）哪儿，哪儿？”

曼努埃尔船上的人朝他们吼回来：“喂！喂……诶（*Ohe! Ohe…e!*）这边；这儿！”

忽然他朝吉他猛击一记，用一种灵感的、浮夸的调子唱道：

“循——着——歌——声——来。”

他的手指在弦间撒野，叮咚之上，他的嗓音逼到最高处，朗诵着，仿佛在一场风暴的中心：

>

>

===Original===

He was improvising. Sometimes he gasped; the rill of softened tinkle ran on, and, glaring watchfully, I fancied I could detect his shape in the white vapour, like a shadow thrown from afar by a tallow dip upon a snowy sheet﻿—the lank droop of his posturing, the greasy locks, the attentive poise of his head, the sentimental rolling of his lustrous and enormous eyes.
I had not forgotten his astonishing display in the cabin of the schooner when, after the confiding of his woes and his ambitions, he had favoured me with a sample of his art. As at that time, when he had been nursing his truculent conceit, he sang, and the unsteady twanging of his guitar lurched and staggered far behind his voice, like a drunken slave in the footsteps of a raving master. Tinkle, tinkle, twang! A headlong rush of muddled fingering; a sudden bang, like a heavy stumble.
“She is the proud daughter of the old Castile! *Olà! Olà!*” he chanted mysteriously at the beginning of every stanza in a rapturous and soft ecstasy, and then would shriek, as though he had been suddenly cast up on the rock. The poet of Rio Medio was rallying his crew of thieves to a rhapsody of secret and unrequited passion. *Twang, ping, tinkle tinkle.* He was the *Capataz* of the valiant Lugareños! The true *Capataz*! The only *Capataz*. *Olà! Olà!* *Twang, twang.* But he was the slave of her charms, the captive of her eyes, of her lips, of her hair, of her eyebrows, which, he proclaimed in a soaring shriek, were like rainbows arched over stars.
It was a love-song, a mournful parody, the odious grimacing of an ape to the true sorrow of the human face. I could have fled from it, as from an intolerable humiliation. And it would have been easy to pull away unheard while he sang, but I had a plan, the beginning of a plan, something like the beginning of a hope. And for that I should have to use the fog for the purpose of remaining within earshot.
Would the fog last long enough to serve my turn? That was the only question, and I believed it would, for it settled lower; it settled down denser, almost too heavy to be stirred by the fitful efforts of the breeze. It was a true night fog of the tropics, that, born after sunset, tries to creep back into the warm bosom of the sea before sunrise.

===Chinese===

他在即兴演唱。有时他喘气；软化了的叮咚细流继续着，而我警觉地瞪视，仿佛能在白汽裡辨出他的形状，像远处一支牛油烛投在雪白床单上的影子——他那瘦长的做派的俯垂，油腻的发绺，头部专注的姿势，那一双水灵而巨大的眼睛的多情滚动。

我没有忘记他在纵帆船舱裡那场惊人的表演，倾诉完他的苦楚和抱负之后，他赏了我一段他的艺术。同那时一样，他养着他那横暴的自负，唱着，他那不稳的吉他铮鸣跌跌撞撞远远落在他嗓音后面，像喝醉的奴隶跟着发狂的主人。叮铃，叮铃，铮！一通仓皇的乱指；忽然砰的一声，像重重一跤。

“她是古老卡斯蒂利亚骄傲的女儿！奥拉！奥拉（*Olà! Olà*）！”他每段开头都神秘地唱，带着狂喜的温柔心醉，随后又会尖吼，仿佛忽然被抛上礁石。裡奥梅迪奥（Rio Medio）的诗人正把他的窃贼船队召向一场隐秘而无回报的狂想曲。铮，乒，叮铃叮铃。他是勇武村民的头目（*Capataz*）！真正的头目！唯一的头目。奥拉！奥拉！铮，铮。可他是她魅力的奴隶，她的眼睛、她的唇、她的头发、她的眉毛的俘虏——那眉毛，他用一声直冲云霄的尖啸宣布，像拱在星星上的虹。

那是一首情歌，一场哀伤的戏仿，一只猿猴对人类面孔真实悲哀的可憎鬼脸。我本可以从它面前逃走，像逃避一场难以忍受的羞辱。趁他唱着，无声地划开本来容易，可我有了一个计划，一个计划的雏形，有点像一个希望的雏形。而为这个，我得借这雾，好留在听得见的距离之内。

这雾能撑得够久、合我的用吗？这是唯一的问题，而我相信能，因为它沉得更低了；沉得更稠了，几乎重得微风断续的努力掀不动它。这是真正的热带夜雾，日落后生，赶在日出前爬回大海温暖的胸怀。

===Original===

Once in Rio Medio, taking a walk in the early morning along the sand-dunes, I had stood watching below me the heads of some people, fishing from a boat, emerge strangely in the dawn out of such a fog. It concealed their very shoulders more completely than water could have done. I trusted it would not come so soon to our heads, emerging, though it seemed to me that already, by merely clambering on Castro’s shoulders, I could attain to clear moonlight; see the highlands of the coast, the masts of the English ship. She could not be very far off if only one could tell the direction. But an unsteady little dinghy was not the platform for acrobatic exercises, and Castro not exactly the man.
The slightest noise would have betrayed us, and moreover, the thing was no good, for even supposing I had got a hurried sight of the ship’s spars, I should have to get down into the fog to pull, and there would be nothing visible to keep us from going astray, unless at every dozen strokes I clambered on Castro’s shoulders again to rectify the direction﻿—an obviously impracticable and absurd proceeding.

> “She is the proud daughter of old Castile, *Olà, Olà*,”

Manuel sang confidentially with a subdued and gallant lilt﻿ ﻿… Obviously impracticable. But I had another idea.
*Tinkle tinkle pinnnng﻿ ﻿… Brrroum. Brrrroum*.

> “My soul yearns for the alms of a smile.

For a forgiving glance yearns my lofty soul﻿ ﻿…”

===Chinese===

有一回在裡奥梅迪奥，清晨沿着沙丘散步，我曾站在高处，看下面几个从船上垂钓的人的脑袋，就这样奇异地从这样的雾裡探出黎明。它遮他们的肩膀，遮得比水还严实。我指望它不至于这么快升到我们头的高度——探出头去——虽然在我看来，只要爬上卡斯特罗的肩头，我就够得着清朗的月光；望得见海岸的高地，那条英国船的桅樯。只要辨得清方向，她就不会很远。可一条摇晃的小艇不是耍杂技的台子，卡斯特罗也不很像那个人。

最轻的声响都会出卖我们，况且那也没有用，因为就算我匆匆望见了船的桅樯，我也得回到雾裡划，而没有什么可见的东西能防止我们走偏，除非每划十几桨我就再爬上卡斯特罗的肩头校正方向——一个显然行不通而且荒唐的举动。

===Original===

he sang. Ah, if one could have added another four feet to one’s stature. Four or five feet only. There seemed to be nothing but a thin veil between me and the moon. No more than a thin haze. But at the level of my eyes everything was hidden. From behind the white veil came the crying of the strings, a screeching, lugubrious and fierce in its artificial transport, as if it were mocking my sad and ardent conviction of unworthiness, the crowning torment, and the inward pride of pure love. In the breathless pauses I could hear the hollow bumping of gunwales knocking against each other; faint splashings of oars; the distant hail of some laggards groping their way on the shrouded sea.
The note of cruel passion that runs in the blood held these cutthroats profoundly silent in their boats, as at home I could imagine a party of smugglers (they would not stick at a murder or two, either) listening, with pensive faces, to a sentimental ditty of some “sweet Nancy,” howled dismally within the walls of a wayside taproom in the smoke of pipes. I seemed to understand profoundly the difference of races that brings with it the feeling of romance or awakens hate. My gorge rose at Manuel’s song. I hated his lamentations. “Alas, alas; in vain, in vain.” He strummed with vertiginous speed, with fury, and the distracted clamour of his voice, wrestling madly with the ringing madness of the strings, ended in a piercing and supreme shriek.
“Finished. It is finished.” A low and applauding murmur flowed to my ears, the austere acclamations of connoisseurs. “Viva, viva, Manuele!”﻿—a squeak of fervid admiration. “Ah, our *Manuelito*.”﻿ ﻿… But a gruff voice discoursed jovially, “Care not, Manuel. What of Paquita with the broken tooth? Is she not left to thee? And *por Dios, hombres*, in the dark all women are alike.”
“I will cram thy unclean mouth with live coals,” Manuel drawled spitefully.
They roared with laughter at this sally. I depicted to myself their shapes, their fierce gesticulations, their earrings, bound heads, rags, and weapons, the vile scowls on their swarthy, grimacing faces. My anxiety beheld them as plainly as anything seen with the eyes of the body. And, with my sharpened hearing catching every word with preternatural distinctness, I felt as if, the ring of Gyges on my finger, I had sat invisible at the council of my enemies.

===Chinese===

他唱着。啊，人若能给自己添高四英尺。只四五英尺。我和月亮之间仿佛只隔一层薄纱。不多于一层薄霾。可在我眼睛的高度，一切都藏着。白纱后面传来琴弦的哭喊，一阵尖啸，人为的狂热裡透着凄厉，仿佛在嘲弄我那悲伤而炽热的自惭——纯粹爱情那加冕的苦楚和内在的骄傲。屏息的间歇裡，我听得见船舷彼此相磕的空响；桨的轻溅；几个掉队者在遮蔽的海上摸路，彼此遥远的招呼。

那流在血裡的残酷激情的音符，使这些刺客在各自的船裡深深沉默，正如在家乡，我可以想象一伙走私贩子（他们也是不惮杀一两个人的）听着某支“甜美的南希”之类的伤感小调，愁容满面，那歌在路边酒肆的墙壁内、烟斗的烟裡凄凄地嚎。我仿佛深刻地懂得了种族的差异——它带来罗曼斯之感，或唤醒仇恨。曼努埃尔的歌使我作呕。我恨他的哀叹。“唉，唉；徒然，徒然。”他以令人眩晕的速度、狂怒地乱弹，他嗓音疯狂的喧嚣，同琴弦轰响的疯狂扭打，收在一个穿透的、至高的尖叫裡。

“完了。完了。”一阵低低的赞许的喃喃流进我耳中，行家们严肃的喝彩。“万岁，万岁，曼努埃尔（*Viva, viva, Manuele*）！”——一声热烈倾慕的尖叫。“啊，我们的曼努埃利托（*Manuelito*）。”……可一条粗嗓门快活地说：“别往心裡去，曼努埃尔。缺了牙的帕基塔算什么？她不是还归你么？再说，凭上帝（*por Dios, hombres*），黑地裡女人全一个样。”

“我要拿活炭塞满你那张脏嘴，”曼努埃尔怨毒地拖长了腔说。

他们对这句妙语哄堂大笑。我在心裡描画他们的形貌、凶猛的手势、耳环、缠头、破烂和兵器、他们黝黑鬼脸上的狞相。我的焦虑把他们看得同肉眼所见一样清楚。我那变得锋利的听觉，把每个字都听得超自然的清楚，我觉得仿佛指上戴着吉格斯的戒指，隐身坐在仇敌们的会议裡。

===Original===

It was noisy, animated, with an issue of supreme interest for us. The ship, seen at midday standing inshore with a light wind, had not approached the bay near enough to be conveniently attacked till just after dusk. They had waited for her all the afternoon, sleeping and gambling on the spit of sand. But something heavy in her appearance had excited their craven suspicions, and checked their ardour. She appeared to them dangerous. What if she were an English man-of-war disguised? Some even pretended to recognize in her positively one of the lighter frigates of Rowley’s squadron. Night had fallen whilst they squabbled, and their flotilla hung under the land, the men in a conflict of rapacity and fear, arguing among themselves as to the ship’s character, but all unanimously goading Manuel﻿—since he *would* call himself their only *Capataz*﻿—to go boldly and find out.
It seems he had just been doing this with the help of a few choicer spirits, and under cover of the fog. They had managed to steal near enough to hear Englishmen conversing on board, orders given, and the yo-hoing of invisible sailors, trimming the yards of the ship to the fitful airs. This last, of course, was decisive. Such sounds are not heard on a man-of-war. She was a merchant ship: she would be an easy prey. And Manuel, in a state of exaltation at his venturesome bravery, had pulled back inshore, to rally all the boats round his own, and lead them to certain plunder. They would soon find out, he declaimed, what it was to have at their head their own valiant Manuel, instead of that vagabond, that stranger, that Andalusian starveling; that traitor, that infidel, that Castro. Hidden away, he seemed to spout all this for our ears alone, as though he could see us in our boat.﻿ ﻿… Patience; patience! Some day he would cut off that interloper’s eyelids, and lay him on his back under a nice clear sun. Castro made a brusque movement; a little shudder of disgust escaped Seraphina.﻿ ﻿… Meantime, Manuel declared, by his audacity, that ship was as good as theirs already. “*Viva el Capataz!*” they cheered.
The cloud-like vapours resting on the sea muffled the short roar; we heard grim laughter, excited cries.

===Chinese===

会开得热闹、生动，而对我们有着至高的利害。那条船，中午被望见乘着微风向岸驶来，直到黄昏刚过才近到便于攻击。他们守了它一下午，在沙洲上睡觉、赌博。可它外形上某种沉重的东西激起了他们怯懦的疑心，遏住了他们的热劲。它显得危险。万一它是一条化了装的英国军舰呢？有几个甚至硬说认出它确是罗利分舰队裡较轻的一条巡防舰。争吵间夜幕落了，他们那支小船队悬在陆岸下，人们在贪欲与恐惧的冲突裡，为那条船的身份互相争辩，却一致撺掇曼努埃尔——既然他非要自称他们唯一的头目——去大胆探个明白。

看来他刚带着几个精选的人物，借着雾的掩护干了这事。他们摸得够近，听见英国人在船上交谈、下口令，和看不见的水手收放帆索的号子。这最后一样当然一锤定音。军舰上听不到这种声音。它是条商船：会是块肥肉。于是曼努埃尔，处于对自身亡命之勇的亢奋裡，划回岸边，把所有小船聚拢到自己周围，率领他们去一场稳到手的劫掠。他们很快就会知道，让勇武的曼努埃尔做他们的头，而不是那个流浪汉、那个外乡人、那个安达卢西亚饿殍；那个奸细、那个异教徒、那个卡斯特罗，是什么滋味。他藏在我们近旁，仿佛专门对着我们的耳朵喷吐这一切，仿佛他在船裡看得见我们。……忍着；忍着！总有一天他要剪掉那篡位者的眼皮，叫他仰面躺在一个清朗的好太阳底下。卡斯特罗猛一动；塞拉菲娜漏出一小声厌恶的战栗。……同时，曼努埃尔宣称，凭他的胆气，那条船已经等于是他们的了。“头目万岁（*Viva el Capataz*）！”他们欢呼。

歇在海上的云絮闷住了短促的吼声；我们听见狞笑、兴奋的喊叫。

===Original===

He began to make a set speech, and his voice, haranguing with vehement inflections in the shining whiteness of a cloud, had an amazing and uncorporeal character; the quality of abstract surprise; of phenomenal emotion shouted into empty space. And for me it had, also, the fascination of a revealed depth.
It was like the oration of an ambitious leader in a farce; he held his hearers with his eloquence, as much as he had done with the song of his grotesque and desecrating love. He vaunted his sagacity and his valour, and overwhelmed with invective all sorts of names﻿—my own and Castro’s among them. He revealed the unholy ideals of all that band of scoundrels﻿—ideals that he said should find fruition under his captaincy. He boasted of secret conferences with O’Brien. There were murmurs of satisfaction.
I don’t wonder at Seraphina’s shudder of horror, of disgust, of dismay, and indignation. Robbed of the inexpugnable shelter of the Casa Riego, she, too, was made to look into the depths; upon the animalism, the lusts, and the reveries of that sordid, vermin-haunted crowd. I felt for her a profound and shamed sorrow. It was like a profaning touch on the sacredness of her mourning for the dead, and on her clear and passionate vision of life.
“*Hombres de Rio Medio! Amigos! Valientes!﻿ ﻿…*” Manuel was beginning his peroration. He would lead them, now, against the English ship. The terrified heretics would surrender. There was always gold in English ships. He stopped his speech, and then called loudly, “Let the boats keep touch with each other, and not stray in that fog.”
“The dog,” grunted Castro. We heard a resolute bustle of preparation; oars were being shipped.
“Make ready, Tomas,” I whispered.
“Ready for what?” he grumbled. “Where shall your worship run from these swine?”
“We must follow them,” I answered.
“The madness of the señor’s countrymen descends upon him,” he whispered with sardonic politeness. “Wherefore follow?”
“To find the English ship,” I answered swiftly.
This, from the moment we had heard Manuel’s guitar, had been my idea. Since the fog that concealed us from their sight made us, too, hopelessly blind, those wretches must guide us themselves out of their own clutches, as it were. I don’t put this forward as an inspired conception.

===Chinese===

他开始发表一通演说，他的嗓音，在云的闪亮洁白裡慷慨激昂抑扬顿挫，有一种惊人的、非肉身的性质；一种抽象的惊异之感；一种对着虚空呐喊的超常情感。而对我，它还有一种揭示深渊的迷惑力。

像一出闹剧裡野心家领袖的演说；他用口才抓住他的听众，同他用他那怪诞渎圣的情歌抓住他们一样牢。他吹嘘自己的精明和勇武，把一切名字骂了个遍——我的和卡斯特罗的也在其中。他揭示了那帮恶棍不圣洁的理想——他说那些理想要在他的统领下结出果实。他夸耀同奥布赖恩的秘密会谈。响起满足的低语。

我不奇怪塞拉菲娜那恐惧、厌恶、惶骇与义懤的战栗。被夺去列戈宅（Casa Riego）那不可攻破的庇护，她也只得朝深渊裡看；看那卑污的、害虫麇集的人群的兽性、欲念和梦呓。我为她感到一种深沉而羞惭的悲哀。那像一只亵渎的手，触在她对亡者的哀悼的神圣上，触在她对生活清明而炽热的远见上。

“裡奥梅迪奥的人们！朋友们！勇士们！……”曼努埃尔开始他的结尾。他此刻要率领他们攻打那条英国船。吓破胆的异端们会投降。英国船上总有金子。他停下演说，随后大声喊：“各船保持联络，别在那雾裡走散。”

“这狗东西，”卡斯特罗哼了一声。我们听见坚决的忙乱准备；桨要入位了。

“准备，托马斯，”我低声说。

“准备什么？”他嘟哝。“老爷要往哪兒躲开这些猪？”

“我们必须跟着他们，”我答。

“贵国同胞的疯劲儿传上您了，”他带着讥诮的客气低语。“为什么要跟？”

“去找那条英国船，”我飞快地答。

这，从我们听见曼努埃尔的吉他那一刻起，就是我的主意。既然遮住他们眼睛的雾也把我们弄得全然瞎了，那就得让这些可怜虫自己领我们出他们的掌心。我不把这说成灵感。

===Original===

It was a most risky and almost hopeless expedient; but the position was so critical that there was no other alternative to sitting still and waiting with folded hands for discovery. Castro seemed more inclined for the latter.
Fortunately, the bandits wasted some time in blasphemous bickerings as to the order of the boats in the procession of attack. I urged my views upon Castro in hurried whispers. His assent was of importance, since he could use an oar very well, and, if left to myself, I could not hope to scull fast enough to keep within hearing of the flotilla.
“Of what use to us would be a ship in Manuel’s power?” he argued morosely. On the other hand, if we waited near her till she had been plundered and released, neither the fog nor the night would last forever.
“My countrymen will beat them off,” I affirmed confidently. “At any rate, let us be on the spot. We may take a hand. And remember, Tomas, they are not led by you, this time.”
“True,” he said, mollified. “But one thing more deserves the consideration of your worship﻿ ﻿… If we follow this plan, we take the señorita among flying bullets. And lead, alas! unlike steel, is blind, or that illustrious man would not now be dead. If we wait here, the señorita, at least, shall take no harm from these ruffians, as I have said.”
“Are you afraid of the bullets?” I asked Seraphina.
Before she had answered, Castro hissed at me:
“Oh, you unspeakable English. Would you sacrifice the daughter, too, only because she is brave?”
His sinister allusion made my blood boil with rage, and suddenly run cold in my veins. Swathed in the brilliant cloud, we heard the sounds of quarrelling and scrambling die away; cries of “Ready! ready!” an unexpected and brutal laugh. Seraphina leaned forward.
“Tomas, I wish this thing. I command it,” she whispered imperiously. “We shall help these English on the ship. We must; I command it. For these are now my people.”
I heard him mutter to himself, “Ah, dear shade of my Carlos. Her people. Where are now mine?” But he shipped his oar, and sat waiting.
In the moment before the picaroons actually started, I became the prey of the most intense anxiety. I knew we were to seaward of the cluster. But of our position relatively to the boats, and to the English ship they would make for, I was profoundly ignorant. The dinghy might be lying right in the way.

===Chinese===

那是一个极其冒险、几乎无望的权宜之计；可处境危急到这地步，除了袖手坐着等被发现，别无他途。卡斯特罗似乎更倾向于后者。

幸好，那帮强盗为船队进攻的次序浪费了一阵渎神的争吵。我匆匆低语把我的看法劝给卡斯特罗。他的同意事关重大，因为他一只手也把桨使得很好，而若只剩我一个，我摇橹摇不到够快，赶不上听见的距离。

“落在曼努埃尔手裡的船，于我们有什么用？”他阴沉地反驳。另一面，倘若我们在船近旁等到它被劫掠、被放开，雾和夜都不会永在。

“我的同胞会打退他们，”我自信地断言。“无论如何，让我们到场。我们也可以插一手。记住，托马斯，这一回他们不是你带的。”

“倒是，”他说，软了。“可还有一件事值得老爷考虑……我们若照这计划办，就是把小姐带进枪林弹雨。而且铅弹，唉！不像钢，是不长眼的，不然那位显贵者也不会死了。我们若等在这裡，小姐至少不会伤在这帮恶棍手裡，像我方才说的。”

“你怕子弹吗？”我问塞拉菲娜。

她还来不及答，卡斯特罗朝我嘶声：

“噢，你们说不出口的英国人。就因为她勇敢，连女儿也要赔上么？”

他那阴森的影射使我血涌如狂怒，忽然又在血管裡变冷。裹在灿烂的云裡，我们听见争吵和忙乱的声音退去；“准备！准备！”的喊声，一声意外的粗野的笑。塞拉菲娜前倾。

“托马斯，我要这个。我命令，”她专断地低语。“我们要帮船上的英国人。我们必须；我命令。因为这些人如今就是我的人了。”

我听见他自言自语地咕哝：“啊，我卡洛斯亲爱的亡灵。她的人。我的如今何在？”可他收桨入位，坐着等了。

在海寇（picaroons）真正出发之前的一刻，我成了最剧烈的焦虑的猎物。我知道我们在那群船的海一侧。可对于我们自己同那些船、同他们要扑的英国船的相对位置，我全然无知。小艇说不定正横在路上。

===Original===

Before I could master the sort of disorder I was thrown into by that thought﻿—which, strange to say, had not occurred to me till then﻿—with a shrill whistle Manuel led off.
We are always inclined to trust our eyes rather than our ears; and such is the conventional temper in which we receive the impression of our senses that I had no idea they were so near us. The destruction of my illusory feeling of distance was the most startling thing in the world. Instantly, it seemed, with the second swing and plash of the oars, the boats were right upon us. They went clear. It was like being grazed by a fall of rocks. I seemed to feel the wind of the rush.
The rapid clatter of rowing, the excited hum of voices, the violent commotion of the water, passed by us with an impetuosity that took my breath away. They had started in a bunch. There must have been amongst them at least one crew of negroes, because somebody was beating a tambourine smartly, and the rowers chorused in a quick, panting undertone, “*Ho, ho, talibambo.﻿ ﻿… Ho, ho, talibambo.*” One of the boats silhouetted herself for an instant, a row of heads swaying back and forth, towered over astern by a full-length figure as straight as an arrow. A retreating voice thundered, “Silence!” The sounds and the forms faded together in the fog with amazing swiftness.
Seraphina, her cloak off, her head bare, stared forward after the fleeting murmurs and shadows we were pursuing. Sometimes she warned us, “More to the left”; or, “Faster!” We had to put forth our best, for Manuel, as if in the very wantonness of confidence, had set a tremendous pace.
I suppose he took his first direction by the light on the point. I cannot tell what guided him after that feeble sheen had become buried in the fog; but there was no check in the speed, no sign of hesitation. We followed in the track of the sound, and, for the most part, kept in sight of the elusive shadow of the sternmost boat. Often, in a denser belt of fog, the sounds of rowing became muffled almost to extinction; or we seemed to hear them all round and, startled, checked our speed. Dark apparitions of boats would surge up on all sides in a most inexplicable way; to the right; to the left; even coming from behind. They appeared real, unmistakable, and, before we had time to dodge them, vanished utterly.

===Chinese===

我还没能定下神来——说来奇怪，这念头直到那时才来——曼努埃尔一声呼哨，领头出发了。

我们总是宁信眼睛不信耳朵；而我们接受感官印象的惯常心境又那样，我竟不知道他们离我们这样近。我那虚幻的距离感被摧毁，是世上最骇人的事。仿佛转瞬之间，随着第二记荡桨，那些船已压到我们身上。它们擦了过去。像被一场滚落的岩石擦身。我仿佛觉出了那股冲的风。

急促的划桨声、兴奋的人语声、猛烈的水的骚动，以一种夺走我呼吸的猛劲从我们身旁掠过。它们是成堆出发的。他们中间起码有一船黑人，因为有谁灵巧地敲着一只铃鼓，桨手们气喘吁吁地齐声低唱：“嗬，嗬，塔利班波……嗬，嗬，塔利班波（*Ho, ho, talibambo*）。”其中一条船显现了一瞬剪影，一排脑袋前后摇晃，船尾上方高耸着一个笔直如箭的全身人像。一个远去的声音雷鸣般喝道：“肃静！”声响和形影一齐以惊人的迅疾淡入雾中。

塞拉菲娜斗篷卸了，头露着，朝我们追踪的那飞逝的低语和影子瞪望。时时她警告我们：“再偏左些”；或者：“快些！”我们得使出全力，因为曼努埃尔仿佛出于自信的放纵，定下了惊人的速度。

我想他起初是凭岬上的灯光定向。那点微光没进雾裡之后，什么在给他引路，我说不上；可速度不见停顿，不见犹豫。我们循着声响的航迹，大半时候望得见末尾那条船那飘忽的影。常常，在一带更浓的雾裡，划桨声闷得几乎消逝；或者我们仿佛四面都听见它们，一惊，收了速。船的黑影会以最不可解的方式四面涌起；在右；在左；甚至从后面来。它们显得真切、确凿，不等我们闪避，又全然消散。

===Original===

Then we had to spurt desperately after the grind of the oars, caught, just in time, in an unexpected direction.
And then we lost them. We pulled frantically. Seraphina had been urging us, “Faster! faster!” From time to time I would ask her, “Can you see them?” “Not yet,” she answered curtly. The perspiration poured down my face. Castro’s panting was like the wheezing of bellows at my back. Suddenly, in a despairing tone, she said:
“Stop! I can neither see nor hear anything now.”
We feathered our oars at once, and fell to listening with lowered heads. The ripple of the boat’s way expired slowly. A great white stillness hung slumbrously over the sea.
It was inconceivable. We pulled once or twice with extreme energy for a few minutes after imaginary whistles or shouts. Once I heard them passing our bows. But it was useless; we stopped, and the moon, from within the mistiness of an immense halo, looked dreamily upon our heads.
Castro grunted, “Here is an end of your plan, Señor Don Juan.”
The peculiar and ghastly hopelessness of our position could not be better illustrated than by this fresh difficulty. We had lost touch﻿—with a murderous gang that had every inducement not to spare our lives. And positively it was a misfortune; an abandonment. I refused to admit to myself its finality, as if it had reflected upon the devotion of tried friends. I repeated to Castro that we should become aware of them directly﻿—probably even nearer than we wished. And, at any rate, we were certain of a mighty loud noise when the attack on the ship began. She, at least, could not be very far now. “Unless, indeed,” I admitted with exasperation, “we are to suppose that your imbecile Lugareños have missed their prey and got themselves as utterly lost as we ourselves.”
I was irritated﻿—by his nodding plume; by his cold, perfunctory, as if sleepy mutters, “Possibly, possibly, *puede ser*.” He retorted: “Your English generosity could wish your countrymen no better luck than that my Lugareños, as your worship pleases to call them, should miss their way. They are hungry for loot﻿—with much fasting. And it is hunger that makes your wolf fly straight at the throat.”
All the time Seraphina breathed no word. But when I raised my voice, she put out a hushing hand to my arm. And, from her intent pose, from the turn of her shadowy head, I knew that she was peering and listening loyally.

===Chinese===

于是我们只得朝某个意外方向裡刚刚捕捉到的桨声绝望地猛冲。

随后我们丢了他们。我们狂乱地划。塞拉菲娜一直催着：“快！快！”我不时问她：“能看见吗？”“还看不见，”她简短地答。汗淌下我的脸。卡斯特罗的喘息像背后风箱的嘶鸣。忽然，她用一种绝望的声调说：

“停！我现在既看不见也听不见了。”

我们立刻平桨，垂头听。船行的涟纹慢慢止息。一片巨大的白寂困倦地罩在海上。

这难以置信。我们朝想象中的呼哨或喊声，一两回极其用力地划了几分钟。有一回我听见它们从我们船头旁边过。可没有用；我们停了，月亮，从一圈巨大光晕的雾霭裡，梦一样照着我们的头。

卡斯特罗哼道：“您的计划到头了，胡安先生。”

我们处境那特有的阴惨的无望，再没有比这个新困难说明得更好的了。我们失了联络——同一帮有一切理由不留我们活口的杀人匪帮。而这竟真是不幸；一场被弃。我拒不向自己承认它的终结，仿佛它折射了患难之交的忠诚。我向卡斯特罗反复说，我们立刻就会再觉察到他们——多半比我们希望的还近。再说，无论如何，对那条船的进攻一开始，我们准能听见一场大响。她，至少，此刻不会很远了。“除非，”我恼火地承认，“我们要假定你那些低能的村民错过了他们的猎物，迷失得同我们自己一样彻底。”

我被惹恼——为他那点头的羽翎；为他那冷淡的、敷衍的、仿佛瞌睡的咕哝，“也许，也许，可能（*puede ser*）”。他反唇相讥：“你们的英国宽宏，不能再给贵同胞更好的运气了，除了盼着我那些村民——随老爷怎么称呼他们——迷路。他们饿着赃物呢——斋戒了这么久。而正饥饿，使狼直扑喉咙。”

塞拉菲娜自始至终一言不发。可我一抬高嗓门，她就伸出一只噤声的手到我臂上。而从她专注的姿势、她那朦胧的头颅的转向，我知道她在忠诚地瞭望和倾听。

===Original===

Minutes passed﻿—very few, I dare say﻿—and brought no sound. The restlessness of waiting made us dip our oars in a haphazard stroke, without aim, without the means of judging whether we pulled to seaward, inshore, north, or south, or only in a circle. Once we went excitedly in chase of some splashing that must have been a leaping fish. I was hanging my head over my idle oar when Seraphina touched me.
“I see!” she said, pointing over the bows.
Both Castro and I, peering horizontally over the water, did not see anything. Not a shadow. Moreover, if they were so near, we ought to have heard something.
“I believe it is land!” she murmured. “You are looking too low, Juan.”
As soon as I looked up I saw it, too, dark and beetling, like the overhang of a low cliff. Where on earth had we blundered to? For a moment I was confounded. Fiery reflections from a light played faintly above that shape. Then I recognized what I was looking at. We had found the ship.
The fog was so shallow that up there the upper bulk of a heavy, square stern, the very rails and stanchions crowning it like a balustrade, jutted out in the misty sheen like the balcony of an invisible edifice, for the lines of her run, the sides of her hull, were plunged in the dense white layer below. And, throwing back my head, I traced even her becalmed sails, pearly gray pinnacles of shadow uprising, tall and motionless, towards the moon.
A redness wavered over her, as from a blaze on her deck. Could she be on fire? And she was silent as a tomb. Could she be abandoned? I had promised myself to dash alongside, but there was a weirdness in that fragment of a dumb ship hanging out of a fog. We pulled only a stroke or two nearer to the stern, and stopped. I remembered Castro’s warning﻿—the blindness of flying lead; but it was the profound stillness that checked me. It seemed to portend something inconceivable. I hailed, tentatively, as if I had not expected to be answered, “Ship, ahoy!”
Neither was I answered by the instantaneous, “Hallo,” of usual watchfulness, though she was not abandoned. Indeed, my hail made a good many men jump, to judge by the sounds and the words that came to me from above. “What? What? A hail?” “Boat near?” “In English, sir.”
“Dive for the captain, one of you,” an authoritative voice directed. “He’s just run below for a minute. Don’t frighten the missus. Call him out quietly.”

===Chinese===

几分钟过去——我想，很少几钟——没有带来声响。等待的不安使我们胡乱下了桨，无的放矢地划着，无从判断我们划向海侧还是岸侧，向北还是向南，或只是在兜圈子。有一回我们激动地追了一阵什么溅水声，必定是一条跳起的鱼。我正垂头闲桨上，塞拉菲娜碰了碰我。

“我看见了！”她说，指着船头外。

卡斯特罗和我，平贴着水面瞭望，什么也没看见。一点影子也没有。况且，他们若这样近，我们本该听见点什么。

“我相信那是陆地！”她喃喃。“你望得太低了，胡安。”

我一抬头，也看见了，黑沉沉地探出，像一道低崖的悬岩。我们到底瞎闯到哪兒了？有一阵我懵了。一点灯火的红光在那形状上方微微摇曳。随后我认出了我看的是什么。我们找到那条船了。

雾这样浅，上头，一个沉重的方形船尾的上半截，连栏杆和栏柱，像一排女墙冠在上面，从雾光裡探出，像一座看不见的大厦的阳台，因为它的船体线条、它的两舷，都浸在下面浓白的一层裡。而我仰起头，连它那困于无风的帆也认了出来，珍珠灰的尖顶般的影子向上耸起，高而静止，朝着月亮。

一片红光在它上面摇曳，像甲板上有一炉火。它着火了吗？而它寂静如墓。它被弃了吗？我本打算猛地靠上去，可那截悬在雾外的哑船有一种怪异。我们只朝船尾多划了一两桨，停住。我想起卡斯特罗的警告——飞铅无眼；可止住我的是那深深的寂静。它仿佛预示着什么不可思议的事。我试探着招呼，仿佛没指望有人应：“船上的！”

也没有得到惯常警觉的当即一声“哈罗”，虽然它并未被弃。确实，从上头传到我这里的声音和话语判断，我这一喊叫好些人跳了起来。“什么？什么？有人喊？”“船在近旁？”“是英语，先生。”

“你们一个去叫船长，”一个权威的声音吩咐。“他刚下舱一分钟。别吓着太太。轻声叫他出来。”

===Original===

Talking, in confidential undertones, followed.
“See him?” “Can’t, sir.” “What’s the dodge, I wonder.” “Astern, I think, sir.” “D﻿—﻿—﻿n this fog, it lies as thick as pea-soup on the water.”
I waited, and after a perplexed sort of pause, heard a stern “Keep off.”

===Chinese===

随后是压低的私语。

“看见他了吗？”“看不见，先生。”“玩的什么花样，我纳闷。”“在船尾，我想，先生。”“这该死的雾，像豌豆汤一样厚厚趴在水上。”

我等着，一段困惑的停顿之后，听见一声严厉的“别过来”。

### III / 三
===Original===

They did not suspect how close I was to them. And their temper struck me at once as unsafe. They seemed very much on the alert, and, as I imagined, disposed to precipitate action. I called out, deadening my voice warily:
“I am an Englishman, escaping from the pirates here. We want your help.”
To this no answer was made, but by that time the captain had come on deck. The dinghy must have drifted in a little closer, for I made out behind the shadowy rail one, two, three figures in a row, looming bulkily above my head, as men appear enlarged in mist.
“ ‘Englishman,’ he says.” “That’s very likely,” pronounced a new voice. They held a hurried consultation up there, of which I caught only detached sentences, and the general tone of concern. “It’s perfectly well known that there *is* an Englishman here.﻿ ﻿… Aye, a runaway second mate.﻿ ﻿… Killed a man in a Bristol ship.﻿ ﻿… What was his name, now?”
“Won’t you answer me?” I called out.
“Aye, we will answer you as soon as we see you.﻿ ﻿… Keep your eyes skinned fore and aft on deck there.﻿ ﻿… Ready, boys?”
“All ready, sir”; voices came from further off.
“Listen to me,” I entreated.
Someone called out briskly, “This is a bad place for pretty tales of Englishmen in distress. We know very well where we are.”
“You are off Rio Medio,” I began anxiously; “and I﻿—”
“Speaks the truth like a Briton, anyhow,” commented a lazy drawl.
“I would send another man to the pump,” a reflective voice suggested. “To make sure of the force, Mr. Sebright, you know.”
“Certainly, sir.﻿ ﻿… Another hand to the brakes, bo’sun.”
“I have been held captive on shore,” I said. “I escaped this evening, three hours ago.”
“And found this ship in the fog? You made a good shot at it, didn’t you?”
“It’s no time for trifling, I swear to you,” I continued. “They are out looking for you, in force. I’ve heard them. I was with them when they started.”
“I believe you.”
“They seem to have missed the ship.”
“So you came to have a friendly chat meantime. That’s kind. Beastly weather, aint it?”
“I want to come aboard,” I shouted. “You must be crazy not to believe me.”
“But we do believe every single word you say,” bantered the Sebright voice with serenity.
Suddenly another struck in, “Nichols, I call to mind, sir.”
“Of course, of course. This is the man.”
“My name’s not Nichols,” I protested.
“Now, now. You mustn’t begin to lie,” remonstrated Sebright.

===Chinese===

他们不怀疑我离他们多近。而他们的脾气我一听就觉得不妙。他们非常警觉，而且，如我想象的，倾向于立即动手。我小心翼翼压着嗓门喊：

“我是英国人，从这儿的海盗手裡逃出来的。我们需要你们的帮助。”

对此无人作答，可那时船长已上了甲板。小艇必定又漂近了些，因为我在朦胧的栏杆后辨出了一、二、三个人影一排，庞然耸立在我头顶上方，正如人在雾中显得放大。

“‘英国人’，他说。”“那很可能，”一个新声音断言。他们在上头匆匆商议，我只听到零散的句子，和总体的忧虑腔调。“这儿有个英国人，这是众所周知的。……是啊，一个逃跑的二副。……在一条布裡斯托尔的船上杀过人。……他叫什么来着？”

“你们不回答我吗？”我喊。

“啊，我们一见你就会回答你。……甲板上前后都给我盯紧了。……准备好了吗，伙计们？”

“都好了，先生”；声音从更远处传来。

“听我说，”我恳求。

有人干脆地喊：“这地方不适合英国落难人的漂亮故事。我们很清楚自己在哪兒。”

“你们在裡奥梅迪奥（Rio Medio）外海，”我焦急地开口；“而我——”

“不管怎样，说话像个英国人，”一条懒洋洋的拖腔评论。

“我要再派一个人去泵那儿，”一个沉思的声音建议。“为保险起见，希布赖特（Sebright）先生，您知道。”

“当然，先生。……再派一个上手压杆，水手长。”

“我被扣在岸上，”我说。“今晚逃出来的，三个钟头前。”

“然后在雾裡找到了这条船？你瞄得挺准，是不是？”

“我发誓不是开玩笑的时候，”我接着说。“他们正倾巢出动找你们。我听见的。他们出发时我就在他们中间。”

“我相信你。”

“他们似乎错过了这条船。”

“于是你先来聊个天。真客气。天气糟透了，是不是？”

“我要上船，”我喊。“你们不信我，准是疯了。”

“可你说的每一个字我们都信呐，”希布赖特的声音安详地打趣。

忽然另一个人插进来：“尼科尔斯（Nichols），我想起来了，先生。”

“当然，当然。就是这人。”

“我不叫尼科尔斯，”我抗议。

“嗳，嗳。不许开始撒谎，”希布赖特告诫。

===Original===

Somebody laughed discreetly.
“You are mistaken, on my honour,” I said. “Nichols left Rio Medio some time ago.”
“About three hours, eh?” came the drawl of insufferable folly in these precious minutes.
It was clear that Manuel had gone astray, but I feared not for long. They would spread out in search. And now I had found this hopeless ship, it seemed impossible that anybody else could miss her.
“You may be boarded any moment by more than a dozen boats. I warn you solemnly. Will you let me come?”
A low whistle was heard on board. They were impressed, “Why should he tell us this?” an undertone inquired.
“Why the devil shouldn’t he? It’s no great news, is it? Some scoundrelly trick. This man’s up to any dodge. Why, the *Jane* was taken in broad day by two boats that pretended they were going to sell vegetables.”
“Look out, or by heavens you’ll be taken by surprise. There’s a lot of them,” I said as impressively as I could.
“Look out, look out. There’s a lot of them,” someone yelled in a sort of panic.
“Oh, that’s your game,” Sebright’s voice said to me. “Frighten us, eh? Never you mind what this skunk says, men. Stand fast. We shall take a lot of killing.” He was answered by a sort of pugnacious uproar, a clash of cutlasses and laughter, as if at some joke.
“That’s right, boys; mind and send them away with clean faces, you gunners. Jack, you keep a good lookout for that poor distressed Englishman. What’s that? a noise in the fog? Stand by. Now then, cook!﻿ ﻿…”
“All ready to dish up, sir,” a voice answered him.
It was like a sort of madness. Were they thinking of eating? Even at that the English talk made my heart expand﻿—the homeliness of it. I seemed to know all their voices, as if I had talked to each man before. It brought back memories, like the voices of friends.
But there was the strange irrelevancy, levity, the enmity﻿—the irrational, baffling nature of the anguishing conversation, as if with the unapproachable men we meet in nightmares.
We in the dinghy, as well as those on board, were listening anxiously. A profound silence reigned for a time.
“I don’t care for myself,” I tried once more, speaking distinctly. “But a lady in the boat here is in great danger, too. Won’t you do something for a woman?”
I perceived, from the sort of stir on board, that this caused some sensation.
“Or is the whole ship’s company afraid to let one little boat come alongside?”

船上响起一声低低的呼哨。他们被打动了。“他为什么要告诉我们这个？”一个低音问。
