The wind stirred slightly her delicate hair, and I looked at her; I looked at her stilled, as one watches the dawn or listens to a sweet strain of music caught from afar. Suddenly dropping Mrs. Williams’ hand, I ran to her.﻿ ﻿…
When I turned round, Williams had joined his wife, and she had slipped her arm under his. Her hand, thin and white, looked like the hand of an invalid on the brawny forearm of that man bursting with health and good condition. By the side of his lustiness, she was almost ethereal﻿—and yet I seemed to see in them something they had in common﻿—something subtle, like the expression of eyes. It *was* the expression of their eyes. They looked at us with commiseration; one of them sweetly, the other with his owlish fixity. As we two, Seraphina and I, approached them together, I heard Williams’ thick, sleepy voice asking, “And so he says he won’t?” To which his wife, raising her tone with a shade of indignation, answered, “Of course not.” No, I was not mistaken. In their dissimilar persons, eyes, faces, there was expressed a common trouble, doubt, and commiseration. This expression seemed to go out to meet us sadly, like a bearer of ill-news. And, as if at the sight of a downcast messenger, I experienced the clear presentiment of some fatal intelligence.
It was conveyed to me late in the afternoon of that same day out of Williams own thick lips, that seemed as heavy and inert as his voice.
“As far as we can see,” he said, “you can’t stay in the ship, Kemp. It would do no one any good﻿—not the slightest good. Ask Sebright here.”
It was a sort of council of war, to which we had been summoned in the saloon. Mrs. Williams had some sewing in her lap. She listened, her hands motionless, her eyes full of desolation. Seraphina’s attitude, leaning her cheek on her hand, reminded me of the time when I had seen her absorbed in watching the green-and-gold lizard in the back room of Ramon’s store, with her hair falling about her face like a veil. Castro was not called in till later on. But Sebright was there, leaning his back negligently against the bulkhead behind Williams, and looking down on us seated on both sides of the long table. And there was present, too, in all our minds, the image of the Rio Medio schooner, hull down on our quarter. In all the trials of sailing, we had not been able to shake her off that day.

等我回过头，威廉斯已站到妻子身边，她的手臂已挽进他的臂弯。她那只手，又白又瘦，搭在那个浑身健壮迸发的男人的粗壮前臂上，像一只病弱之人的手。同他的壮实一比，她几乎飘渺——可我又仿佛看见他们身上有什么共通的东西——某种微妙的，像眼神一样的东西。那*正是*他们眼神里的东西。他们怜悯地望着我们；一个望得温柔，一个瞪着猫头鹰似的专注。当塞拉菲娜和我一同走近他们时，我听见威廉斯那又粗又瞌睡的嗓子在问：“这么说，他不肯？”他的妻子提高嗓音，带一点忿意，答：“当然不肯。”是的，我没有听错。在他们迥异的身形、眼睛、面孔上，写着同一种忧心、疑虑和怜悯。这表情仿佛迎着我们悲哀地走来，像一名报凶信的使者。而像人望见垂头的信使那样，我清清楚楚地预感到某种噩耗。
它就在当天傍晚较晚的时辰，从威廉斯本人那两片厚嘴唇里传给了我；那嘴唇同他的嗓音一样沉重呆滞。
“依我们看，”他说，“你不能再待在船上了，肯普。对谁都没好处——丝毫无好处。问这儿的希布赖特。”
这是餐厅里召集的一场类似军事会议的会。威廉斯太太膝上摊着针线。她听着，两手不动，眼里盛满凄凉。塞拉菲娜一手托腮的姿态，叫我想起从前在拉蒙铺子后屋里见她看那只绿金蜥蜴出神的样子，头发像面纱一样垂在脸旁。卡斯特罗到晚些才被叫进来。但希布赖特在场，散漫地把背靠在威廉斯身后的舱壁上，俯视着长桌两侧坐着的我们。而在我们所有人的心里，还坐着一个影子：那条里奥梅迪奥的双桅船，在我们尾后只剩桅顶。这一天任凭怎样变着法子驶，我们都没能甩脱她。

“I don’t want to hide from you, Mr. Kemp,” Sebright began, “that it was I who pointed out to the captain that you would be only getting the ship in trouble for nothing. She’s an old trader and favourite with shippers; and if we once get to loggerheads with the powers, there’s an end of her trading. As to missing Havana this trip, even if you, Mr. Kemp, could give a pot of money, the captain could never show his nose in there again after breaking his charter-party to help steal a young lady. And it isn’t as if she were nobody. She’s the richest heiress in the island. The biggest people in Spain would have their say in this matter. I suppose they could put the captain in prison or something. Anyway, goodbye to the Havana business for good. Why, old Perkins would have a fit. He got over one runaway match.﻿ ﻿… All right, Mrs. Williams, not another word.﻿ ﻿… What I meant to say is that this is nothing else but a love story, and to knock on the head a valuable old-established connection for it.﻿ ﻿… Don’t bite your lip, Mr. Kemp. I mean no disrespect to your feelings. Perkins would start up to break things﻿—let alone his heart. I am sure the captain and Mrs. Williams think so, too.”
The festive and subdued captain of the *Lion* was staring straight before him, as if stuffed. Mrs. Williams moved her fingers, compressed her lips, and looked helplessly at all of us in turn. “Besides altering his will,” Sebright breathed confidentially at the back of my head. I perceived that this old Perkins, whom I had never seen, and was never to see in the body, whose body no one was ever to see any more (he died suddenly on the echoing staircase, with a flat candlestick in his hand; was already dead at the time, so that Mrs. Williams was actually sitting in the cabin of her very own ship)﻿—I perceived that old Perkins was present at this discussion with all the power of a malignant, bad-tempered spirit. Those two were afraid of him. They had defied him once, it is true﻿—but even that had been done out of fear, as it were.
Dismayed, I spoke quickly to Seraphina. With her head resting on her hand, and her eyes following the aimless tracings of her finger on the table, she said:
“It shall be as God wills it, Juan.”
“For Heaven’s sake, don’t!” said Sebright, coughing behind me. He understood Spanish fairly well. “What I’ve said is perfectly true.

Nevertheless the captain was ready to risk it.”
“Yes,” ejaculated Williams profoundly, out of almost still lips, and otherwise so motionless all over that the deep sound seemed to have been produced by some person under the table. Mrs. Williams’ fingers were clasped on her lap, and her eyes seemed to beg for belief all round our faces.
“But the point is that it would have been no earthly good for you two,” continued Sebright. “That’s the point I made. If O’Brien knows anything, he knows you are on board this ship. He reckons on it as a dead certainty. Now, it is very evident that we could refuse to give *you* up, Mr. Kemp, and that the admiral (if the flagship’s off Havana, as I think she must be by now) would have to back us up. How you would get on afterwards with old Groggy Rowley, I don’t know. It isn’t likely he has forgotten you tried to wipe the floor with him, if I am to take the captain’s yarn as correct.”
“A regular hero,” Williams testified suddenly, in his concealed, from-under-the-table tone. “He’s not afraid of any of them; not he. Ha! ha! Old Topnambo must have.﻿ ﻿…” He glanced at his wife, and bit his tongue﻿—perhaps at the recollection of his unsafe conjugal position﻿—ending in disjointed words, “In his chaise﻿—warrant﻿—separationist﻿—rebel,” and all this without moving a limb or a muscle of his face, till, with a low, throaty chuckle, he fluttered a stony sort of wink to my address.
Sebright had paused only long enough for this ebullition to be over. The cool logic of his surmise appalled me. He didn’t see why O’Brien or anybody in Havana should want to interfere with me personally. But if I wanted to keep my young lady, it was obvious she must not arrive in Havana on board a ship where they would be sure to look for her the very first thing. It was even worse than it looked, he declared. His firm conviction was that if the *Lion* did not turn up in Havana pretty soon, there would be a Spanish man-of-war sent out to look for her﻿—or else Mr. O’Brien was not the man we took him for. There was lying in harbour a corvette called the *Tornado*, a very likely looking craft. I didn’t expect them to fight a corvette. No doubt there would be a fuss made about stopping a British ship on the high seas; but that would be a cold comfort after the lady had been taken away from me.

希布赖特只停到这一阵发作过去。他那套推断的冷静逻辑叫我胆寒。他不明白奥布赖恩或哈瓦那的什么人为什么要来同我个人过不去。可我若想留住我的小姐，那么明摆着，她绝不能坐在一条船上进哈瓦那——人家上那儿头一件事就是搜这条船。照他看，事情比表面还糟，他说。他斩钉截铁地相信：狮子号要是不赶紧在哈瓦那露面，就会有一条西班牙军舰开出来找她——不然，奥布赖恩先生就不是我们认定的那个人了。港里正泊着一条叫托纳多号的巡航舰，一条看着顶利落的船。我没指望他们去同巡航舰打仗。在公海上拦一条英国船，无疑要闹一场风波；可等人家把小姐从我身边带走之后，那点风波不过是冷安慰。

She was a person of so much importance that even our own admiral could be induced﻿—say, by the Captain-General’s remonstrances﻿—to sanction such an action. There was no saying what Rowley would do if they only promised to present him with half a dozen pirates to take home for a hanging. Why! that was the very identical thing the flagship was kept dodging off Havana for! And O’Brien knew where to lay his hands on a gross of such birds, for that matter.
“No,” concluded Sebright, overwhelming me from behind, as I sat looking, not at the uncertainties of the future, but at the paralyzing hopelessness of the bare tomorrow. “The *Lion* is no place for you, whether she goes into Havana or not. Moreover, into Havana she must go now. There’s no help for it. It’s the deuce of a situation.”
“Very well,” I gasped. I tried to be resolute. I felt, suddenly, as if all the air in the cabin had gone up the open skylight. I couldn’t remain below another moment; and, muttering something about coming back directly, I jumped up and ran out without looking at anyone lest I should give myself away. I ran out on deck for air, but the great blue emptiness of the open staggered me like a blow over the heart. I walked slowly to the side, and, planting both my elbows on the rail, stared abroad defiantly and without a single clear thought in my head. I had a vague feeling that the descent of the sun towards the waters, going on before my eyes with changes of light and cloud, was like some gorgeous and empty ceremonial of immersion belonging to a vast barren faith remote from consolation and hope. And I noticed, also, small things without importance﻿—the hirsute aspect of a sailor; the end of a rope trailing overboard; and Castro, so different from everybody else on board that his appearance seemed to create a profound solitude round him, lounging before the cabin door as if engaged in a deep conspiracy all by himself. I heard voices talking loudly behind me, too.
I noted them distinctly, but with perfect indifference. A long time after, with the same indifference, I looked over my shoulder. Castro had vanished from the quarterdeck. And I turned my face to the sea again as a man, feeling himself beaten in a fight with death, might turn his face to the wall.

“不行，”希布赖特下结论，从我背后压过来——我坐在那里，望着的不是未来的种种不定，而是光秃秃的明天那叫人瘫软的无望。“狮子号不是您的安身之处，进不进哈瓦那都一样。再说，她如今非进哈瓦那不可。没有别的法子。这局面真是糟透了。”
“很好，”我喘着气说。我努力拿出决断。忽然，我觉得舱里的空气全从开着的天窗跑了，一秒也待不下去；咕哝了一句马上回来，便跳起身跑了出去，谁也不看，生怕露了馅。我跑上甲板透气，可海上那片浩大的蓝色空虚，像当胸给了我一拳，打得我趔趄。我慢慢走到船边，两肘往栏杆上一架，挑衅地瞪向四外，脑子里没有一个清晰的念头。我模糊地觉得，眼前那太阳向水面沉落的过程，随着光与云的变幻，像一场华丽而空洞的浸礼，属于一个远离安慰与希望的浩大荒凉的信仰。我还留意到一些无关紧要的小事——一个水手的毛发；一段拖出舷外的绳头；还有卡斯特罗，他同船上谁都两样，那副模样仿佛在自身周围造出一片深寂，闲闲地立在舱门前，像独自一人经营着一桩深谋。我还听见身后有人大声说话。
我听得清清楚楚，却全然无动于衷。过了好一阵，我带着同样的无动于衷回头望了一眼。卡斯特罗已从尾楼消失。我重新把脸转向大海，像一个自觉败给了死亡的人，把脸转向墙壁。

===Original===

I had fought a harder battle with a more cruel foe than death, with the doubt of myself; an endless contest, in which there is no peace of victory or of defeat. The open sea was like a blank and unscalable wall imprisoning the eternal question of conduct. Right or wrong? Generosity or folly? Conscience or only weak fear before remorse? The magnificent ritual of sunset went on palpitating with an inaudible rhythm, with slow and unerring observance, went on to the end, leaving its funeral fires on the sky and a great shadow upon the sea. Twice I had honourably stayed my hand. Twice﻿ ﻿… to this end.
In a moment, I went through all the agonies of suicide, which left me alive, alas, to burn with the shame of the treasonable thought, and terrified by the revolt of my soul refusing to leave the world in which a young girl lived! The vast twilight seemed to take the impress of her image like wax. What did Seraphina think of me? I knew nothing of her but her features, and it was enough. Strange, this power of a woman’s face upon a man’s heart﻿—this mastery, potent as witchcraft and mysterious like a miracle. I should have to go and tell her. I did not suppose she could have understood all of Sebright’s argumentation. Therefore, it was for me to explain to what a pretty pass I had brought our love.
I was so greatly disinclined to stir that I let Sebright’s voice go on calling my name half a dozen times from the cabin door. At last I faced about.
“Mr. Kemp! I say, Kemp! Aren’t you coming in yet?”
“To say goodbye,” I said, approaching him.
It had fallen dark already.
“Goodbye? No. The carpenter must have a day at least.”
Carpenter! What had a carpenter to do in this? However, nothing mattered﻿—as though I had managed to spoil the whole scheme of creation.
“You didn’t think of making a start tonight, did you?” Sebright wondered. “Where would be the sense of it?”
“Sense,” I answered contemptuously. “There is no sense in anything. There is necessity. Necessity.”
He remained silent for a time, peering at me.
“Necessity, to be sure,” he said slowly. “And I don’t see why you should be angry at it.”
I was thinking that it was easy enough for him to keep cool﻿—the necessity being mine. He continued to philosophize with what seemed to me a shocking freedom of mind.
“Must try to put some sense into it. That’s what we are here for, I guess.

我刚打完一场比死亡更艰苦的仗，对手比死亡更残酷：那便是对自己的怀疑；一场无休止的较量，没有胜利的安宁，也没有失败的安宁。开阔的海面像一堵空白而不可攀越的墙，囚着那个永恒的诘问：行止之问。对还是错？是慷慨还是愚蠢？是良知，还是仅仅是悔恨前头的软弱？日落的壮丽祭仪，以听不见的节律搏动着，以迟缓而分毫不差的仪轨，一路行到尽头，把葬礼的火留在天上，把一大片影子留在海上。两次，我体面地缩回了手。两次……落到这般下场。
一瞬之间，我尝遍了自杀的种种苦楚，可它偏留我活着，唉，叫我被这叛逆念头的羞耻烧灼，又惊恐于我灵魂的造反——它不肯离开这个有一位少女活着的人世！浩大的暮色，像蜡一样印上了她的容貌。塞拉菲娜怎么看我？我对她一无所知，只有她的眉目，而这已尽够。奇怪啊，一个女人的脸对男人心的这份权力——这份统驭，灵验如巫术，神秘如奇迹。我得去告诉她。我不信她能听懂希布赖特的全部推论。所以，该由我去解释，我把我们的爱情带到了怎样一个田地。
我懒得挪步到那个地步，任凭希布赖特的声音在舱门口喊了我半打遍名字。末了我转过身。
“肯普先生！喂，肯普！还不进来吗？”
“来道个别，”我说着走近他。
天已经黑了。
“道别？不。木匠总得干上一天。”
木匠！木匠同这有什么相干？也罢，什么都无所谓了——仿佛我已把造化的整个盘算都搅黄了。
“您总不至于想今夜就动身吧？”希布赖特纳罕道。“那有什么道理？”
“道理，”我轻蔑地答。“天下事没有道理，只有必要。必要。”
他沉默了一阵，端详我。
“必要，可不，”他慢慢说。“可我不明白您为它生什么气。”
我心想，他当然凉快——必要的又不是他。他接着发他的哲理，那份心思的自由，在我看来放肆得吓人。
“总得想法子往里搁点道理。咱们活在世上，大约就为的这个。

===Original===

Anyhow, there’s some room for sense in arranging the way a thing is to be done, be it as hard as it may. And I don’t see any sense, either, in exposing a woman to more hardship than is absolutely necessary. We have talked it out now, and I can do no more. Do go inside for a bit. Mrs. Williams is worrying the Señorita, rather, I’m afraid.”
I paused a moment to try and regain the command of my faculties. But it was as if a bombshell had exploded inside my skull, scattering all my wits to the four winds of heaven. Only the conviction of failure remained, attended by a profound distress.
I fancy, though, I presented a fairly bold front. The lamp was lit, and small changes had occurred during my absence. Williams had turned his bulk sideways to the table. Mrs. Williams had risen from her place, and was now sitting upright close to Seraphina, holding one little hand enclosed caressingly between her frail palms, as if she had there something alive that needed cherishing. And in that position she looked up at me with a strange air of worn-out youth, cast by a rosy flush over her forehead and face. Seraphina still leaned her head on her other hand, and I noted, through the soft shadow of falling hair, the heightened colour on her cheek and the augmented brilliance of her eye.
“How I wish she had been an English girl,” Mrs. Williams sighed regretfully, and leaned forward to look into Seraphina’s half-averted face.
“My dear, did you quite, quite understand what I have been saying to you?”
She waited.
“*Si Señora*,” said Seraphina. None of us moved. Then, after a time, turning to me with sudden animation, “This woman asked me if I believed in your love,” she cried. “She is old. Oh, Juan, can the years change the heart? your heart?” Her voice dropped. “How am I to know that?” she went on piteously. “I am young﻿—and we may not live so long. I believe in mine.﻿ ﻿…”
The corners of her delicate lips drooped; but she mastered her desire to cry, and steadied her voice which, always rich and full of womanly charm, took on, when she was deeply moved, an imposing gravity of timbre.
“But I am a Spaniard, and I believe in my lover’s honour; in your﻿—your English honour, Juan.”
With the dignity of a supreme confidence she extended her hand. It was one of the culminating moments of our love.

===Chinese===

不管怎样，一件事怎么个做法，里头总还容得下道理，事再难也一样。再说，我也看不出有什么道理，叫一个女人去受绝对必要的苦楚以外的更多苦。现在我们把话都说尽了，我无能为力了。进去待一会儿吧。威廉斯太太怕是把小姐缠得有些烦了。”
我停了一停，想收回对我神志的指挥权。可这好比一颗炮弹在我头盖骨里炸了开来，把我浑身的神志崩上四面天风。只剩失败的确认还在，拖着一 profound 的苦痛。
不过我想，我撑的还算一副硬朗门面。灯点上了；我不在的当儿起了些小变化。威廉斯把大块身子侧对桌子转了过来。威廉斯太太已离座起身，紧挨着塞拉菲娜端坐，把那只小手娇怜地拢在她纤弱的双掌之间，仿佛掌心里护着一件活物。她就这样仰起脸望我，带着一种奇异的、韶华耗尽的少年气，是扑在前额和脸上的玫瑰色晕染出来的。塞拉菲娜依旧另一只手托着头；透过垂发的柔影，我看见她颊上加了颜色的红、眼中添了亮度的光。
“我多希望她是个英国姑娘，”威廉斯太太惋惜地叹道，欠身去看塞拉菲娜半偏的脸。
“亲爱的，我方才对您说的话，您完完全全明白了吗？”
她等着。
“是，夫人，”塞拉菲娜说。我们谁都没动。过了一会儿，她转向我，忽然生动起来：“这个女人问我，信不信你的爱，”她喊道。“她老了。哦，胡安，岁月能改变心吗？你的心？”她的声音低下去。“我怎么知道呢？”她凄然接着说。“我年轻——而我们未必活得那么久。我信我自己的。……”
她纤秀的唇角垂下来；可她按住了哭意，稳住了嗓音——那嗓音本就丰满而富于女性的魅力，每遇深深动情，便添上一重庄重的音色。
“可我是西班牙人，我信我爱人的荣誉；信你的——你那英国人的荣誉，胡安。”
她以至高信赖的尊严伸出手来。那是我们爱情登峰造极的时刻之一。

===Original===

For love is like a journey in mountainous country, up through the clouds, and down into the shadows to an unknown destination. It was a moment rapt and full of feeling, in which we seemed to dwell together high up and alone﻿—till she withdrew her hand from my lips, and I found myself back in the cabin, as if precipitated from a lofty place.
Nobody was looking at us. Mrs. Williams sat with downcast eyelids, with her hands reposing on her lap: her husband gazed discreetly at a gold moulding on the deck-beam; and the upward cast of his eyes invested his red face with an air of singularly imbecile ecstasy. And there was Castro, too, whom I had not seen till then, though I must have brushed against him on entering. He had stood by the door a mute, and, as it were, a voluntarily unmasked conspirator with the black round of the hat lying in front of his feet. He, alone, looked at us. He looked from Seraphina to me﻿—from me to Seraphina. He looked unutterable things, rolling his crow-footed eyes in pious horror and glowering in turns. When Seraphina addressed him, he hastened to incline his head with his usual deference for the daughter of the Riegos.
She said, “There are things that concern this caballero, and that you can never understand. Your fidelity is proved. It has sunk deep here.﻿ ﻿… It shall give you a contented old age﻿—on the word of Seraphina Riego.”
He looked down at his feet with gloomy submission.
“There is a proverb about an enamoured woman,” he muttered to himself, loud enough for me to overhear. Then, stooping deliberately to pick up his hat, he flourished it with a great sweep lower than his knees. His dumpy black back flitted out of the cabin; and almost directly we heard the sharp click of his flint and blade outside the door.

===Chinese===

因为爱情像在山地里行路，穿云而上，入影而下，去一个未知的终点。那是一个出神而饱满的时刻，我们仿佛一同高居于世上，孤独相对——直到她把手从我唇边抽回，我发觉自己已回到舱里，像从高处猛地跌落。
没有人在看我们。威廉斯太太垂着眼皮坐着，双手安放在膝上；她的丈夫知趣地盯着船梁上的一道金饰；他眼睛朝上翻着，给他那张红脸添了一副傻得出神的表情。还有卡斯特罗——我进门时必定擦过他身边，却直到此刻才看见。他一直立在门边，一言不发，像个自愿亮明身份的阴谋家，那顶黑圆帽就摊在脚前。只有他望着我们。他从塞拉菲娜望到我，从我望到塞拉菲娜。他眼里翻滚着说不出的东西，鸦爪般的眼角打着虔诚的惊惶，一阵阵地发狠。塞拉菲娜一唤他，他连忙低头，一如他对列戈家女儿素来的恭顺。
她说：“有些事关乎这位骑士，是您永远不会懂的。您的忠心已得了验证，深深地烙在了这里。……凭塞拉菲娜·列戈的一句话，它必给您一个安稳的晚年。”
他阴顺地低头看着自己的脚。
“有句俗话，说恋爱中的女人，”他自言自语，声音刚好落进我耳朵。随后，他不慌不忙俯身拾帽，抡开大弧，挥到膝下。他那矮墩墩的黑背影闪出船舱；几乎紧接着，我们在门外听见他的火石与刀刃清脆地一击。

### VI / 六
===Original===

How often the activity of our life is the least real part of it! Life, looked upon as a whole, presents itself to my fancy as a pursuit with open arms of a winged and magnificent dream, hovering just over our heads and casting its glory upon our hopes. It is in this simple vision, which is one and enduring, and not in the changing facts, that we must look for meaning and for truth. The three quiet days we spent together on board the *Lion* remain to me memorable and full of import, eventless and containing the very quintessence of existence. We shared the sunshine, always together, very close, turning hand in hand to the sea, whose unstained blueness continued under our feet the blue above our heads, as though we had been snatched up into the sky. The insignificant words we exchanged seemed informed by a sustaining certitude and an admirable gravity, as though there had been some quality of unerring wisdom in the blind love of man and woman. From the inexhaustible treasure of her feelings she drew words, glances, gestures that appeased every uneasiness of my heart. In some brief moment of illumination whose advent my man’s eyes had utterly missed, she had learned all at once everything there was to know. She knew. She no longer needed to survey my actions, my words, my thoughts; but she accorded me the sincere flattery of spellbound attention, and it was made intoxicating by her smile. In those short days of a pause, when, like a swimmer turning on his back, we lived in the trustful confidence of the sustaining depths, instead of struggling with the agitation of the surface﻿—in these days we had the time to look at each other profoundly; and I saw her smile come back again a little changed, more meaning and a little less mirthful, as if her lips had been made stiff by sorrow. But she was young; and youth, the time of softness, of tenderness, of enthusiasm, and of pity, presents a surface as hard as marble to the finality of death.
Breathing side by side, drinking in the sunshine, and talking of ourselves not at all, but casting the sense of our love like a magnificent garment over the wide significance of a world already conquered, we could not help being made aware of the currents of excitement and sympathy that converged upon our essential isolation from the life of the ship.

===Chinese===

我们的生活的忙碌，往往正是它最不真实的部分！生活，作为整体看，在我想象裡呈现为：张开双臂追逐一个长翼的、辉煌的梦，它悬在我们头顶上方，把光辉投在我们的希望上。我们必须在这单纯的一瞥裡——它浑一而恒久——而不是在流转的事实裡，寻找意义和真理。我们在狮子号（Lion）上共同度过的安静三天，于我至今难忘而意味深长，无事发生，却含着存在的精髓。我们共享阳光，始终在一起，很近，手挽手转向大海，它无瑕的蓝在我们脚下延续着头顶的蓝，仿佛我们被擭上了天。我们交换的无足轻重的话语，仿佛灌注着一种撑持的确信和可敬的庄重，仿佛男女盲目的爱裡有某种不出错的智慧的品格。从她感情的不竭宝库裡，她取出话语、眼色、手势，安抚我心中每一阵不安。在我这双男人的眼睛全然错过的一场顿悟的短暂时刻裡，她已一下子学会了该知道的一切。她知道了。她不再需要审视我的行动、我的言语、我的思想；但她给我一种出神的专注的真诚奉承，而她的微笑使它醉人。在那停顿的短短几天裡——像游泳人翻过身来仰浮，我们活在对托着我们的深处的信靠裡，而不与水面的激荡搏斗——那几天我们得以深深地互相凝视；我看见她的微笑回来了，有点变了，更多意味，少了些欢快，仿佛她的唇被悲伤弄得僵硬了。可她年轻；而青春，柔软、温存、热忱与怜悯的时代，对死亡的终结呈现一面大理石般硬的表面。

并肩呼吸，痛饮阳光，全然不谈我们自己，只把我们的爱的感觉像一件辉煌的外衣，罩上这个已被征服的世界的辽阔意义，我们不禁觉出那一股股兴奋与同情的潜流，向我们这本质的孤立——与船的生活的隔绝——汇聚而来。

===Original===

It was the excitement of the adventure brewing for our drinking according to Sebright’s recipe. People approached us﻿—spoke to us. We attended to them as if called down from an elevation; we were aware of the kind tone; and, remaining indistinct, they retreated, leaving us free to regain the heights of the lovers’ paradise﻿—a region of tender whispers and intense silences. Suddenly there would be a short, throaty laugh behind our backs, and Williams would begin, “I say, Kemp; do you call to mind so-and-so?” Invariably some planter or merchant in Jamaica. I never could.
Williams would grunt, “No? I wonder how you passed your time away these two years or more. The place isn’t that big.” His purpose was to cheer me up by some gossip, if only he could find a common acquaintance to talk over. I believe he thought me a queer fish. He told me once that everybody he knew in Jamaica had that precise opinion of me. Then with a chuckle and muttering, “Warrants﻿—assault﻿—Topnambo﻿—ha, ha!” he would leave us to ourselves, and continue his waddle up and down the poop. He wore loose silk trousers, and the round legs inside moved like a contrivance made out of two gateposts.
He was absurd. They all were that before our sweet reasonableness. But this atmosphere, full of interest and good will, was good to breathe. The very steward﻿—the same who had been hiding in the lazarette during the fight﻿—a hunted creature, displaying the most insignificant anatomy ever inhabited by a quailing spirit, devoted himself to the manufacture of strange cakes, which at teatime he would deposit smoking hot in front of Seraphina’s place. After each such exploit, he appeared amazed at his audacity in taking so much upon himself. The carpenter took more than a day, tinkering at an old ship’s boat. He was a Shetlander﻿—a sort of shaggy hyperborean giant with a forbidding face, an appraising, contemplative manner, and many nails in his mouth. At last the time came when he, too, approached our oblivion from behind, with a large hammer in his hand; but instead of braining us with one sweep of his mighty arm, he remarked simply in uncouth accents, “There now; I am thinking she will do well for what ye want her. I can do no more for ye.”
We turned round, arm-in-arm, to look at the boat.

===Chinese===

那是按希布赖特（Sebright）的方子为我们酿着的冒险的兴奋。人们走近我们——同我们说话。我们应接他们，像从高处被唤下来；我们觉出那好意的腔调；而他们保持模糊，退开了，留我们自由地重登恋人天堂的高处——一个温柔的耳语与强烈的寂静的国度。我们背后会忽然响起一声短促的、喉咙裡的笑，威廉斯开口了：“我说，肯普；你还记得某某人吗？”无一例外是牙买加（Jamaica）的某个种植园主或商人。我从来记不得。

威廉斯会咕哝：“不记得？我纳闷这两年多你是怎么打发的。那地方可没多大。”他的用意是拿点闲话给我解闷，只要他能找到一个共同的熟人聊聊。我相信他当我是条怪鱼。他有一回告诉我，他在牙买加认识的每一个人对我都有恰恰同样的看法。随后他咯咯一笑，咕哝着“拘票——殴人——托普南博——哈，哈！”丢下我们自己走开，继续他在尾楼上摇摇摆摆的踱步。他穿宽松的绸裤，裡头两条圆腿移动着，像一副用两根门柱造的机关。

他可笑。在我们甜蜜的通情达理面前，他们全可笑。可这充满兴味与善意的气氛，呼吸起来是好的。连那个乘务员——海战时躲进食品库的那位——一个被追猎的生灵，展示着一具曾被畏怯灵魂住过的最不起眼的骨架——也专心制造古怪的糕点，喝茶时他会把它们冒着热气摆在塞拉菲娜的座位前。每立此功，他都为自己胆敢如此自作主张而显得惊愕。木匠花了一天多，修补一条旧艇。他是个设得兰人——一个毛茸茸的极北巨人模样的家伙，一脸峻厉，一副估价沉思的神气，嘴裡叨着许多钉子。终于到了那时辰，他也提着一把大锤从背后接近我们的忘我；但他没有抡起有力的臂膀一锤砸碎我们，只用粗陋的腔调简单地说：“好了；我想她够你们用的了。我能为你们做的就这么多。”

我们手挽手转过身，去看那条艇。

===Original===

There she was, lying careened on the deck, with patched sides, in a belt of chips, shavings, and sawdust; a few pensive sailors stood about, gazing down at her with serious eyes. Sebright, bent double, circled slowly on a prowl of minute inspection. Suddenly straightening himself up, he pronounced a curt “She’ll do”; and, without looking at us at all, went off busily with his rapid stride.
A light sigh floated down upon our heads. Williams and his wife appeared on the poop above us like an allegorical couple of repletion and starvation, conceived in a fantastic vein on a balcony. A cigar smouldered in his stumpy red fingers. She had slipped a hand under his arm, as she would always do the moment they came near each other. She never looked more wasted and old-maidish than when thus affirming her wifely rights. But her eyes were motherly.
“Ah, my dears!” (She usually addressed Seraphina as “miss,” and myself as “young sir.”) “Ah, my dears! It seems so heartless to be sending you off in such a small boat, even for your own good.”
“Never fear, Mary. Repaired. Carry six comfortably,” reassured Williams in a tremendous mutter, like a bull.
“But why can’t you give them one of the others, Owen? That big one there?”
“Nonsense, Mary. Never see boat again. Wouldn’t grudge it. Only Sebright is quite right. Didn’t you hear what Sebright said? Very sensible. Ask Sebright. He will explain to you again.”
It was Sebright, with his asperity and his tact, with fits of brusqueness subdued by an almost affectionate contempt, who conducted all their affairs, as I have seen a trustworthy and experienced old nurse rule the infinite perplexities of a room full of children. His clear-sightedness and mental grip seemed independent of age and experience, like the ability of genius. He had an imaginative eye for detail, and, starting from a mere hint, would go scheming onwards with astonishing precision. His plan, to which we were committed﻿—committed helplessly and without resistance﻿—was based upon the necessity of our leaving the ship.
He had developed it to me that evening, in the cabin, directly Castro had gone out. He had already got Williams and his wife to share his view of our situation. He began by laying it down that in every desperate position there was a loophole for escape.

===Chinese===

她就在那儿，侧卧在甲板上，两舷打着补丁，围在一圈木片、刨花和锯末裡；几个沉思的水手站在四周，用严肃的眼睛俯视她。希布赖特弯着腰，缓缓兜圈，做一番细致的巡查。忽然直起身，草草断言“她行”；根本不看我们，迈着快步忙碌地走了。

一声轻叹飘落在我们头上。威廉斯和他的妻子出现在我们上方的尾楼上，像一对寓意画裡的饱足与饥馑，奇幻地构思在一座阳台上。一支雪茄在他粗短的红手指裡炯着。她一只手挽进他的臂弯，一如他们每次彼此走近时她必做的。她从不像这样肯定自己为妻的权利时那样枯槁而老处女气。可她的眼睛是慈母的。

“啊，我亲爱的孩子们！”（她惯常称塞拉菲娜“小姐”，称我“年轻先生”。）“啊，亲爱的孩子们！送你们乘这样一条小船走，哪怕是为你们自己好，也显得这样狠心。”

“别怕，玛丽。修好了。坐六个人舒舒服服，”威廉斯船长（Captain Williams）用公牛似的低沉咕哝宽慰道。

“可你们为什么不能给他们一条别的，欧文？那边那条大的？”

“胡说，玛丽。船就要不回来了。我也舍不得。只是希布赖特完全在理。你没听见希布赖特说的吗？很有见识。问希布赖特去。他会再给你解释。”

正是希布赖特，凭他的尖刻和圆熟，凭一阵阵被近乎慈爱的轻蔑驯服的粗暴，主持着他们的一切事务，如同我见过的一位可靠而经验丰富的老保姆，统御满屋孩子的无穷纷扰。他的清明和心智的把握仿佛独立于年龄与经验之外，像天才的才能。他对细节有想象力的眼睛，从一点暗示出发，能以惊人的精确一路谋划下去。我们已委身于他的计划——无助地、不加抗拒地委身——它基于我们必须离船的必要。

当天傍晚，卡斯特罗一出去，他就在舱裡把它向我铺开了。他已让威廉斯夫妇接受了他对我们处境的看法。他先立下一条：每一个绝望的处境裡都有一个逃逸的孔窍。

===Original===

Like other great men, he was conscious of his ability, and was inclined to theorize at large for a while. You had to accept the situation, go with it in a measure, and as you had walked into trouble with your eyes shut, you had only to continue with your eyes open. Time was the only thing that could defeat one. If you had no time, he admitted, you were at a dead wall. In this case he judged there would be time, because O’Brien, warned already, would sit tight for a few days, being sure to get hold of us directly the *Lion* came into port. It was only if the *Lion* failed to turn up within a reasonable term in Havana, that he would take fright, and take measures to hunt her up at sea. But I might rest assured that the *Lion* was going to Havana as fast as the winds would allow her.
What was, then, the situation? he continued, looking at me piercingly above Williams’ cropped head. I had run away for dear life from Cuba (taking with me what was best in it, to be sure, he interjected, with a faint smile towards Seraphina). I had no money, no friends (except my friends in this cabin, he was good enough to say); warrants out against me in Jamaica; no means to get to England; no safety in the ship. It was no use shirking that little fact. We must leave the *Lion*. This was a hopeless enough position. But it was hopeless only because it was not looked upon in the right way. We assumed that we had to leave her forever, while the whole secret of the trick was in this, that we need only leave her for a time. After O’Brien’s myrmidons had gone through her, and had been hooted away empty-handed, she became again, if not absolutely safe, then at least possible﻿—the only possible refuge for us﻿—the only decent means of reaching England together, where, he understood, our trouble would cease. Williams nodded approval heavily.
“The friends of Miss Riego would be glad to know she had made the passage under the care of a respectable married lady,” Sebright explained, in that imperturbable manner of his, which reflected faintly all his inner moods﻿—whether of recklessness, of jocularity or anxiety﻿—and often his underlying scorn. His gravity grew perfectly portentous. “Mrs. Williams,” he continued, “was, of course, very anxious to do her part creditably.

===Chinese===

像其他大人物一样，他自知其才，乐于先高谈一阵理论。你得接受处境，在一定程度上顺流而行；既然你是闭着眼走进麻烦的，你只需睁着眼走下去。时间是唯一能击败人的东西。他承认，你若没有时间，就撞死墙了。这一案裡他判断会有时间，因为奥布赖恩既已得了警报，会按兵不动几天，笃定狮子号一进港就能攥住我们。只有狮子号过了合理的期限还没在哈瓦那（Havana）露面，他才会惊慌，采取措施到海上搜她。而我尽可能心，狮子号正以风所许可的速度赶往哈瓦那。

那么，处境是什么？他接着说，越过威廉斯剪短的头顶锐利地看着我。我为逃命跑出了古巴（Cuba）（带走了那地方最好的东西，确实，他朝塞拉菲娜微微一笑插了一句）。我没有钱，没有朋友（除了这舱裡的朋友，他好意地说）；牙买加有通缉我的拘票；没有办法去英国；在船上也不安全。回避这一个小事实没有用。我们必须离开狮子号。这是一个够无望的处境。可它无望，只因为它没有被正确看待。我们假定必须永远离开她，而这把戏的全部秘密在于：我们只需离开她一时。等奥布赖恩的爪牙搜过她、被嘲骂着空手轰走之后，她就算不绝对安全，至少也重新成为可能——我们唯一可能的避难所——唯一体面的一同抵达英国的手段，在那裡，据他理解，我们的麻烦就会终止。威廉斯沉重地点头赞成。

“列戈小姐的朋友们会很乐意知道，她是在一位可敬的已婚女士的照料下完成这段航程的，”希布赖特以他那种不动声色的方式解释，那方式淡淡映出他全部的内心情绪——无论是莽撞、戏谑还是焦虑——也常常映出他深藏的轻蔑。他的庄重变得煞有介事。“威廉斯太太，”他接着说，“自然非常急于体面地尽她的一份。

===Original===

As it happened, the *Lion* was chartered for London this voyage; and notwithstanding her natural desire to rejoin, as soon as possible, her home and her aged uncle in Bristol, she intended to go with the young lady in a hackney coach to the very door.”
I had previously told them that the lately appointed Spanish ambassador in London was a relation of the Riegos, and personally acquainted with Seraphina, who, nearly two years before, had been on a short visit to Spain, and had lived for some months with his family in Madrid, I believe. No trouble or difficulty was to be apprehended as to proper recognition, or in the matter of rights and inheritance, and so on. The ambassador would make that his own affair. And for the rest I trusted the decision of her character and the strength of her affection. I was not afraid she would let anyone talk her out of an engagement, the dying wish of her nearest kinsman, sealed, as it were, with the blood of her father. This matter of temporary absence from the *Lion*, however, seemed to present an insuperable difficulty. We could not, obviously, be left for days floating in an open boat outside Havana harbour, waiting till the ship came out to pick us up. Sebright himself admitted that at first he did not see how it could be contrived. He didn’t see at all. He thought and thought. It was enough to sicken one of every sort of thinking. Then, suddenly, the few words Castro had let drop about the sugar estate and the relay of mules came into his head﻿—providentially, as Mrs. Williams would say. He fancied that the primitive and grandiose manner for a gentleman to keep a relay of mules﻿—any amount of mules﻿—in case he should want to send a letter or two, caused the circumstance to stick in his mind. At once he had “our little hidalgo” in, and put him through an examination.
“He turned fairly sulky, and tried constantly to break out against you, till Dona Seraphina here gave him a good talking to,” Sebright said.
Otherwise it was most satisfactory. The place was accessible from the sea through a narrow inlet, opening into a small, perfectly sheltered basin at the back of the sand-dunes. The little river watering the estate emptied itself into that basin.

碰巧，狮子号这一趟是租给伦敦的；不顾她自己尽快回到布裡斯托尔的家和年迈伯父身边的天性，她打算陪这位年轻小姐坐出租马车，一直送到门口。”

我先前已告诉他们，新任西班牙驻伦敦大使是列戈家的亲戚，同塞拉菲娜本人相识——差不多两年前她短期访问过西班牙，我相信，在马德里他家住过几个月。关于得体的认领、权利和继承等等，不必担心任何麻烦。大使会把那当成他自己的事。至于其余，我信她性格的决断和她爱情的力量。我不怕她会让人家说服她放弃一桩婚约，她最近血亲的临终之愿，可以说，用她父亲的血封了印的。可是这暂时离开狮子号一事，似乎呈现一道不可逾越的难关。显然，我们不能一连几天漂在哈瓦那港外一条敞口船裡，等船出来接我们。希布赖特自己承认，起初他看不出怎么安排。他全然看不出。他想啊想。想得叫人对一切思维倒胃。随后，忽然，卡斯特罗漏出的那几句关于糖庄和换乘骡子的话进了他的脑子——照威廉斯太太的说法，是天意。他想，是一位绅士保有换乘骡队——多少匹都行——以备他要送一两封信的那种原始而堂皇的方式，使这情节粘在了他心裡。他立刻把“我们的小贵人”请来，进行了一番盘问。

“他赌起了气，不断想朝你发作，直到堂娜·塞拉菲娜这裡好好说了他一顿，”希布赖特说。

其余都极为满意。那地方从海上经一条窄窄的进口可以进入，通到沙丘背后一个小巧而全然避风的小湾。灌溉庄园的小河就泄进那湾裡。

One could land from a boat there, he understood, as if in a dock﻿—and it was the very devil if I and Miss Riego could not lie hidden for a few days on her own property, the more so that, as it came out in the course of the discussion, while I had “rushed out to look at the sunset,” that the manager, or whatever they called him﻿—the fellow in charge﻿—was the husband of Dona Seraphina’s old nurse-woman. Of course, it behoved us to make as little fuss as possible﻿—try to reach the house along bypaths early in the morning, when all the slaves would be out at work in the fields. Castro, who professed to know the locality very well indeed, would be of use. Meantime, the *Lion* would make her way to Havana, as if nothing was the matter. Why should there be?﻿ ﻿… Rio Medio? What about Rio Medio? Hadn’t been within miles and miles of Rio Medio; tried this trip to beat up well clear of the coast. Search the ship? With pleasure﻿—every nook and cranny. He didn’t suppose they would have the cheek to talk of the pirates; but if they did venture﻿—what then? Pirates? That’s very serious and dishonourable to the power of Spain. Personally, had seen nothing of pirates. Thought they had all been captured and hanged quite lately. Rumours of the *Lion* having been attacked obviously untrue. Some other ship, perhaps.﻿ ﻿… That was the line to take. If it didn’t convince them, it would puzzle them altogether. Of course, Captain Williams, in his great regard for me, had abandoned the intention of making an affair of state of the outrage committed on his ship. He would not lodge any complaint in Havana﻿—nothing at all. The old women of the Admiralty wouldn’t be made to sit up this time. No report would be sent to the admiral either. Only, if the ship were interfered with, and bothered under any pretence whatever, once they had been given every facility to have one good look everywhere, the admiral would be asked to stop it. And the Spanish authorities would have not a leg to stand on either, for this simple reason, that they could not very well own to the sources of their information. Meantime, all hands on board the *Lion* had to be taken into confidence; that could not be avoided.

从船上在那儿可以登岸，他说他理解，就像进了船坞——而我和列戈小姐若不能在她自己的产业上躲几天，那才见了鬼，尤其因为——随着讨论展开，趁我“冲出去看落日”的当口——那个经理，或者随他们怎么称呼——管事的——是堂娜·塞拉菲娜老乳母的丈夫。当然，我们得尽量少声张——一清早趁所有奴隶都下地干活时，沿小径摸到宅子。卡斯特罗自称对那地方很熟，会派上用场。其间，狮子号装作若无其事地驶往哈瓦那。无疑，各式各样可恶的警役（*alguazils*）和海关鹰犬会一路狂吠着蜂拥上船。他们将大受欢迎。船上有生人吗？绝无。为什么要有？……裡奥梅迪奥（Rio Medio）？裡奥梅迪奥怎么了？多少英裡都没挨近过裡奥梅迪奥；这一趟特意远远避开海岸抢行。搜船？欢迎之至——每个角落每条缝。他不信他们有脸提海盗；可他们要是敢提——又怎样？海盗？那对西班牙的威权是非常严重、非常不体面的。本人嘛，海盗的影子都没见过。想是近来已尽数捕获绞决了。狮子号遭攻击的传闻显然不实。兴许是别的船。……就采取这个口径。就算说服不了他们，也会叫他们彻底糊涂。当然，威廉斯船长出于对我的极大尊重，已放弃把他船上的遭难闹成国家事件的打算。他不在哈瓦那提出任何控告——一点也不。这回不叫海军部的老太婆们坐起来了。也不向海军上将送报告。只是，倘若船受了干扰，无论借什么借口找麻烦——等他们得到了到处细看一遍的充分便利之后——就会请上将出面制止。而西班牙当局也将无立足之地，理由简单：他们不能太痛快地供出他们情报的来源。其间，狮子号上的全体人手都必须知内情；这避免不了。

He, Sebright, answered for their discretion while sober, anyhow; and he promised me that no leave or money would be given in Havana, for fear they should get on a spree, and let out something in the grogshops on shore. We all knew what a sailor-man was after a glass or two. So that was settled. Now, as to our rejoining the *Lion*. This, of necessity, must be left to me. Counting from the time we parted from her to land on the coast, the *Lion* would remain in Havana sixteen days; and if we did not turn up in that time, and the cargo was all on board by then, Captain Williams would try to remain in harbour on one pretence or another a few days longer. But sixteen days should be ample, and it was even better not to hurry up too much. To arrive on the fifteenth day would be the safest proceeding in a way, but for the cutting of the thing too fine, perhaps. With all these mules at our disposal, Sebright didn’t see why we should not make our way by land, pass through the town at night, or in the earliest morning, and go straight on board the *Lion*﻿—perhaps use some sort of disguise. He couldn’t say. He was out of it there. Blackened faces or something. Anyway, we would be looked out for on board night and day.
Later on, however, we had learned from Castro that the estate possessed a sailing craft of about twenty tons, which made frequent trips to Havana. These sugar *droghers* belonging to the plantations (every estate on the coast had one or more) went in and out of the harbour without being taken much notice of. Sometimes the battery at the water’s edge on the north side or a customhouse guard would hail them, but not often﻿—and even then only to ask the name, where from, and for the number of sugar-hogsheads on board. “By heavens! That’s the very thing!” rejoiced Sebright. And it was agreed that this would be our best way. We should time our arrival for early morning, or else at dusk. The craft that brought us in should be made, by a piece of unskillful management, to fall aboard the *Lion*, and remain alongside long enough to give us time to sneak in through an open deck-port.
The whole occurrence must be so contrived as to wear the appearance of a pure accident to the onlookers, should there be any. Shouting and an exchange of abuse on both parts should sound very true.

===Chinese===

他，希布赖特，为他们的谨慎担保——至少清醒的时候；他答应我，在哈瓦那不放假、不发饷，生怕他们上了岸寻欢，在酒馆裡走漏什么。我们都知道水手灌下一两杯之后是什么德行。就这样说定了。现在说我们重回狮子号。这必然只能交给我。从我们离船登岸那时算起，狮子号将在哈瓦那停十六天；我们若不在这期间露面，而货又都已上船，威廉斯船长会设法找这样那样的借口再留港几天。可十六天应当绰绰有余，甚至以不太赶为好。第十五天到，在某种意义上是最稳妥的做法，只是时间掐得太紧了些。有这么多骡子听凭调遣，希布赖特看不出我们为何不能取陆路，夜裡或清早穿过城，径直上狮子号——兴许用某种化装。他说不上来。他就管不到那儿了。抹黑的脸之类。总之，船上会昼夜有人守望我们。

不过后来我们从卡斯特罗那裡得知，那座庄园有一条二十吨上下的帆船，常跑哈瓦那。这些庄园的运糖驳船（沿海每座庄园都有一两条）进出港口，不大受人理会。有时北边水边的炮台或海关哨卡会招呼它们，但不常有——即便有，也只是问船名、来处，和船上糖桶的数目。“老天！正是这个东西！”希布赖特欢喜道。于是商定这是我们最好的路子。我们要掐准清晨、或黄昏时分到达。载我们进港的那条船，要经一番笨拙的操纵，撞靠上狮子号，并排停靠足够久，好给我们时间从一扇开着的甲板舱门溜进去。

整个事件必须安排得——万一有旁观者——在他们眼裡呈现为纯粹的意外。双方的大呼小叫和对骂要显得逼真。

Then the *drogher*, getting herself clear, would proceed innocently to the customhouse steps, where all such coasters had to report themselves on arrival. “Never fear. We shall put in some loud and scandalous cursing,” Sebright assured me. “The boys will greatly enjoy that part, I dare say.”
Remained to consider the purpose of the schooner that had come out of Rio Medio to hang on our skirts. It was doubtful whether it was in our power to shake her off. Sebright was full of admiration for her sailing qualities, coupled with infinite contempt for the “lubberly gang on board.”
“If I had the handling of her, now,” he said, “I would take my position as near as I liked, and stick there. “You know I never pretended my plan was quite safe. But have you got another?”
I made no answer, because I had no other, and could not think of one. Incredible as it may appear, not only my heart, but my mind, also, in the awakened comprehension of my love, refused to grapple with difficulties. My thoughts raced ahead of ships and pursuing men, into a dream of cloudless felicity without end. And I don’t think Sebright expected any suggestion from me.
