Whereas we shall keep well clear of the land when the time comes, and drop you in the dark without as much check on our way as there is in the wink of an eye. Hey?﻿ ﻿… Mind, Mr. Kemp, you take the boat out of sight up that little river, in case they should have a fancy, as they go along after us, to peep into that inlet. As I have said it wouldn’t do to trust too much in any fool’s folly.”
And now the time was approaching; the time to awake and step forth out of the temple of sunshine and love﻿—of whispers and silences. It had come. The night before both Williams and Sebright had been on deck, working the ship with an anxious care to take the utmost advantage of every favouring flaw in the contrary breeze. In the morning I was told there was a norther brewing. A norther is a tempestuous gale. I saw no signs of it. The realm of the sun, like the vanished one of the stars, appeared to my senses to be profoundly asleep, and breathing as gently as a child upon the ship. The *Lion*, too, seemed to lie wrapped in an enchanted slumber from the waterline to the tops of her upright masts. And yet she moved with the breath of the world, but so imperceptibly that it was the coast that seemed to be nearing her like a line of low vapour blown along the water. Between Williams and Sebright Castro pointed with his one arm, and a splutter of guttural syllables fell like hail out of his lips. The other two seemed incredulous. He stamped with both his feet angrily. Finally they went below together, to look at the chart, I suppose. They came up again very fast, one after another, and stood in a row, looking on as before. Three more dissimilar human beings it would have been difficult to imagine.
Dazzling white patches, about the size of a man’s hand, came out between sky and water. They grew in width, and ran together with a hummocky outline into a continuous undulation of sand-dunes. Here and there this rampart had a gap like a breach made by guns. Mrs. Williams, behind me, blew her nose faintly; her eyes were red, but she did not look at us. No eye was turned our way, and the spell of the coast was on her, too. A low, dark headland broke out to view through the dunes, and stood there conspicuous amongst the heaps of dazzling sand, like a small man frowning. A voice on deck pronounced:
“That’s right. Here’s his landmark. The fellow knew very well what he was talking about.”

===Chinese===

到时候我们却要远远避开陆地，在黑地裡把你们放下去，途中连眨眼那么一下的迟滞都没有。嘿？……记住，肯普先生，把船划上看不见的地方，藏进那条小河，以防他们跟在我们后面经过时，起意朝那进口窥一眼。如我所说，任何蠢货的愚蠢都不可信托太过。”

如今时候临近了；从阳光与爱的殿堂——耳语与寂静的殿堂——醒来跨出的时辰。它到了。前一夜，威廉斯和希布赖特都在甲板上，怀着焦虑的细心操船，要把逆风裡每一阵顺气的风用到极致。早晨我被告知，一场北风在酝酿。北风是一场狂暴的大风。我看不出征兆。太阳的疆域，同消失了的星辰的疆域一样，在我的感官裡显得酣睡，像个孩子一样轻轻呼吸着这条船。狮子号，从水线到挺直的桅顶，也仿佛裹在一场着魔的酣睡裡。可她随世界的呼吸移动着，只是那样难以觉察，倒像是海岸像一线贴水低吹的薄雾，在向她靠近。在威廉斯和希布赖特之间，卡斯特罗用他那只独臂指点着，一串喉音的音节像冰雹从他唇间落下。那两位似乎不信。他双足愤怒地顿地。末了他们一同下了舱，我想是去看海图。他们又很快上来，一个接一个，像先前那样站成一排。再难想象出三个更不相同的人了。

一片一片炫目的白斑，约莫手掌大小，在天与水之间显出来。它们展宽，连成一道丘岗起伏的轮廓，成为绵延的沙丘。这道壁垒处处有豁口，像被炮火轰开的。威廉斯太太在我背后轻轻擤鼻子；她眼睛红了，可不看我们。没有一只眼睛朝我们这边转，海岸的咒也罩在她身上。一座低低的黑色海岬从沙丘间显现，矗立在那些炫目的沙堆之间，像一个小个子的皱眉人。甲板上一个声音宣布：

“对了。这就是他的陆标。那家伙说得很清楚自己在讲什么。”

===Original===

It was Sebright’s voice, and Castro, strolling away triumphantly, affected to turn his back on the land. He had recognized the formation of the coast about the inlet long before anybody else could distinguish the details. His word had been doubted. He was offended, and passed us by, wrapping himself up closely. One of Seraphina’s locks blew against my cheek, and this last effort of the breeze remained snared in the silken meshes of her hair.
“There’s not enough wind to fill the sail of a toy boat,” grumbled Sebright; “and you can’t pull this heavy gig ashore with only that one-armed man at the other oar.” He was sorry he could not send us off with four good rowers. The norther might be coming on before they could return to the ship, and﻿—apart from the presence of four English sailors on the coast being sure to get talked about﻿—there was the difficulty in getting them back on board in Havana. We could, no doubt, smuggle ourselves in; but six people would make too much of a show. On the other hand, the absence of four men out of the ship’s company could not be accounted for very well to the authorities. “We can’t say they all died, and we threw them overboard. It would be too startling. No; you must go alone, and leave us at the first breath of wind; and that, I fear, ’ll be the first of the norther, too.”
He threw his head back, and hailed, “Do you see anything of that schooner from aloft there?”
“Nothing of her, sir,” answered a man perched, with dangling feet, astride the very end of the topsail yardarm. He paused, scanned the space from under the flat of his hand, and added, shouting with deliberation, “There’s﻿—a﻿—haze﻿—to seaward, sir.” The ship, with her decks sprinkled over with men in twos and threes, sent up to his ears a murmur of satisfaction.
If we could not see her, she could not see us. This was a favourable circumstance. To the infinite gratification of everyone on board, it had been discovered at daylight that the schooner had lost touch with us during the hours of darkness﻿—either through unskillful handling, or from some accidental disadvantage of the variable wind. I had been informed of it, directly I showed myself on deck in the morning, by several men who had radiant grins, as if some great piece of luck had befallen them, one and all.

===Chinese===

那是希布赖特的声音，卡斯特罗得意地踱开，装作背对陆地。他早在任何人能分辨细节之前很久，就认出了进口一带海岸的形态。他的话遭了怀疑。他生气了，紧裹着身子从我们旁边走过。塞拉菲娜的一绺头发吹上我的脸颊，微风这最后的努力被她头发的丝网缠住了。

“这点风连玩具船的帆都吹不满，”希布赖特咕哝；“而这条沉重的大艇，光靠那一边一个独臂人摇另一支桨，是划不上岸的。”他很抱歉不能派四个好桨手送我们。北风也许在他们回到船上之前就来了，而且——撇开四个英国水手出现在海岸上必定招人议论不谈——要他们回船上船也难。我们自然可以偷渡进去；可六个人太招摇。另一面，船上少了四个人，对当局也不好交代。“我们总不能说他们都死了，扔海裡了。太骇人。不；你们得自己走，一有风就离开我们；而那风，我怕，也将是北风的开头。”

他仰起头，喊：“上桅那边！望得见那条纵帆船吗？”

“望不见，先生，”一个跨坐在上帆桁桁端、双脚悬荡的人答。他停了停，用手掌平檐扫视海天，随后从容地喊加：“海——上——有——雾，先生。”船上，甲板三三两两散布的人，向那耳朵送去一阵满意的低语。

我们若看不见她，她也就看不见我们。这是个有利的情况。天亮时全船发现，那条纵帆船在黑暗的时辰裡失去了同我们的联络——或是操纵拙劣，或是多变的风偶然不利——船上人人喜出望外。早晨我一上甲板就有好几个人来告诉我，个个咧着发光的笑，仿佛人人都撞了大运。

===Original===

They shared their unflagging attention between the land and the sea-horizon, pointing out to each other, with their tattooed arms, the features of the coast, nodding knowingly towards the open. At midday most of them brought out their dinners on deck, and could be seen forward, each with a tin plate in the left hand, gesticulating amicably with clasp knives. A small white handkerchief hung from Mrs. Williams’ fingers, and now and then she touched her eyes lightly, one after the other. Her husband and Sebright, with a grave mien, stamped busily around the binnacle aft, changing places, making way for each other, stooping in turns to glance carefully along the compass card at the low bluff, like two gunners laying a piece of heavy ordnance for an important shot. The steward, emerging out of the companion, rang a handbell violently, and remained scared at the failure of that appeal. After waiting for a moment, he produced a further feeble tinkle, and sank down out of sight, with resignation.
A white sun, as if blazing with the pallor of fury, swung past the zenith in a profound and universal stillness. There was not a wrinkle on the sea; it presented a lustrous and glittering level, like the polished facet of a gem. In the cabin we sat down to the meal, not even pretending a desire to eat, exchanging vague phrases, hanging our heads over the empty plates. But the regular footsteps of the boatswain left in charge hesitated, stopped near the skylight. He said in an imperfectly assured voice, “Seems as if there was a steadier draught coming now.” At this we rose from the table impetuously, as though he had shouted an alarm of fire, and Mrs. Williams, with a little cry, ran round to Seraphina. Leaving the two women locked in a silent embrace, the captain, Sebright and myself hurried out on deck.
Every man in the ship had done the same. Even the shiny black cook had come out of his galley, and was already comfortably seated on the rail, baring his white teeth to the sunshine.
“Just about enough to blow out a farthing dip,” said Sebright, in a disappointed mutter.
He thought, however, we had better not wait for more. There would be too much presently. Some sailors hauled the boat alongside, the rest lined the rail as for a naval spectacle, and Williams stared blankly. We were waiting for Seraphina, who appeared, attended by Mrs.

===Chinese===

他们把不倦的注意力分给陆地和海平线，用刺着花的手臂互相指点海岸的特征，朝外海会意地点头。中午，多数人把饭端上甲板，在船头，人人左手一只锡盘，右手攥着折刀友善地比划。一条白手帕从威廉斯太太指间垂下，她时时轮流轻按两眼。她的丈夫和希布赖特，一脸郑重，在船尾罗经柜边忙碌地转，换位，互让，轮流俯身沿着罗经卡朝那座低岬仔细瞄，像两个炮手为一发要紧的炮弹标定一件重炮。乘务员从升降口冒出来，猛摇一只手铃，被这呼吁的失败吓住。等了片刻，他又弄出一声微弱的叮当，认命地缩下去不见了。

一轮白晃晃的太阳，仿佛因盛怒的苍白而燃烧，在一片深沉普遍的寂静裡越过天顶。海上没有一道皱；它呈现一片亮泽闪烁的平面，像宝石抛光的棱面。舱裡我们坐下用饭，连吃的意思都装不出，交换着含糊的话句，垂头对着空盘。可是留班的水手长那规律的脚步犹豫了，停在天窗近旁。他用一种不完全有把握的声音说：“像是来了股更稳的风。”一听这话我们从桌边猛地起身，仿佛他喊了火警，威廉斯太太轻呼一声，奔到塞拉菲娜身边。把两个女人留在无言的拥抱裡，船长、希布赖特和我急忙奔上甲板。

船上每个人都做了同样的事。连那个黑亮的厨子也出了他的厨房，已经舒舒服服坐上栏杆，朝阳光齜着白牙。

“也就够吹煍一支法辛蜡烛，”希布赖特失望地咕哝。

不过他想，我们最好别再等更多的了。待会儿就会太多。几个水手把艇拖到船侧，其余的人沿栏杆站成排，像看一场海军盛典，威廉斯茫茫然瞪着。我们在等塞拉菲娜，她由威廉斯太太陪着出现了，

===Original===

Williams, looking more kind, bloodless, and ascetic than ever. But my girl’s cheeks glowed; her eyes sparkled audaciously. She had done up her hair in some way that made it fit her head like a cap. It became her exceedingly, and the decision of her movements, the white serenity of her brow, dazzled me as if I had never seen her before. She seemed less childlike, older, ripe for this adventure in a new development of strength and courage. She inclined her head slowly at the gaping sailors, who had taken their caps off.
As soon as she appeared, Castro, who had been leaning against the bulwark, started up, and with a muttered “Adios, Señores,” went down the overside ladder and ensconced himself in the bow of the boat. The leave-taking was hurried over. Williams gave no sign of feeling, except, perhaps, for the greater intensity of his stare, which passed beyond our shoulders in the very act of handshaking. Sebright helped Seraphina down into the boat, and ran up again nimbly. Mrs. Williams, with her slim hand held in both mine, uttered a few incoherent words﻿—about men’s promises and the happiness of women, as I thought; but, truth to say, my own suppressed excitement was too considerable for close attention. I only knew that I had given her my confidence, that complete and utter confidence which neither wisdom nor power alone, can command. And, suddenly, it occurred to me that the heiress of a splendid name and fortune, down in the boat there, had no better friend in the world than this woman, who had come to us out of the waste of the sea, opening her simple heart to our need, like a pious and naive hermit in a wilderness throwing open the door of his cell to strange wayfarers.
“Mrs. Williams,” I stammered. “If we﻿—if I﻿—there’s no saying what may happen to any of us. If she ever comes to you﻿—if she ever is in want of help.﻿ ﻿…”
“Yes, yes. Always, always﻿—like my own daughter.”
And the good woman broke down, as if, indeed, I were taking her own daughter away.
“Nonsense, Mary!” Williams advanced, muttering tremendously. “They are not going round the world. Dare say get ashore in time for supper.”
He stared through her without expression, as if she had been thin air, but she seized his arm, of course, and he gave me, then, an amazingly rapid wink which, I suppose, meant that I should go.﻿ ﻿…
“All right there?”

===Chinese===

后者显得比以往更善良、更无血色、更苦修。可我的姑娘双颊灼灼；她的眼睛大胆地放光。她把头发盘成了紧贴头顶的一顶小帽模样。那非常衬她，而她动作的决断、额头的白皙安详，使我目眩，仿佛从没见过她。她似乎少了孩子气，年长了些，成熟得足以担当这场新的力量与勇气之历险。她朝张口结舌摘了帽的水手们缓缓颔首。

她一露面，倚在舷墙上的卡斯特罗便一跃而起，咕哝一声“再会，先生们（*Adios, Señores*）”，顺舷梯下去，蜷进了艇首。道别匆匆了结。威廉斯没有露感情的迹象，也许除了他的瞪视更紧张了些，那瞪视在握手的当口越过我们的肩膀。希布赖特把塞拉菲娜扶下艇去，又轻快地跑上来。威廉斯太太把她纤细的手握在我的两只手裡，说了几句不连贯的话——关于男人的承诺和女人的幸福，我想；但说实在的，我自己压着的激动太剧烈，顾不上细听。我只知道我已给了她我的信任，那种智慧和权势单独都唤不来的、完全彻底的信任。忽然我想起，那个辉煌姓氏与家财的继承人，在下面船裡，世上再没有比这女人更好的朋友了——她从海的荒芜裡来到我们身边，为我们的需要敞开她单纯的心，像荒野裡一位虔敬而天真的隐士，向陌生的行路人敞开他小室的门。

“威廉斯太太，”我讷讷地说。“要是我们——要是我——我们中任何一个都难说会碰上什么。她若有一天来找您——她若有一天需要帮助。……”

“是，是。随时，随时——像我自己女儿一样。”

这好女人哭出了声，仿佛我带走的真是她自己的女儿。

“胡说，玛丽！”威廉斯上前，瓮声瓮气地咕哝。“他们又不是环游世界。敢说到时候赶上岸吃晚饭。”

他毫无表情地看穿她，仿佛她是稀薄的空气，可她当然抓住了他的胳膊，于是他朝我极快地眨了一下眼，我想，意思是叫我走。……

“下面好了吗？”

===Original===

asked Sebright from above, as soon as I had taken my seat in the stern sheets by the side of Seraphina. He was standing on the poop deck ready with a sign for letting go the end of our painter on deck; but before I could answer in the affirmative, Castro, ensconced forward under his hat, drew his ready blade across the rope, as it were a throat.
At once a narrow strip of water opened between the boat and the ship, and our long-prepared departure, hastened thus by half a second, seemed to strike everybody dumb with surprise, as if we had taken wings to ourselves to fly away. Hastily I grasped the tiller to give the boat a sheer, and heard a sort of loud gasp in the air above. A row of heads, posed on chins all along the rail, stared after us with unanimous fixity. Mrs. Williams averted her face on her husband’s shoulder. Behind the couple, Sebright raised his cap gravely.
Our little sail filled to a breeze which was much too feeble to produce a perceptible effect on the ship, and we left behind us her towering form, as one recedes from a tall white spire on a plain. I laid the boat’s head straight for the dwarf headland, marking the mouth of the inlet on the interminable range of sand-dunes. We drove on with a smart ripple, but before we felt sufficiently settled to exchange a few words the animated sound languished suddenly, paused altogether, and, with a renewed murmur under our feet seemed to lose itself below the glassy waters.

===Chinese===

我在船尾座塞拉菲娜身边坐定后，希布赖特在上面问。他站在尾楼甲板上，手裡拿着放开拖缆的信号；可我还来不及应声说是，蜷在前头帽檐底下的卡斯特罗，已把他那随时待命的刃横过缆绳一划，仿佛割一条喉咙。

船与船之间立刻裂开一线窄水，我们这准备已久的启程，被这样提前了半秒，似乎叫人人都惊得哑了，仿佛我们给自己插上翅膀飞走了。我急忙抓住舵柄给艇一个偏转，听见头顶空气中一声大大的抽气。一排脑袋，下巴搁在栏杆上，齐齐定定地目送我们。威廉斯太太把脸扭到丈夫肩上。那对夫妇身后，希布赖特庄严地举了举帽。

我们的小帆鼓上一阵风，那风太弱，对大船产生不出可觉的效果，我们把那高塔般的形体留在身后，像人在平原上离一座白色高尖塔远去。我把艇头对准那座侏儒海岬，它标着无穷无尽的沙丘带上进口的位置。我们带着轻快的涟纹驶去，可还没等我们定下神来交谈几句，那活泼的水声忽然衰了，全然停了，随后脚下一阵新起的低语，仿佛没入了那琉璃般的水下。

### VII / VII
===Original===

The calm had returned. The sea, changing from the warm glitter of a gem, and attuned to the grays and blacks of space, resembled a monstrous cinder under a sky of ashes.
The sun had disappeared, smothered in these clouds that had formed themselves all at once and everywhere, like some swift corruption of the upper air. For the best part of the afternoon the ship and the boat remained lying at right angles, within half a mile of each other. What light was left in the world, cut off from the source of life, seemed to sicken with a strange decay. The long stretch of sands and the sails of the motionless vessel stood out lividly pale in universal gloom. And yet the state of the atmosphere was such that we could see clear-cut the very folds in the steep face of the dunes, and the figures of the people moving on the poop of the *Lion*. There was always somebody there that had the aspect of watching us. Then, with some excitement, we saw them on board haul up the mainsail and lower the gig.
The four oars beat the sombre water, rising and falling apparently in the same place. She was an interminable time coming on, but as she neared us I was surprised at her dashing speed. Sebright, who steered, laid her alongside smartly, and two of his men, clambering over without a word, lowered our lug at once.
“We came to reef your sail for you. You couldn’t manage that very well with a one-armed crew,” said the young mate quietly in the enormous stillness. In his opinion, we couldn’t expect now any wind till the first squall came down. This flurry, as he called it, would send us in smoking, and he was sure it would help the ship, as well, into Havana, in about twenty-four hours. He didn’t think that it would come *very* heavy at first; and, once landed, we need not care how hard it blew.
He tendered me over the gunwale a pocket-flask covered with leather, and with a screwed silver stopper in the shape of a cup. It was from the captain; full of prime rum. We were pretty sure to get wet. He thrust, also, into my hands a gray woollen shawl. Mrs. Williams thought my young lady might be glad of it at night. “The dear old woman has shut herself up inside their stateroom, and is praying for you now,” he concluded. “Look alive, boys.”
His men did not answer him, but at some words he addressed to Castro, the latter, in the bows and looking at the coast, growled with a surly impatience.

===Chinese===

平静又回来了。大海脱去了宝石般温暖的光泽，与太空的灰黑融为一体，在灰烬色的天空下，像一块狰狞的煤渣。
太阳不见了，被那些四面八方骤然涌起的云闷死在里面，仿佛高空里一场迅疾的腐烂。大半个下午，大船和小艇彼此成直角地停着，相距不过半英里。世上剩下的光，既与生命之源隔绝，似乎也染上一种奇怪的病变，衰败下去。长长的沙洲和那纹丝不动的船帆，在一片普遍的昏暗中显出死一般的苍白。然而大气通透得出奇，我们连沙丘陡壁上的道道褶皱、狮子号（*Lion*）尾楼上走动的人影，都看得清清楚楚。那上面总有人像是在望着我们。随后，我们带着几分兴奋，看见船上的人收起主帆，放下了小艇。
四支桨拍打着阴沉的水面，起起落落，似乎总在原地。它来了，来得没完没了；可等它近了，那股冲刺般的速度又让我吃惊。掌舵的希布赖特（Sebright）利落地把它贴上我们艇侧，他手下两人一言不发地翻过船来，立刻动手收低了我们的大三角帆。
“我们是来替你们缩帆的。你们这么一条独臂人手的船，自己可弄不好这个。”年轻的大副在这无边的寂静里轻声说。依他看，头一阵暴风压下来之前，别指望有风。那阵“骚动”——他这样称呼它——会载着我们一溜烟送进港去，他也确信它同样会把大船送进哈瓦那（Havana），不出二十四小时。他觉得开头不至于来得太猛；而一旦上了岸，风刮得多凶都不干我们的事了。
他从舷边递过来一只小酒瓶，皮子包着，旋着一只杯形的银盖。是船长送的，满装上好的朗姆酒。我们十有八九要淋成落汤鸡。他还往我手里塞了一条灰色羊毛披肩。威廉斯太太想，夜里我的小姐兴许用得着。“那位亲爱的老太太已经把自己关在他们房舱里，这会儿正为你们祈祷呢。”他末了说。“伙计们，麻利些。”
他的水手没有应声；可他对卡斯特罗说了几句什么，后者正坐在船头望着海岸，粗声粗气地咕哝起来，一脸乖戾的不耐烦。

===Original===

He was perfectly sure of the entrance. Had been in and out several times. Yes. At night, too. Sebright then turned to me. After all, it was not so difficult. The inlet bore due south from us, and the wind would come true from the north. Always did in these bursts. I had only to keep dead before it. “The clouds will light you in at the last,” he added meaningly, glancing upwards.
The two sailors, having finished reefing, hoisted, lowered, and hoisted again the yard to see that the gear ran clear, and without one look at us, stepped back into the gig, and sat down in their places. For a moment longer we lay together, touching sides. Sebright extended his hand from boat to boat.
“You are in God’s care now, Kemp,” he said, looking up at me, and with an unexpected depth of feeling in his tone. “Take no turn with the sheet on any account, and if you feel it coming too heavy, let fly and chance it. Did I tell you we have sighted the schooner from aloft? No? We can just make her out from the main-yard away astern under the land. That don’t matter now.﻿ ﻿… Señorita, I kiss your hands.” He liked to air his Spanish.﻿ ﻿… “Keep cool whatever happens. Dead before it﻿—mind. And count on sixteen days from tomorrow. Well. No more. Give way, boys.”
He never looked back. We watched the boat being hoisted and secured. Shortly afterwards, as we were observing the *Lion* shortening sail, the first of the rain descended between her and us like a lowered veil. For a time she remained mistily visible, dark and gaunt with her bared spars. The downpour redoubled; she disappeared; and our hearts were stirred to a faster beat.
The shower fell on us, around us, descending perpendicularly, with a steady force; and the thunder rolled far off, as if coming from under the sea. Sometimes the muffled rumbling stopped, and let us hear plainly the gentle hiss and the patter of the drops falling upon a vast expanse. Suddenly, mingled with a loud detonation right over our heads, a burst of light outlined under the bellying strip of our sail the pointed crown of Castro’s hat, reposing on a heap of black clothing huddled in the bows. The darkness swallowed it all. I swung Seraphina in front of me, and made her sit low on the stern sheets beneath my feet. A lot of foam boiled up around the boat, and we had the sensation of having been sent flying from a catapult.

===Chinese===

他对那个入口有十足的把握。进进出出过好几回了。是的。夜里也走过。希布赖特随即转向我。说到底，这不算难。水道正在我们正南，风会从正北来。这类风暴发作时向来如此。我只需始终正对着它行驶。“到最后，云会替你们照路的。”他意味深长地补了一句，往上一瞥。
两个水手缩好帆，又把帆桁升起、落下、再升起，试试滑车顺不顺，然后看也不看我们一眼，跨回小艇，各就各位。我们又并排贴着船舷停了片刻。希布赖特从这条船向那条船伸过手来。
“如今你们是托付给上帝照看了，肯普。”他说，抬眼望着我，语气里有一种出乎意料的深情。“千万别去动帆脚索；要是觉得风来得太猛，就干脆松帆，听天由命。我告诉过你没有，我们从桅顶上望见那条纵帆船了？没有？从主桅桁上，陆地遮着，船尾远处，勉强认得出它来。如今这也无关紧要了。……小姐（Señorita），我吻您的手。”他喜欢显摆他的西班牙语。……“无论出什么事，保持镇定。正对着风走——记住。从明天起，数着十六天。好。不多说了。伙计们，划。”
他再没有回头。我们望着小艇被吊上去、系牢。没过多久，正当我们望着狮子号收帆时，头一场雨落了下来，像一道垂下的面纱，隔在大船与我们之间。有一阵子它还朦朦胧胧看得见，赤裸的桅桁衬出它又黑又瘦的轮廓。雨陡然加倍倾泻；它不见了；我们的心被搅得跳得更急了。
雨落在我们身上、四周，笔直地泻下，力道沉稳；雷声在远处滚动，仿佛发自海底。有时那闷闷的隆隆声停了，让我们清清楚楚听见雨点落在辽阔水面上的轻嘶与淅沥。突然，一声炸雷正当头顶，一道爆亮的光，在我们那面鼓胀的帆下勾出卡斯特罗帽子的尖顶——它正安放在船头一堆蜷作一团的黑衣上。黑暗把这一切吞没了。我把塞拉菲娜拽到身前，让她在尾座上、贴着我脚边低低坐下。艇的四周腾起大片白沫，我们只觉得自己像被弹弓射了出去。

===Original===

Everything was black﻿—perfectly black. At intervals, headlong gusts of rain swept over our heads. I suppose I did keep sufficiently cool, but in every flash of lightning the wind, the sea, the clouds, the rain, and the boat appeared to rush together thundering upon the coast. The line of sands, bordered with a belt of foam, zigzagged dazzlingly upon an earth as black as the clouds; only the headland, with every vision, remained sombre and unmoved. At last it rose up right before the boat. Blue lightning streamed on a lane of tumbling waters at its foot. Was this the entrance? With the vague notion of shortening sail, I let the sheet go from my hand. There was a jerk, the crack of snapped wood, and the next flash showed me Castro emerging from the ruins of mast and sail. He uprose, hurling the wreck from him overboard, then flickered out of sight with his arm waving to the left, and I bore accordingly on the tiller. In a moment I saw him again, erect forward, with the arm pointing to the right, and I obeyed his signal. The clouds, straining with water and fire, were, indeed, lighting us on our way. A wave swelled astern, chasing us in; rocking frightfully, we glanced past a stationary mass of foam﻿—a sandbar﻿—breakers.﻿ ﻿… It was terrible.﻿ ﻿… Suddenly, the motion of the boat changed, and the flickers of lightning fell into a small, landlocked basin. The wind tore deep furrows in it, howling and scuffling behind the dunes. Spray flew from the whole surface, the entire pool of a bay seemed to heave bodily upwards, and I saw Castro again, with his face to me this time. His black cloak was blowing straight out from his throat, his mouth yawned wide; he shouted directions, but in an instant darkness sealed my eyes with its impenetrable impress. It was impossible to steer now; the boat swung and reeled where she listed; a violent shock threw me sideways off my seat. I felt her turning over, and, gathering Seraphina in my arms, I leaped out before she capsized. I leaped clear out into shallow water.
I should never in my life have thought myself capable of such a feat, and yet I did it with assurance, with no effort that I can remember. More than that﻿—I managed, after the leap, to keep my feet in the clinging, staggering clutch of water charged with sand, which swirled heavily about my knees.

===Chinese===

天地一片黑——纯粹的黑。一阵阵骤急的风雨当头扫过。我想我确实够镇定，可是在每一道闪电里，风、海、云、雨，连同这条艇，都仿佛轰然一同向海岸猛冲过去。那一线沙洲镶着一道白沫的边，在黑得像云的大地上灼灼地曲折发亮；唯有那座海岬，每一次显现，都阴沉而纹丝不动。终于，它就在艇的正前方耸起。蓝色的闪电泻在它脚下一条翻腾的水路上。这就是入口么？我心里模模糊糊想着收帆，手一松，放开了帆脚索。猛地一拽，木头断裂一声脆响，下一道闪光里，只见卡斯特罗从桅杆和帆的残骸中钻出来。他直起身，把那堆破烂甩出船外，随即手臂向左一挥，人闪没了影，我便照着压舵；片刻后又见他挺立船头，手臂指向右，我依他的信号行事。那满载着水与火的云，果真在为我们照路。一道浪从船尾涌起，赶着我们进湾；艇可怕地摇晃着，擦过一团凝住不动的白沫——沙洲——碎浪。……可怕极了。……突然，艇的动态一变，闪电的微光落进一个小小的、陆地环抱的盆地里。风在盆地里犁出深深的沟，在沙丘背后呼啸厮打。浪花从整个水面上飞起，整个一湾水仿佛整体向上掀动，我又看见了卡斯特罗，这一回他脸对着我。他的黑斗篷从颈间笔直地吹开，嘴张得大大的；他高喊着指令，可一眨眼，黑暗便用它那不可穿透的印记封住了我的眼睛。这时候掌舵已经不可能了；艇随意地摇摆、踉跄；猛烈的一撞把我从座位上掀向一边。我觉出它正在翻，便一把将塞拉菲娜搂进怀里，赶在它倾覆之前跳了出去。我干干净净地跳进了浅水。
我这辈子从不会想到自己能做出这样的事，可我做得分外笃定，不记得费过一点力气。不止如此——跳下去之后，我还在那裹挟着泥沙、黏缠踉跄的水的抓握里站住了脚，那水在我膝头沉沉地打着旋。

===Original===

It kept on hurling itself at my legs from behind, while I waded across the narrow strip of sand with an inspired firmness of step defying all the power of the elements. I felt the harder ground at last, but not before I had caught a momentary glimpse of a black and bulky object tumbling over and over in the advancing and withdrawing liquid flurry of the beach.
“Sit still here on the ground,” I shouted to Seraphina, though flights of spray enveloped us completely. “I am going back for Castro.”
I faced about, putting my head down. He had been undoubtedly knocked over; and an old man, with only one hand to help himself with, ran a very serious risk of being buffeted into insensibility, and thus coming to his death in some four feet of water. The violent glare disclosed a body, entangled in a cloak, rolling about helplessly between land and water, as it were. I dashed on in the dark; a wave went over my head as I stooped, nearly waist-deep, groping. His rotary motion, in that smother, made it extremely difficult to obtain any sort of hold. A little more, and he would have knocked my legs from under me, but it was as if my grim determination were by itself of a saving nature. He submitted to being hauled up the beach, passively, like a sack. It was a heavy drag on the sand; I felt him bump behind me on the edge of the harder ground, and a deluge fell uninterruptedly from above. He lay prone on his face, like a corpse, between Seraphina and myself. We could not remain there, however.
But where to go? What to do? In what direction to look for a refuge? Was there any shelter near by? How were we to reach it? How were we to move at all? No doubt he had expired; and the earth, swept, deluged, glimmering fiercely and devastated with an awful uproar, appeared no longer habitable. A thunderclap seemed to crash new life into him; the world flared all round, as if turning to a spark, and he was seen sitting up dazedly, like one called up from the dead. Through it all he had preserved his hat.
It was fixed firmly down under his chin with a handkerchief, the side rims over his ears like flaps, and, for the rest, presenting the appearance of a coal-scuttle bonnet behind, as well as in front. We followed its peculiar aspect.

===Chinese===

它不断从背后向我的双腿砸来，而我涉过那道窄窄的沙带，脚步带着一种如有神助的坚定，全然不把天地之威放在眼里。我终于踩到坚实的地面，不过在那之前，我瞥见一样黑乎乎的庞然大物，在海滩上前奔后撤的浪沫里翻滚不休。
“就坐在这儿地上别动。”我朝塞拉菲娜喊道，尽管一阵阵飞沫把我们整个裹住。“我回去救卡斯特罗。”
我掉转身，低下头迎上去。他无疑是被打倒了；一个老头子，只凭一只手自救，很可能被打得人事不省，就此死在四英尺来深的水里。炫目的闪光里显出一具身躯，缠在斗篷里，仿佛在陆地与水之间无可奈何地滚来滚去。我在黑暗里猛冲过去；我弯腰摸索、几乎齐腰深的时候，一道浪从我头顶漫过。在那片窒闷的混沌里，他旋转式的翻滚让抓住他任何一处都难上加难。只差一点，他就把我的腿都撞飞了，可我那股狠下来的决心本身，仿佛就有救人的效力。他听任自己被拖上沙滩，一动不动，像条口袋。在沙上拖行沉重得很；我觉出他在坚实地面边缘、在我身后一路磕碰，头顶的倾盆大雨下个不停。他脸朝下直挺挺躺着，像具尸体，横在我和塞拉菲娜之间。然而我们不能留在那里。
可是去哪儿？做什么？往哪边找栖身之处？近旁可有遮蔽？我们怎么到得了那儿？我们又怎么挪得动？他想必已经断气了；而这大地，被横扫，被浇透，凶光闪闪，在可怖的喧嚣中满目疮痍，仿佛再不是人住的地方。一声霹雳，仿佛把新的生命砸进了他体内；四野轰然一亮，世界像烧作一点火星，只见他迷迷糊糊坐起来，像被人从死人堆里唤起。历经这一切，他的帽子居然还在。
它用一条手帕牢牢兜在下巴底下，两侧帽檐护住耳朵，像两片挡风，其余部分，前前后后，看去都像一顶煤斗似的兜帽。我们便跟着这顶形貌古怪的帽子走。

===Original===

Driving on under this indestructible headgear, he flickered in and out of the world, while, with entwined arms and leaning back against the wind with all our might, Seraphina and myself were borne along in his train. He knew of a shelter; and this knowledge, perhaps, and also his evident familiarity with the topography of the country, made him appear indomitably confident in the storm.
A small plain of coarse grass was bounded by the steep spur of a rise. To the left a little river would burst, all at once, in all its windings into a bluish sulphurous glow; and between the crashes of thunder there was heard the long-drawn, whistling swish of the rushes and canebrakes springing on the boggy ground. We skirted the rise. The rain beat against it; the lightning showed its streaming and furrowed surface. We stumbled in the gusts. We felt under our feet, mud, sand, rocky inequalities of the ground, and the moving stones in the bed of a torrent, which broke headlong against our ankles. The entrance of a deep ravine opened.
Its lower sides palpitated with the ceaseless tossing of dwarf trees and bushes; and, motionless above the sombre tumult of the slopes, the monumental stretch of bare rock rose on high, level at the top, and emitting a ghastly yellow sheen in the flashes. The thunderclaps rolled ponderously between the narrowing walls of that chasm, that was all aflame one moment, and all black the next. A torrent springing at its head, and dashing with inaudible fury along the bottom, seemed to gleam placidly amongst the rounded forms of inky bushes and pale boulders below our path. Enormous eddies of wind from above made us stop short and totter breathless, clinging to each other.
Castro sustained Seraphina on the other side; but frequently he had to leave us and move ahead, looking for the way. There was, in fact, a half-obliterated path winding along the less steep of the two sides; and we struggled after our guide with the unthinking fortitude of despair. He was being disclosed to us so suddenly, extinguished so swiftly, that he appeared, always, as if motionless and posturing in a variety of climbing attitudes. The rise of the bottom was very steep, and the last hundred yards really stiff. We did them practically on our hands and knees. The dislodged stones bounded away from under our feet, unheard, like puffballs.

===Chinese===

他顶着这顶打不坏的头盔一路挺进，在闪电里忽隐忽现；塞拉菲娜和我挽紧臂膀，拼尽全力向后仰着顶风，被他一路拽着走。他知道一处藏身之地；也许是这份有数，加上他对这一带地形显而易见的熟稔，使他在风暴里显出一副压不垮的笃定。
一小片长着粗草的平地，尽头是一道陡峭隆起的山脊。左边一条小河，会突然间连同它所有的曲折，一齐爆现在一片硫磺味的蓝光里；雷声与雷声之间，听得见沼地上灯芯草和藤丛弹起时那悠长呼啸的飒飒声。我们绕着山脊走。雨砸在坡上；闪电照出它雨水横流、沟壑纵横的样子。我们在阵风里跌跌撞撞。脚下感到的是泥、是沙、是高低不平的岩石，还有一股激流河床上滚动的石头，水流一头撞在我们的脚踝上。一道深谷的入口敞开了。
谷壁下部，矮树和灌木翻腾摇撼个不停，像在悸动；在两侧山坡阴沉的骚乱之上，那一大片纪念碑似的裸岩巍然耸起，顶端平齐，在闪光里泛着惨黄的辉光。霹雳在峡谷愈来愈窄的两壁之间沉重地滚过，这峡谷前一刻通体是火，下一刻又通体是黑。一股激流从谷首奔出，以听不见的狂怒冲过谷底，在我们小径的下方，在墨黑灌木和灰白巨石浑圆的形体之间，仿佛只是静静闪烁。高空砸下的巨大风涡逼得我们猛地站住，气喘不迭，摇摇欲倒，只好彼此紧抓。
卡斯特罗在另一边搀着塞拉菲娜；可他不得不时常丢下我们，抢到前头去探路。其实有一条磨得半没了影的小径，沿着较缓的那一侧坡蜿蜒而上；我们跟着向导挣扎前行，怀着一种不假思索的、绝望的坚韧。他总在闪电里骤然显现，又倏忽熄灭，于是每一回看上去都像静止的一般，摆出种种攀爬的姿势。谷底上行的坡极陡，最后一百码实在够呛。我们几乎是手脚并用爬完的。踩松的石头从脚下蹦开去，无声无息，像一颗颗马勃菌。

===Original===

At the top I tried to make of my body a shelter for Seraphina. The wind howled and roared over us. “Up! *Vamos!* The worst is yet before us,” shrieked Castro in my ear.
What could he mean by this? The play of lightning opened to view only a vast and rolling upland. Fire flowed in sheets undulating with the expanses of long grass amongst the trees, here and there, in coal-black clumps, and flashed violently against a low edge of forests very dark and far away.
“Let us go!” he cried. “Courage, Señorita!”
Courage! The populace said of her that she had never needed to put her foot to the ground. If courage consists, for a being so tender, in toiling and enduring without faltering and plaint﻿—even to the very limit of physical power﻿—then she was the most courageous woman in the world, as she was the most charming, most faithful, most generous, and the most worthy of love. I tried not to think of her racked limbs, for the very pain and pity of it. We retraced our steps, but now following the edge of that precipice out of which we had emerged. I had peremptorily insisted on carrying her. She put her arms round my neck and, to my uplifted heart, she weighed no heavier than a feather. Castro, grasping my arm, guided my steps and gave me support against the wind.
There was a distinct lull. Even the thunder had rolled away, dwindling to a deep mutter. Castro fell on his knees in front of me.
“It is here,” I heard him scream.
I set Seraphina down. A hooked dart of fire tore in two the thick canopy of clouds. I started back from the edge.
“What! Here?” I yelled.
“Señor﻿—*Si!* There is a cavern below.﻿ ﻿…”
I had seen a ledge clinging to the face of the rock.
It was a cornice inclining downwards upon the wall of the precipice, as you see, sometimes, a flight of stairs built against the outside wall of a house. And it resembled a stair roughly, with long, sloping steps, wet with rain.
“*Por Dios*, Señor, do not let us stay to think here, or we shall perish in this tempest.”
He howled, gesticulated, shrieked with all the strength of his lungs. He knew these tornadoes. Brute beasts would be found lying dead in the fields in the morning. This was the beginning only. The lightning showed his kneeling form, the eager upturned face, and a finger pointing urgently into the abyss. The wind was nothing! Nothing to what would come after.

===Chinese===

到了顶上，我竭力拿自己的身子给塞拉菲娜挡风。风在头顶呼啸咆哮。“起来！*Vamos*（走）！最厉害的还在前头呢。”卡斯特罗在我耳边尖声喊。
这话是什么意思？闪电的光里只展开一片辽阔起伏的高地。火的巨澜随着树间长草的广野起伏流淌，树这里一丛、那里一丛，黑得像煤，又猛烈地闪向远处一道低矮幽暗的森林边缘。
“走吧！”他喊道。“鼓起勇气，小姐！”
勇气！百姓们说起她，说她从来不消自己把脚踏到地面上。倘若对一个如此娇弱的人，勇气便是毫不动摇、毫无怨言地劳苦与忍受——哪怕忍到体力的极限——那么她是世上最有勇气的女人，正如她也是最迷人、最忠贞、最慷慨、最值得被爱的女人。我竭力不去想她那备受折磨的四肢，一想便心痛怜惜。我们循原路折回，只是这一回沿着我们钻出来的那道绝壁的边缘走。我斩钉截铁地坚持要抱她。她搂住我的脖颈，在我昂扬的心里，她轻得不及一根羽毛。卡斯特罗抓着我的手臂，为我引路，替我顶着风。
风势明显缓了。连雷声也滚远了，弱成低低的咕哝。卡斯特罗在我面前扑通跪下。
“就在这儿。”我听见他尖叫。
我把塞拉菲娜放下。一道钩状的火矛把厚厚的云幕撕成两半。我从崖边猛地缩回。
“什么！这儿？”我吼道。
“先生——*Si*（是）！下面有一个洞。……”
我已看见一道岩檐贴在崖壁上。
那是一道贴着绝壁倾斜而下的檐道，就像你有时见到贴着房屋外墙搭起的石阶。它大致像一道楼梯，踏步又长又斜，淋着雨水。
“*Por Dios*（看在上帝份上），先生，别让我们在这儿站着琢磨了，不然要死在这场风暴里了。”
他嚎着，比划着，扯开喉咙拼命尖叫。他懂这种龙卷风暴。明早田野里会找到倒毙的牲口。这还只是开头。闪电照出他跪着的身影、急切仰起的脸，和一根急急指向深渊的手指。这风算不得什么！比起后头要来的，什么都不是。

===Original===

As he shrieked these words I was feeling the crust of the earth vibrate, absolutely vibrate, under the soles of my feet, with the sound of thunder.
He unfastened his cloak, and was seen to struggle above his head with the hovering and flapping cloth, as though he had captured a black and pugnacious bird. We mastered at last a corner each, and then we started to twist the whole, as if to wring the water out. We produced, thus, a sort of short rope, the thickness of a cable, and the descent began.
“Do not look behind you. Do not look,” Castro screeched.
The first downward steps were terrible, but as soon as our heads had sunk below the level of the plain it was better, for we had turned about to the rock, moving sideways, cautiously, one step at a time, as if inspecting its fractured roughness for traces of a mysterious inscription. Castro, with one end of the twisted cloak in his hand, went first; I held the other; and between us, Seraphina, the rope at her back, imitated our movements, with her loosened hair flying high in the wind, and her pale, rigid head as if deaf to the crashes. I saw the drawn stillness of her face, her dilated eyes staring within three inches of the strata. The strain on our prudence was tremendous. The knowledge of the precipice behind must have affected me. Explain it as you will, several times during that descent I felt my brain slip away from my control, and suggest a desire to fling myself over backwards. The twigs of the bushes, growing a little below the outer edge of the path, swished at my calves. Castro stopped. The cornice ended as a broken stairway hangs upon nothing. A tall, narrow arch stood back in the rock, with a sill three feet high at least. Castro clambered over; his head and torso, when he turned about, were lighted up blindingly between the inner walls at every flash. Seeing me lay hold of Seraphina, he yelled:
“Señor, mind! It’s death if you stagger back.”
I lifted her up, and put her over like a child; and, no sooner in myself, felt my strength leave all my limbs as water runs out of an overturned vessel. I could not have lifted up a child’s doll then. Directly, with a wild little laugh, she said to me:
“Juan﻿—I shall never dare come out.”
I hugged her silently to my breast.
Castro went ahead. It was a narrow passage; our elbows touched the sides all the way.

===Chinese===

他尖声喊出这些话时，我正觉出地壳在震，真真切切地震，随着雷声，从我脚底传上来。
他解开斗篷，只见他在头顶上同那块盘旋扑打的布搏斗，仿佛擒住了一只黑黑的、好斗的鸟。我们终于一人制服一只角，然后动手把整块布拧起来，像拧水那样。我们就此搓出一根短短的绳索，有船缆那么粗，下降开始了。
“别回头看。千万别看。”卡斯特罗尖声喊。
开头往下那几步可怕极了，可等我们的头一沉到高地平面以下，就好受些了：我们已转过身面朝岩石，侧着身子，小心翼翼，一步一挪，像是在它破裂的粗粝表面察看一种神秘铭文的痕迹。卡斯特罗攥着拧成的斗篷绳一端，走在前面；我牵着另一端；塞拉菲娜夹在我们中间，绳背在身后，模仿着我们的动作，散开的长发在风里高高飘飞，苍白而僵直的头颅仿佛对那一声声炸响充耳不闻。我看见她脸上绷紧的沉静，她放大的眼睛瞪着三英寸外的岩层。我们全部的谨慎承受着莫大的重压。知道身后便是深渊，这念头必定搅扰了我。随你怎么解释，下降途中我有好几次觉得脑子脱离了我的掌控，竟怂恿起一种向后倒栽下去的欲望。长在小径外缘稍下处的灌木枝条，扫打着我的小腿。卡斯特罗停住了。檐道到了头，像一段断裂的楼梯悬在半空。一道又高又窄的拱门凹进岩壁，门槛至少三英尺高。卡斯特罗翻了过去；他转身时，头和上身在每一次闪光里都被内壁照得雪亮刺目。见我伸手去扶塞拉菲娜，他喊道：
“先生，当心！你往后一晃就没命了。”
我把她抱起来，像个孩子似的送了过去；我自己刚一进去，便觉出力气从四肢里流尽，像水从倾覆的容器里流干。那时我连一个娃娃也举不起来了。随即，她带着一声狂野的轻笑，对我说：
“胡安——我再也不敢出去了。”
我默默把她搂在胸前。
卡斯特罗在前头走。那是一条窄窄的甬道；我们的两肘一路蹭着两壁。

===Original===

He struck at his flint regularly, sparks streamed down from his hand; we felt a freshness, a sense of space, as though we had come into another world. His voice directed us to turn to the left, then cried in the dark, “Stand still.” A blue gleam darted after us, and retired without having done anything against the tenebrous body of gloom, and the thunder rolled far in, unobstructed, in leisurely, organ-like peals, as if through an amazingly vast emptiness of a temple. But where was Castro? We heard snappings, rustlings, mutters; sparks streamed, now here, now there. We dared not move. There might have been steep ridges﻿—deep holes in that cavern. And suddenly we discovered him on all-fours, puffing out his cheeks above a small flame kindled in a heap of dry sticks and leaves.
It was an abode of darkness, enormous, without sonority. Feeble currents of air, passing on our faces, gave us a feeling of being in the open air on a night more black than any known night had been before. One’s voice lost itself in there without resonance, as if on a plain; the smoke of our blaze drove aslant, scintillating with red sparks, and went trailing afar, as if under the clouds of a starless sky. Ultimately, it must have escaped through some imperceptible crevices in the roof of rock. In one place, only, the light of the fire illuminated a small part of the rugged wall, where the shadows of our bodies would surge up, repeating our movements, and suddenly be gone from our sight. Everywhere else, pressing upon the reflection of the flames, the blind darkness of the vault might have extended away for miles and miles.
Castro thought it probable. He made me observe the incline of the floor. It sloped down deep and far. For miles, no doubt. Nobody could tell; no one had seen the end of it. This cavern had been known of old. This brushwood, these dead leaves, that would make a couch for her Excellency, had been stored for years﻿—perhaps by men who had died long ago. Look at the dry rot. These large piles of branches were found stacked up when he first beheld this place. *Caramba!* What toil! What fatigue! Let us thank the saints, however.
Nevertheless, he shook his head at the strangeness of it.

===Chinese===

他有节奏地打着火石，火星从他手里流泻而下；我们觉出一阵清凉，一种空旷之感，仿佛走进了另一个世界。他的声音指点我们向左转，随后又在黑暗里喊道：“站着别动。”一道蓝光追着我们窜进来，又退了出去，对那团浓重的幽暗一无所撼；雷声远远滚进来，毫无遮拦，一阵阵从容不迫、管风琴般的轰鸣，仿佛穿过一座大得惊人的、空空荡荡的殿堂。
可是卡斯特罗在哪儿？我们听见噼啪声、窸窣声、咕哝声；火星忽而在这里、忽而在那里迸溅。我们不敢动。那洞里说不定有陡坎——有深坑。突然，我们发现他四肢着地趴在那里，鼓着腮帮，俯身在一堆干枝枯叶间燃起的小火苗上。
这是一座黑暗的居所，巨大，没有回声。微弱的气流拂过我们的脸，给我们一种身在旷野的感觉，仿佛置身于一个比以往任何已知的夜都更黑的夜里。人在里面说话，声音散了便无声无息，像在平原上一样；我们那堆火冒出的烟斜斜地扑出去，闪着红色的火星，袅袅拖向远处，仿佛飘在无星天空的云底下。到头来，它想必是从岩顶几道无从察觉的裂缝里逸出去的。只有一处，火光照亮了崎岖岩壁的一小片，我们的身影会在那里腾起，复演着我们的动作，又倏然从眼前消失。在其余所有地方，穹顶那盲目的黑暗压着火光的反光，说不定绵延出去好几里又好几里。
卡斯特罗觉得多半如此。他让我留意洞底的坡度。它深深远远地斜下去。好几里，毫无疑问。谁也说不准；没有人见过它的尽头。这洞穴古来就为人所知。这些柴枝，这些枯叶——正好给阁下铺一个卧处——已经存了多年，也许是早已死去的人们存下的。瞧那干腐的样子。他头一回见到这个地方时，这些成大垛的树枝就堆在那儿了。*Caramba*（该死）！多少苦工！多少劳累！不过，让我们感谢圣徒们吧。
尽管如此，对这里头的蹊跷，他还是摇了摇头。

===Original===

His cloak, spread out wide, was drying in the light, while he busied himself with his hat, turning it before the blaze in both hands, tenderly; and his tight little figure, lit up in front from head to foot, steamed from every limb. His round, plump shoulders and gray-shock head smoked quietly at the top. Suddenly, the fine mesh of wrinkles on his face ran together, shrinking like a torn cobweb; a spasmodic sound, quite new to me, was heard. He had laughed.
The warmth of the fire had penetrated our chilled bodies with a feeling of comfort and repose. Williams’ flask was empty; and this was a new Castro, mellowed, discoursive, almost genial. It was obvious to me that, had it not been for him, we two, lost and wandering in the storm, should have died from exposure and exhaustion﻿—from some accident, perhaps. On the other hand I had indubitably saved his life, and he had already thanked me in high-flown language; very grave, but exaggerating the horrors of his danger, as a woman might have done for the better expression of gratitude. He had been greatly shocked. Spaniards, as a race, have never, for all their conquests, been on intimate terms with the sea. As individuals I have often observed in them, especially in the lower classes, a sort of dread, a dislike of salt water, mingled with contempt and fear.
Castro, lifting up his right arm, protested that I had given a proof of very noble devotion in rushing back for an old man into that black water. Ough! He shuddered. He had given himself up﻿—*por Dios!* He hinted that, at his age, he could not have cared much for life; but then, drowning in the sea was a death abhorrent to an old Christian. You died brutally﻿—without absolution, and unable, even, to think of your sins. He had had his mouth filled with horrid, bitter sand, too. Tfui! He gave me a thousand thanks. But these English were wonderful in their way.﻿ ﻿… Ah! *Caramba!* They were.﻿ ﻿…
A large protuberance of the rocky floor had been roughly chipped into the semblance of a seat, God only knows by what hands and in what forgotten age. Seraphina’s inclined pose, her torn dress, the wet tresses lying over her shoulders, her homeless aspect, made me think of a beautiful and miserable gipsy girl drying her hair before a fire.

===Chinese===

他的斗篷摊得开开的，在火光里烘着；他自己忙着侍弄那顶帽子，双手捧着，在火前温存地转来转去；他那紧绷绷的小小身躯从头到脚被火照亮，每个肢体都冒着热气。圆圆厚实的肩膀，一头灰白的乱发，顶上静静地冒着烟。忽然，他脸上那细密的皱纹网拢到一起，像一张扯破的蛛网似的皱缩起来；一阵抽搐似的声音响了，我从未听过。他笑了。
火的暖意渗进我们冻透的身体，带来一种舒适与安歇。威廉斯的酒瓶空了；这是一个焕然一新的卡斯特罗，和悦了，健谈了，几乎称得上亲切。我心里明白，若不是有他，我们两个在风暴里迷路乱闯的人，早就会冻毙力竭而死——也许还会死于什么意外。另一方面，我确凿无疑地救了他的命，他已经用夸张的言辞谢过我；神情十分庄重，却把险境的可怕渲染得过了头，像个女人那样，为了把感激表达得更周全。他受的惊吓实在不小。西班牙人这个种族，纵然有过那么多征服，却从来不曾与海亲近。作为个人，我常常在他们身上、尤其是在下层人身上，观察到一种畏惧，一种对咸水的嫌恶，掺着轻蔑与恐惧。
卡斯特罗抬起右臂，郑重申明：我为救一个老人冲回那片黑水里去，是极高尚的赤诚的明证。呕！他打了个寒噤。他本来已经认命了——*por Dios*！他暗示说，到了他这把年纪，本不至于把命看得太重；可是，淹死在海里，对一个老基督徒是可憎的死法。死得那样横暴——得不到赦罪，甚至连想一想自己的罪孽都来不及。他的嘴里还灌满了可怕的、苦涩的沙子。呸！他给了我一千个感谢。不过这些英国人自有他们的了不起。……啊！*Caramba*！确实了不起。……
岩地上一处凸起的大石，被粗粗凿成了座椅的模样，只有上帝知道出自谁的手、在哪个被遗忘的年代。塞拉菲娜斜倚的姿态、撕破的衣裙、披在肩头的湿发、无家可归的模样，使我想起一个美丽而凄苦的吉卜赛姑娘，正在火前烘干她的头发。

===Original===

A little foot advanced, gleamed white on the instep in front of the ruddy glare; her clasped fingers nursed one raised knee; and, shivering no longer, her head drooping in still profile, she listened to us, frowning thoughtfully upon the flames.
In the guise of a beggar-maid, and fair, like a fugitive princess of romance, she sat concealed in the very heart of her dominions. This cavern belonged to her, as Castro remarked, and the bay of the sea, and the earth above our heads, the rolling upland, herds of cattle, fields of sugarcane﻿—even as far as the forest away there; the forest itself, too. And there were on that estate, alone, over two hundred Africans, he was able to tell us. He boasted of the wealth of the Riegos. Her Excellency, probably, did not know such details. Two hundred﻿—certainly. The estate of Don Vincente Salazar was on the other side of the river. Don Vincente was at present suffering the indignity of a prison for a small matter of a quarrel with another caballero﻿—who had died lately﻿—and all, he understood, through the intrigues of the prior of a certain convent; the uncle, they said, of the dead caballero. Bah! There was something to get. These fat friars were like the lean wolves of Russia﻿—hungry for everything they could see. Never enough, *Cuerpo de Dios*! Never enough! Like their good friend who helped them in their iniquities, the Juez O’Brien, who had been getting rich for years on the sublime generosity of her Excellency’s blessed father. In the greatness of his nobility, Don Balthasar of holy memory had every right to be obstinate.﻿ ﻿… *Basta!* He would speak no more; only there is a saying in Castile that fools and obstinate people make lawyers rich.﻿ ﻿…
“*Vuestra Señoria*,” he cried, checking himself, slapping his breast penitently, “deign to forgive me. I have been greatly exalted by the familiarity of the two last men of your house﻿—allowed to speak freely because of my fidelity.﻿ ﻿… Alas! Alas!”
Seraphina, on the other side of the fire, made a vague gesture, and took her chin in her hand without looking at him.
“Patience,” he mumbled to himself very audibly. “He is rich, this picaro, O’Brien. But there is, also, a proverb﻿—that no riches shall avail in the day of vengeance.”
Noticing that we had begun to whisper together, he threw himself before the fire, and was silent.
“Promise me one thing, Juan,” murmured Seraphina.

===Chinese===

一只小脚向前伸来，在红彤彤的火光前，脚背闪着白光；她十指相扣，抱着一条支起的膝头；她不再发抖了，头低垂着，侧影静定，听我们说话，对着火焰若有所思地蹙着眉。
一身乞女的装束，却美丽，像传奇里出逃的公主，她端坐在自己领地的最深处，隐而不露。这洞穴是属于她的，卡斯特罗这样说，还有那海湾，我们头顶的大地、起伏的高地、成群的牛、一片片甘蔗田——一直到那边远处的森林；连森林本身也是。单是这片庄园上，就有两百多个非洲人，他告诉我们。他夸耀列戈家的豪富。阁下多半不知道这些细情。两百个——错不了。唐·文森特·萨拉查（Don Vincente Salazar）的庄园在河对岸。唐·文森特眼下正蒙着牢狱之辱，为的是同另一位绅士（caballero）闹了点小小的意气——那位不久前死了——而这一切，据他了解，全出自某座修道院院长的阴谋；据说是那位死去的绅士的伯叔。哼！这里头有油水可捞。这些脑满肠肥的修士，就像俄国的瘦狼——见着什么馋什么。永远不够，*Cuerpo de Dios*（上帝的圣体啊）！永远不够！就像他们那位帮着他们为非作歹的好朋友，法官（Juez）奥布赖恩，靠着阁下那位圣善父亲惊人的慷慨，多年来发家致富。凭着他那份高贵的伟大，圣德的唐·巴尔塔萨完全有资格固执。……够了（*Basta*）！他不再多说了；只是卡斯蒂利亚有句俗话，傻瓜和犟脾气的人养肥了律师。……
“夫人阁下（*Vuestra Señoria*），”他喊道，急急刹住话头，悔罪似地拍着胸口，“请您开恩恕罪。承蒙贵府最后两位主子抬举，容我放肆直言——都是因为我的一片忠心。……唉！唉！”
塞拉菲娜在火的另一边做了个含糊的手势，手托着下巴，看也不看他。
“忍着点儿。”他自言自语地咕哝，声音大得人人都听得见。“这个奥布赖恩，这条无赖，有钱。可是还有一句谚语——报应之日，万贯家财也无济于事。”
见我们开始低声耳语，他往火前一躺，不出声了。
“答应我一件事，胡安。”塞拉菲娜低声说。

===Original===

I was kneeling by the side of her seat.
“By all that’s holy,” I cried, “I shall force him to come out and fight fair﻿—and kill him as an English gentleman may.”
“Not that! Not that!” she interrupted me. She did not mean me to do that. It was what she feared. It would be delivering myself into that man’s hands. Did I think what that meant? It would be delivering her, too, into that man’s power. She would not survive it. And if I desired her to live on, I must keep out of O’Brien’s clutches.
“In my thoughts I have bound my life to yours, Juan, so fast that the stroke which cuts yours, cuts mine, too. No death can separate us.”
“No,” I said.
And she took my head in her hands, and looked into my eyes.
“No more mourning,” she whispered rapidly. “No more. I am too young to have a lover’s grave in my life﻿—and too proud to submit.﻿ ﻿…”
“Never,” I protested ardently. “That couldn’t be.”
“Therefore look to it, Juan, that you do not sacrifice your life which is mine, either to your love﻿—or﻿—or﻿—to revenge.” She bowed her head; the falling hair concealed her face. “For it would be in vain.”
“The cloak is perfectly dry now, Señorita,” said Castro, reclining on his elbow on the edge of the darkness.
We two stepped out towards the entrance, leaving her on her knees, in silent prayer, with her hands clasped on her forehead, and leaning against the rugged wall of rock. Outside, the earth, enveloped in fire and uproar, seemed to have been given over to the fury of a devil.
Yes. She was right. O’Brien was a formidable and deadly enemy. I wished ourselves on board the *Lion* chaperoned by Mrs. Williams, and in the middle of the Atlantic. Nothing could make us really safe from his hatred but the vastness of the ocean. Meantime we had a shelter, for that night, at least, in this cavern that seemed big enough to contain, in its black gloom of a burial vault, all the dust and passions and hates of a nation.﻿ ﻿…
Afterwards Castro and I sat murmuring by the diminished fire. He had much to say about the history of this cave. There was a tradition that the ancient buccaneers had held their revels in it. The stone on which the señorita had been sitting was supposed to have been the throne of their chief. A ferocious band they were, without the fear of God or devil﻿—mostly English. The Rio Medio picaroons had used this cavern, occasionally, up to a year or so ago.

===Chinese===

我跪在她的座旁。
“凭一切神圣起誓，”我喊道，“我要逼他出来，堂堂正正地决斗——像个英国绅士那样杀了他。”
“不要那样！不要那样！”她打断我。她要的不是那个。那正是她害怕的。那等于把我自己送进那人的手里。我想过那意味着什么吗？那也等于把她送进那人的掌心。她活不成的。倘若我要她活下去，我就必须躲开奥布赖恩的魔爪。
“在我的心里，我已把我的生命同你的缚在一起，胡安，缚得那么紧，砍断你那一刀，也砍断我这一刀。什么死亡都拆不开我们。”
“拆不开。”我说。
她双手捧住我的头，直望进我的眼睛。
“不要再哀伤了。”她急急地低语。“不要再有了。我太年轻，不该在生命里立一座爱人的坟——我也太高傲，不肯屈服。……”
“绝不，”我热烈地抗辩，“绝不会有那样的事。”
“所以你要记住，胡安，不要把你那条属于我的性命，牺牲给你的爱——或者——或者——牺牲给复仇。”她低下头；垂落的头发遮住了她的脸。“因为那将是枉然。”
“斗篷这会儿干透了，小姐。”卡斯特罗说，单肘支着身子，躺在黑暗的边上。
我们两个朝洞口走去，把她留在那里跪着，默默祷告，双手交叠抵着额头，倚着那面粗粝的岩壁。外面，天地被火与喧嚣裹着，仿佛已经交给了一个魔鬼的狂怒。
是的。她是对的。奥布赖恩是个可怕而致命的仇敌。但愿我们已经登上狮子号，有威廉斯太太照应着，正在大西洋中央。除了大洋的浩瀚，没有什么能让我们真正躲开他的仇恨。眼下我们总算有个栖身之处，至少今夜有，就在这个洞穴里——它那墓窖般阴森的黑黯，仿佛大得容得下一个民族的全部尘埃、情欲与仇恨。……
后来，卡斯特罗和我在渐弱的火边坐着低语。关于这洞穴的来历，他有许多可讲。有个传说，说古时候的海盗曾在这里纵酒作乐。小姐方才坐的那块石头，据说就是他们首领的宝座。那是一伙凶悍的人，不畏上帝也不畏魔鬼——多半是英国人。里奥梅迪奥（Rio Medio）的海寇（picaroons），直到一年多以前，还偶尔用这个洞。

===Original===

But there were always ugly affairs with the people on the estate﻿—the vaqueros. In his younger days Don Balthasar, having whole leagues of grass land here, had introduced a herd of cattle; then, as the Africans are useless for that work, he had ordered some peons from Mexico to be brought over with their families﻿—ignorant men, who hardly knew how to make the sign of the cross. The quarrels had been about the cattle, which the Lugareños killed for meat. The peons rode over them, and there were many wounds on both sides. Then, the last time a Rio Medio schooner was lying here (after looting a ship outside), there was some gambling going on (they played round this very stone), and Manuel﻿—(*Si*, Señor, this same Manuel the singer﻿—*Bestia!*)﻿—in a dispute over the stakes, killed a peon, striking him unexpectedly with a knife in the throat. No vengeance was taken for this, because the Lugareños sailed away at once; but the widow made a great noise, and some rumours came to the ears of Don Balthasar himself﻿—for he, Castro, had been honoured with a mission to visit the estate. That was even the first occasion of Manuel’s hate for him﻿—Castro. And, as usual, the Intendente after all settled the matter as he liked, and nothing was done to Manuel. Don Balthasar was old, and, besides, too great a noble to be troubled with the doings of such vermin.﻿ ﻿… And Castro began to yawn.
At daybreak﻿—he explained﻿—he would start for the hacienda early, and return with mules for Seraphina and myself. The buildings of the estate were nearly three leagues away. All this tract of the country on the side of the sea was very deserted, the sugarcane fields worked by the slaves lying inland, beyond the habitations. Here, near the coast, there were only the herds of cattle ranging the savannas and the peons looking after them, but even they sometimes did not come in sight of the sea for weeks together. He had no fear of being seen by anybody on his journey; we, also, could start without fear in daylight, as soon as he brought the mules. For the rest, he would make proper arrangements for secrecy with the husband of Seraphina’s nurse﻿—Enrico, he called him: a silent Galician; a graybeard worthy of confidence.
One of his first cares had been to grub out of his soaked clothes a handful of tobacco, and now he turned over the little drying heap critically.

===Chinese===

可是跟庄园上的人——那些牧人（vaqueros）——总闹出不愉快的事。他年轻的时候，唐·巴尔塔萨因为在这儿有着整整几里格的草地，引进了一群牛；后来，因为非洲人干不来那活，又叫人从墨西哥迁来一些雇工（peons），连家眷一起——都是些没见识的人，几乎不会画十字。争端都是为了牛，村人（Lugareños）宰了牛吃肉。雇工们骑马冲撞他们，两边都有许多人挂彩。后来，最近一次一条里奥梅迪奥的纵帆船停在这儿时（刚在外海劫了一条船），有人赌起了钱（他们就是围着这块石头赌的），曼努埃尔——（*Si*，先生，就是那个唱歌的曼努埃尔——*Bestia*（畜生）！）——为赌注起了争执，出其不意，一刀捅进一个雇工的喉咙，把他杀了。这事无人寻仇，因为那伙村人立刻扬帆走了；可寡妇闹得沸沸扬扬，一些风声传到了唐·巴尔塔萨本人耳朵里——因为他，卡斯特罗，曾蒙差遣来察看庄园。那甚至就是曼努埃尔恨他——卡斯特罗——的头一遭。而和往常一样，行政长官（Intendente）末了照自己的意思把事情了结，曼努埃尔什么也没摊上。唐·巴尔塔萨老了，再说，那么伟大的贵族，犯不着为这类虫豸的行径烦心。……卡斯特罗打起呵欠来。
天一亮——他解释说——他一早动身去庄园，带着骡子回来接塞拉菲娜和我。庄园的房舍在将近三里格开外。靠海这一带的乡野荒凉得很，奴隶们耕种的甘蔗田都在内地，在人居之外。这儿，近海的地方，只有游荡在大草原上的牛群和照看它们的雇工，可就连他们，有时一连几星期也见不着海。他上路不怕被任何人瞧见；我们呢，等他牵来骡子，也可以白天放心动身。至于其余的，他会同塞拉菲娜奶妈的丈夫妥善安排好保密的事——他管他叫恩里科（Enrico）：一个沉默寡言的加利西亚人；一个值得托付的白胡子老汉。
他最先操心的几件事之一，就是从湿透的衣服里抠出一撮烟丝，这会儿他正挑剔地翻着那一小堆烘着的烟丝。

===Original===

He hunted up a fragment of maize leaf somewhere upon his bosom. His face brightened. “*Bueno*,” he muttered, very pleased.
“Señor﻿—good night,” he said, more humanized than I had supposed possible; or was it only that I was getting to know him better? “And thanks. There’s that in life which even an old tired man.﻿ ﻿… Here I, Castro﻿ ﻿… old and sad, Señor. Yes, Señor﻿—nothing of mine in all the world﻿—and yet.﻿ ﻿… But what a death! Ouch! the brute water﻿ ﻿… *Caramba!* Altogether improper for a man who has escaped from a great many battles and the winter of Russia.﻿ ﻿… The snow, Señor.﻿ ﻿…”
He drowsed, garrulous, with the blackened end of his cigarette hanging from his lower lip, swayed sideways﻿—and let himself go over gently, pillowing his head on the stump of his arm. The thin, viperish blade, stuck upwards from under his temple, gleamed red before the sinking fire.
I raised a handful of flaring twigs to look at Seraphina. A terrible night raged over the land; the inner arch of the opening growled, winking bluishly time after time, and, like an enchanted princess enveloped in a beggar’s cloak, she was lying profoundly asleep in the heart of her dominions.

===Chinese===

他又在怀里什么地方摸出一小片玉米叶。他的脸亮了。“*Bueno*（好），”他咕哝道，十分满意。
“先生——晚安。”他说，比我想象的更有人情味了；还是说，只是因为我越来越了解他了？“还有，多谢。人这一辈子里，有些东西，连一个又老又累的人也。……我，卡斯特罗，在这儿……老了，也悲哀了，先生。是的，先生——这世上没有一样东西是我的——可是。……可那是怎样的一个死法哟！哎哟！那蛮横的水……*Caramba*！对一条从多少次战役里、从俄罗斯的寒冬里逃出命来的汉子，实在不成体统。……那雪啊，先生。……”
他打着盹，话还絮絮不休，烟卷熏黑的蒂子还挂在下唇上，身子往旁边一歪——便顺势软软倒下去，把头枕在断臂的残桩上。那把细薄的、毒蛇似的刀刃，从他太阳穴底下斜斜翘起，在渐渐沉下去的火光前泛着红。
我举起一把燃亮的枝条，去看塞拉菲娜。一个可怖的夜在大地上肆虐；洞口内层的拱壁一阵阵发出低吼，一次次眨着幽蓝的光，而她，像一位裹着乞女斗篷的、中了魔法的公主，正沉沉睡在她领地的最深处。

### VIII / 八
===Original===

The first thing I noted, on opening my eyes, was that Castro had gone already; I was annoyed. He might have called me. However, we had arranged everything the evening before. The broad day, penetrating through the passage, diffused a semicircle of twilight over the flooring. It extended as far as the emplacement of the fire, black and cold now with a gray heap of ashes in the middle. Farther away in the darkness, beyond the reach of light, Seraphina on her bed of leaves did not stir. But what was that hat doing there? Castro’s hat. It asserted its existence more than it ever did on the head of its master; black and rusty, like a battered cone of iron, reposing on a wide flange near the ashes. Then he was not gone. He would not start to walk three leagues, bareheaded. He would appear presently; and I waited, vexed at the loss of time. But he did not appear. “Castro,” I cried in an undertone. The leaves rustled; Seraphina sat up.
We were pleased to be with each other in an inexpugnable retreat, to hear our voices untinged by anxiety; and, going to the outer end of the short passage, we breathed with joy the pure air. The tops of the bushes below glittered with drops of rain, the sky was clear, and the sun, to us invisible, struck full upon the face of the rock on the other side of the ravine. A great bird soared, all was light and silence, and we forgot Castro for a time. I threw my legs over the sill, and sitting on the stone surveyed the cornice. The bright day robbed the ravine of half its horrors. The path was rather broad, though there was a frightful sheer drop of ninety feet at least. Two men could have walked abreast on that ledge, and with a handrail one would have thought nothing of it. The most dangerous part yet was at the entrance, where it ended in a rounded projection not quite so wide as the rest. I bantered Seraphina as to going out. She said she was ready. She would shut her eyes, and take hold of my hand. Englishmen, she had heard, were good at climbing. Their heads were steady. Then we became silent. There were no signs of Castro. Where could he have gone? What could he be doing? It was unimaginable.
I grew nervous with anxiety at last, and begged Seraphina to go in. She obeyed without a word, and I remained just within the entrance, watching. I had no means to tell the time, but it seemed to me that an hour or two passed.

===Chinese===

我睁开眼睛后注意到的第一件事，是卡斯特罗已经不在了；我有些恼火。他本可以叫醒我的。不过，头天晚上我们已经把一切都安排妥当了。白昼的光线穿过那条通道漫进来，在洞口的地上铺开半圆形的一片微明。它一直延伸到生火的地方，火堆如今又黑又冷，中间堆着一摊灰白的灰烬。再往里去，在光照不到的黑暗深处，塞拉菲娜躺在她的树叶铺上，一动不动。可是那儿放着的那顶帽子是怎么回事？卡斯特罗的帽子。它比在主人头上时更加咄咄逼人地宣示着自己的存在；黑黢黢、锈乎乎的，像一只被打瘪的铁皮漏斗，宽宽的帽边贴着灰烬搁在那里。这么说，他没有走。他总不至于光着头上路，走三里格。他一会儿就会露面；我等着，为白白流失的时间而恼火。可他没有露面。“卡斯特罗。”我低声唤道。树叶窸窣作响；塞拉菲娜坐了起来。
我们很高兴彼此相伴，待在这处无法攻入的藏身之地，听着对方的嗓音里不再掺杂焦虑；我们走到短通道外端的洞口，满怀喜悦地呼吸纯净的空气。下方灌木的顶上闪着雨珠，天空明净，看不见的太阳正照在沟壑对面那面岩壁上。一只大鸟翱翔着，四野一片光亮与寂静，我们一时把卡斯特罗忘在了脑后。我跨过窗台，坐在石头上打量那条岩檐。明亮的白昼洗去了沟壑一半的恐怖。那条小路相当宽，虽然旁边是至少九十英尺的骇人直落。两个人可以在那条岩脊上并肩而行，若再有一道扶手，谁也不会把它当回事。最危险的一段还是在入口处，路的尽头是一处浑圆的凸岩，比别处窄一些。我打趣塞拉菲娜，问她敢不敢出去走走。她说她准备好了。她会闭上眼睛，抓紧我的手。她听说英国人擅长攀爬。他们的头脑很稳。随后我们都沉默了。没有卡斯特罗的踪影。他能去哪儿呢？他会在做什么呢？难以想象。
我终于焦虑得沉不住气了，便求塞拉菲娜回到里面去。她一言不发地照办了，我守在入口内侧，一直望着外面。我没有办法知道时间，但我觉得已经过去了一两个钟头。

===Original===

Hadn’t we better, I thought, start at once on foot for the hacienda? I did not know the way, but by descending the ravine again to the sea, and walking along the bank of the little river, I was sure to reach it. The objection to this was that we should miss Castro. Hang Castro! And yet there was something mysterious and threatening in his absence. Could he﻿—could he have stepped out for some reason in the dark, perhaps, and tumbled off the cornice? I had seen no traces of a slip﻿—there would be none on the rock; the twigs of the growth below the edge would spring back, of course. But why should he fall? The footing was good﻿—however, a sudden attack of vertigo.﻿ ﻿… I tried to look at it from every side. He was not a somnambulist, as far as I knew. And there was nothing to eat﻿—I felt hungry already﻿—or drink. The want of water would drive us out very soon to the spring bubbling out at the head of the ravine, a mile in the open. Then why not go at once, drink, and return to our lair as quickly as possible?
But I did not like to think of her going up and down the cornice. I remembered that we had a flask, and went in hastily to look for it. First, I looked near the hat; then, Seraphina and I, bent double with our eyes on the ground examined every square inch of twilight; we even wandered a long way into the darkness, feeling about with our hands. It was useless! I called out to her, and then we desisted, and coming together, wondered what might have become of the thing. He had taken it﻿—that was clear.
But if, as one might suppose, he had taken it away to get some water for us, he ought to have been back long before. I was beginning to feel rather alarmed, and I tried to consider what we had better do. It was necessary to learn, first, what had become of him. Staring out of the opening, in my perplexity, I saw, on the other side of the ravine, the lower part of a man from his waist to his feet.
By crouching down at once, I brought his head into view. This was not Castro. He wore a black sombrero, and on his shoulder carried a gun. He turned his back on the ravine, and began to walk straight away, sinking from my sight till only his hat and shoulders remained visible. He lifted his arm then﻿—straight up﻿—evidently as a signal, and waited. Presently another head and shoulders joined him, and they glided across my line of sight together.

===Chinese===

我思忖，我们不如立刻动身，步行赶往庄园去？我不认识路，但只要再下到沟壑底的海边，沿着小河的河岸走，我肯定能走到那里。这样做的弊端是会与卡斯特罗错过。让卡斯特罗见鬼去吧！然而他的不在场，总带着一种神秘而威胁的意味。他会不会——会不会出于什么缘故在黑暗中走了出去，比如，从岩檐上跌了下去？我没有看到失足的痕迹——岩石上本来也不会留下什么；岩边下方的灌木枝条自然会弹回原状。可他为什么会跌下去？立足处是牢靠的——不过，一阵突然的眩晕。……我试着从各个方面去想。据我所知，他并没有梦游的毛病。而且这里没有东西可吃——我已经觉得饿了——也没有水喝。缺水很快就会逼得我们到沟壑顶端那眼露天的泉水去，那可是一里格的露天路程。那么何不立刻就去，喝足了水，再尽快回到我们的巢穴里来呢？
可我不愿意想到她在岩檐上走上走下。我想起我们还有一只水壶，急忙进洞去找。我先在帽子附近找；然后我和塞拉菲娜弯着腰、眼睛盯着地面，把那片微明里的每一寸地方都查遍了；我们甚至摸黑往深处走了很远，用手四下探摸。徒劳无功！我唤了她一声，我们这才罢手，走到一处，猜想着那东西的下落。是他拿走了——这很清楚。
可如果按常理推测，他是拿了它去为我们取水，那他早就该回来了。我开始感到相当惊慌，竭力盘算我们该怎么办。首先必须弄清他的下落。我正茫然地望着洞口外面，忽然看见沟壑对岸出现了一个男人的下半身，从腰到脚。
我立刻蹲低身子，把他的头也收进视野。这不是卡斯特罗。他戴一顶黑色阔边帽，肩上扛着一支枪。他背对着沟壑，径直向前走去，渐渐沉出我的视线，最后只剩帽子和双肩还看得见。接着他抬起手臂——笔直向上——显然是个信号，然后等着。很快又一颗头颅和一副肩膀同他会合，两人一齐从我的视线上滑行而过。

===Original===

But I had recognized their bandit-like aspect with infinite consternation. *Lugareños!*
I caught Seraphina’s hand. My first thought was that we should have to steal out of the cavern with the first coming of darkness. Castro must be lying low in hiding somewhere above. The thing was plain. We must try to make our way to the hacienda under the cover of the night, unseen by those two men. Evidently they were emissaries sent from Rio Medio to watch this part of the coast against our possible landing. I was to be hunted down, it seems: and I reproached myself bitterly with the hardships I was bringing upon her continually. Thinking of the fatigues she had undergone﻿—(I did not think of dangers﻿—that was another thing﻿—the romance of dying together like all the lovers in the tradition of the world)﻿—I shook with rage and exasperation. The firm pressure of her hands calmed me. She was content. But what if they took it into their heads to come into the cavern?
The emptiness of the blue sky above the sheer yellow rock opposite was frightful. It was a mere strip, stretched like a luminous bandage over our eyes. They were, perhaps, even now on their way round the head of the ravine. I had no weapon except the butt of my pistol. The charges had been spoilt by the salt water, of course, and I had been tempted to fling it out of my belt, but for the thought of obtaining some powder somewhere. And those men I had seen were armed. At once we abandoned the neighbourhood of the entrance, plunging straight away into the profound obscurity of the cave. The rocky ground under our feet had a gentle slope, then dipped so sharply as to surprise us; and the entrance, diminishing at our backs, shone at last no larger than the entrance of a mouse-hole. We made a few steps more, gropingly. The bead of light disappeared altogether when we sat down, and we remained there hand-in-hand and silent, like two frightened children placed at the centre of the earth. There was not a sound, not a gleam. Seraphina bore the crushing strain of this perfect and black stillness in an almost heroic immobility; but, as to me, it seemed to lie upon my limbs, to embarrass my breathing like a numbness full of dread; and to shake that feeling off I jumped up repeatedly to look at that luminous bead, that point of light no bigger than a pearl in the infinity of darkness.

===Chinese===

可我已经认出他们那副土匪模样，顿时惊恐到了极点。*Lugareños！*
我一把抓住塞拉菲娜的手。我的第一个念头是：我们必须赶在天色刚黑下来时悄悄溜出山洞。卡斯特罗必定正蛰伏在上方什么地方。事情很明白。我们必须设法借着夜色的掩护前往庄园，不让那两个人看见。他们显然是里奥梅迪奥派来监视这一带海岸、防备我们可能登陆的密探。看来我是要被追捕到底了：我一再带给她种种磨难，为此我痛心疾首地自责。想到她经受的种种劳顿——（危险我倒没有想到——那是另一回事——像世间一切恋人那样一同死去，自有其浪漫之处）——我气得浑身发抖，愤懑难平。她的手坚定地一握，让我平静下来。她心满意足。可万一他们起了念头，要进山洞里来呢？
对面光秃秃的黄岩之上，那一线蓝天空得吓人。那不过是一条窄带，像一条发光的绷带蒙在我们眼上。说不定此刻他们正绕向沟壑的顶端。除了手枪的枪柄，我没有任何武器。弹药自然早被海水泡坏了，若不是还想着往后在什么地方弄点火药，我早把它从腰带上扔掉了。而我看见的那两个人是带枪的。我们立刻放弃了洞口一带，径直扎进洞穴深处的浓黑里。脚下的岩石地面先是缓缓倾斜，随即陡然下沉，让我们吃了一惊；身后洞口的光越来越小，最后亮得不过一个鼠洞口那么大。我们又摸索着走了几步。坐下之后，那粒光点便完全消失了，我们手拉手坐在那里，一言不发，像两个被安置在地心的、吓坏了的孩子。没有一点声音，没有一丝光亮。塞拉菲娜以近乎英雄般的镇定，承受着这彻底的、漆黑的沉寂的重压；而于我，它仿佛压在我的四肢上，像一种充满恐惧的麻木，妨碍我的呼吸；为了甩掉这种感觉，我一再跳起来，去看那粒发亮的光珠——那颗在无边的黑暗中不过珍珠大小的光点。

===Original===

And once, just as I was looking, it shut and opened at me slowly, like the deliberate drooping and rising of the lid upon a white eyeball.
Somebody had come in.
We watched side by side. Only one. Would he go out? The point of light, like a white star setting in a coal-black firmament, remained uneclipsed. Whoever had entered was in no haste to leave. Moreover, we had no means of telling what another obscuring of the light might mean; a departure or another arrival. There were two men about, as we knew; and it was even possible that they had entered together in one wink of the light, treading close upon each other’s heels. We both felt the sudden great desire to know for certain. But, especially, we needed to find out if perchance this was not Castro who had returned. We could not afford to lose his assistance. And should he conclude, we were out﻿—should he risk himself outside again, in order to find us and be discovered himself, and thus lost to us when we felt him so necessary? And the doubt came. If this man was Castro, why didn’t he penetrate further, and shout our names? He ought to have been intelligent enough to guess.﻿ ﻿… And it was this doubt that, making suspense intolerable, put us in motion.
We circled widely in that subterranean darkness, which, unlike the darkest night on the surface of the earth, had no suggestion of shape, no horizon, and seemed to have no more limit than the darkness of infinite space. On this floor of solid rock we moved with noiseless steps, like a pair of timid phantoms. The spot of light grew in size, developed a shape﻿—stretching from a pearly bead to a silvery thread; and, approaching from the side, we scanned from afar the circumscribed region of twilight about the opening. There was a man in it. We contemplated for a time his rounded back, his drooping head. It was gray. The man was Castro. He sat rocking himself sorrowfully over the ashes. He was mourning for us. We were touched by this silent faithfulness of grief.
He started when I put my hand on his shoulder, looked up, then, instead of giving any signs of joy, dropped his head again.
“You managed to avoid them, Castro?” I said.
“Señor, behold. Here I am. I, Castro.”
His tone was gloomy, and after sitting still for a while under our gaze, he slapped his forehead violently.

===Chinese===

而有一次，正当我望着它时，它缓缓地对我一合一睁，像一只白眼球上的眼皮慢吞吞地垂下，又抬起来。
有人进来了。
我们并排守望着。只进来了一个。他会出去吗？那光点像一颗白星沉落在漆黑的天宇里，始终没有被遮住。进来的人不急于离开。再说，我们也无从判断光线再一次被遮蔽意味着什么：是离去，还是又来了一个。我们知道外头有两个人；甚至有可能他们前后脚一齐进来，赶在同一次光暗交替里。我们俩忽然涌起一股强烈的欲望：要弄个水落石出。尤其是，我们必须查明，这会不会是卡斯特罗回来了。我们不能失去他的助力。倘若他断定我们已经出去——倘若他为了找我们再一次冒险走到外面，自己被他们发现，从而在我们最需要他的时候失去他，那怎么好？疑心随之而来。如果这个人是卡斯特罗，他为什么不往里走，不喊我们的名字？他应该足够聪明，猜得到。……正是这个疑问使悬念变得无法忍受，催我们行动起来。
我们在那地下的黑暗里绕了一个大圈。这黑暗不同于地表上最黑的夜，没有丝毫形状的暗示，没有地平线，仿佛与无限太空的黑暗一样没有边际。在这整块岩石的地面上，我们脚步无声地移动，像一对怯懦的幽灵。那光点渐渐变大，显出了形状——从一粒珍珠似的光珠拉成一条银线；我们从侧面接近，远远地打量洞口四周那一小圈微明里的一切。里面有一个人。我们注视了一阵他那浑圆的背影、那垂着的头。头发是灰白的。那人是卡斯特罗。他坐在灰烬前，哀哀地摇着身子。他在为我们悲伤。这份沉默的、忠贞的哀恸令我们动容。
我把手放到他肩上，他吓了一跳，抬起头来，随即非但没有露出半点欣喜，反而又垂下了头。
“你躲开他们了，卡斯特罗？”我说。
“先生，您瞧。我在这儿呢。我，卡斯特罗。”
他的口气阴郁，在我们的注视下呆坐了片刻之后，猛地一巴掌拍在自己的额头上。

===Original===

He was in his tantrums, I judged, and, as usual, angry with me﻿—the cause of every misfortune. He was upset and annoyed beyond reason, as I thought, by this new difficulty. It meant delay﻿—a certain measure of that sort of danger of which we had thought ourselves free for a time﻿—night travelling for Seraphina. But I had an idea to save her this. We did not all want to go. Castro could start, alone, for the hacienda after dark, and bring, besides the mules, half a dozen peons with him for an escort. There was nothing really to get so upset about. The danger would have been if he had let himself be caught. But he had not. As to his temper, I knew my man; he had been amiable too long. But by this time we were so sure of his truculent devotion that Seraphina spoke gently to him, saying how anxious we had been﻿—how glad we were to see him safe with us.﻿ ﻿… He would not be conciliated easily, it seemed, and let out only a bloodcurdling dismal groan. Without looking at her, he tried hastily to make a cigarette. He was very clever at it generally, rolling it with one hand on his knee somehow; but this time all his limbs seemed to shake, he lost several pinches of tobacco, dropped the piece of maize leaf. Seraphina, stooping over his shoulder, took it up, twisted the thing swiftly. “Take, amigo,” she said.
He was looking up at her, as if struck dumb, roiling his eye wildly. He jumped up.
“You﻿—Señorita! For a miserable old man! You break my heart.”
And with long strides he disappeared in the darkness, leaving us wondering.
We sat side by side on the couch of leaves. With Castro there I felt we were quite equal to dealing with the two Lugareños if they had the unlucky idea of intruding upon us. Indeed, a vigilant man, posted on one side of the end of the passage, could have disputed the entrance against ten, twenty, almost any number, as long as he kept his strength and had something heavy enough to knock them over. Faint sounds reached me, as if at a great distance Castro had been shouting to himself. I called to him. He did not answer, but unexpectedly his short person showed itself in the brightest part of the light.
“Señor!” he called out with a strange intonation. I got up and went to him. He seemed to be listening intently with his ear turned to the opening. Then suddenly:
“Look at me, Señor. Am I Castro﻿—the same Castro? old and friendless?”

===Chinese===

我判断他又在发脾气了，而且照例是在生我的气——我是一切灾祸的根由。我想，他被这个新的难题搅得烦乱懊恼，失了分寸。这意味着耽搁——意味着一段时间里，我们原以为已经摆脱的那类危险又回来了——意味着塞拉菲娜要走夜路。可我有个法子让她免掉这一遭。我们用不着全都上路。卡斯特罗可以等天黑之后独自动身去庄园，除了骡子，再带上六七个雇工当护卫一起来。实在没有什么好这样心神不定的。危险原本在于他会不会被人抓住。可他没有被抓住。至于他的脾气，我了解我这个人；他和善得太久了。而此刻，我们对他的暴戾的忠心已经如此深信不疑，塞拉菲娜便柔声对他说话，说我们方才多么焦急——如今看见他安然回到我们身边，又是多么欢喜。……他似乎不肯轻易消气，只发出一声令人毛骨悚然的凄恻长叹。他看也不看她，慌忙着手卷一支烟。平常他干这个十分在行，总能单手在膝盖上把烟卷出来；可这一回他的四肢仿佛都在发抖，撒落了好几撮烟丝，那片玉米叶也掉了。塞拉菲娜俯身从他肩上拾起来，利落地捻好了烟。“拿着，朋友（*amigo*）。”她说。
他仰头望着她，仿佛惊得说不出话，眼珠狂乱地打转。他跳了起来。
“您——小姐！为着我这么个苦命的老头！您把我的心都揉碎了。”
他迈开大步走进黑暗里不见了，留下我们面面相觑。
我们并肩坐在树叶铺就的榻上。有卡斯特罗在，我觉得哪怕那两个 Lugareños 当真起了倒霉的念头闯进来，我们也能从容应付。的确，只要有一个警惕的人守在通道口的一侧，就能守住那道入口，对付十个、二十个、几乎任何数目的敌人，只要他力气还在，手里又有件够分量、能把人砸翻的东西。我隐约听见声响，仿佛卡斯特罗在远处什么地方对自己叫嚷。我喊他。他没有应声，可出人意料地，他矮小的身影出现在光线最亮的地方。
“先生！”他用一种古怪的声调喊道。我起身朝他走去。他似乎正凝神倾听，耳朵偏向洞口。忽然，他说：
“您看着我，先生。我还是卡斯特罗吗——还是原来那个卡斯特罗吗？又老又没人依靠？”

===Original===

He stood biting his forefinger and looking up at me from under his knitted eyebrows. I didn’t know what to say. What was this nonsense?
He ejaculated a sort of incomprehensible babble, and, passing by me, rushed towards Seraphina; she sat up, startled, on her couch of leaves. Falling before her on his plump knees, he seized her hand, pressed it against his ragged moustache.
“Excellency, forgive me! No﻿—no forgiveness! Ha! old man! Ha﻿—thou old man.﻿ ﻿…”
He bowed before her shadowy figure, that sustained the pale oval of the face, till his forehead struck the rock. Plunging his hand into the ashes, he poured a fistful with inarticulate low cries over his gray hairs; and the agitation of that obese little body on its knees had a lamentable and grotesque inconsequence, as inexplicable in itself as the sorrow of a madman. Full of wonder before his abject collapse, she murmured:
“What have you done?”
He tried to fling himself upon her feet, but my hand was in his collar, and after an unmerciful shaking, I sat him down by main force. He gulped, blinked the whites of his eyes, then, in a whisper full of rage:
“Horror, shame, misery, and malediction; I have betrayed you.”
At once she said soothingly, “Tomas, I do not believe this”; while I thought to myself: How? Why? For what reason? In what manner betrayed? How was it possible? And, if so, why did he come back to us? But, as things stood, he would never dare approach a Lugareño. If he had, they would never have let him go again.
“You told them we were here?” I asked, so perfectly incredulous that I was not at all surprised to hear him protest, by all the saints, that he never did﻿—never would do. Never. Never.﻿ ﻿… But why should he? Was he the prey of some strange hallucination? Rocking himself, he struck his breast with his clenched hand, then suddenly caught at his hair and remained perfectly motionless. Minutes passed; this despairing stillness inspired in me a feeling of awe at last﻿—the awe of something inconceivable. My head buzzed so with the effort to think that I had the illusions of faint murmurs in the cave, the very shadows of murmurs. And all at once a real voice﻿—his voice﻿—burst out fearfully rapid and voluble.
He had really gone out to get a provision of water. Waking up early, he saw us sleeping, and felt a great pity for the señorita. As to the caballero﻿—his saviour from drowning, alas!

===Chinese===

他站在那里咬着食指，皱起的眉头底下仰视着我。我不知道说什么好。这是什么昏话？
他咕哝出一串不知所云的呓语，从我身边擦过，直冲塞拉菲娜而去；她正在树叶铺上惊得坐起身来。他扑通一声跪倒在她跟前，肥硕的双膝着地，抓住她的手，按在自己斑白的髭须上。
“大人，饶恕我！不——不必饶恕！哈！老头儿！哈——你这老头儿。……”
他朝着她那朦胧的身影深深下拜——那身影托着一张苍白的鹅蛋脸——直拜到额头磕在岩石上。他把手插进灰烬，抓起一把，一边发出含混的低喊，一边倾倒在花白的头发上；那肥胖的小小身躯跪在那里激动着，又可悲又滑稽，全无道理可讲，就像疯子的悲哀一样无从解释。面对他这般自弃的崩溃，她满心惊疑，喃喃地问：
“你做了什么？”
他想要扑倒在她的脚上，可我的手已经揪住他的领子，毫不留情地摇晃了一阵之后，我硬把他按坐了下来。他咽了口唾沫，眨动着白眼珠，随即用一种盛满怒气的耳语说：
“恐怖、耻辱、苦难、诅咒；我把你们出卖了。”
她立刻温言道：“托马斯，我不信这个。”我心里却在想：怎么会？为什么？出于什么缘由？以什么方式出卖的？这怎么可能？果真如此，他为什么还回到我们身边来？不过照眼下的情形看，他绝不敢去接近什么 Lugareño。倘若他真的去过，那些人也绝不会放他回来。
“你告诉他们我们在这儿了？”我问。我压根儿不信，因此听他指着众圣徒起誓，说他从没有——绝不会做这种事，也丝毫不觉得意外。绝没有。绝没有。……可他为什么要那样？难道他被什么奇异的幻觉攫住了？他摇晃着身子，握紧的拳头捶着自己的胸口，忽然又两手抓住头发，纹丝不动了。几分钟过去了；这绝望的静止终于在我心里唤起一种敬畏——对某种不可想象之事的敬畏。我费尽心思去想，脑袋嗡嗡作响，以致起了幻觉，仿佛洞中有低低的人语，人语之影。蓦地，一个真实的声音——他的声音——以可怕的速度喷涌而出，滔滔不绝。
他果真是出去取水的。一早醒来，他看见我们还在睡，心里对小姐生出大怜悯。至于那位绅士——唉，他那从溺水中救起的恩人！

===Original===

﻿—the señorita would need every ounce of his strength. He would let us sleep till his return from the spring; and, there being a blessed freshness in the air, he caught up the flask and started bareheaded. The sun had just risen. Would to God he had never seen it! After plunging his face in the running water, he remained on his knees and busied himself in rinsing and filling the flask. The torrent, gushing with force, made a loud noise, and after he had done screwing the top on, he was about to rise, when, glancing about carelessly, he saw two men leaning on their *escopetas* and looking at him in perfect silence. They were standing right over him; he knew them well; one they called El Rubio; the other, the little one, was José﻿—squinting José. They said nothing; nothing at all. With a sudden and mighty effort he preserved his self-command, affected unconcern and, instead of getting up, only shifted his pose to a sitting position, took off his shoes and stockings, and proceeded to bathe his feet. But it was as if a blazing fire had been kindled in his breast, and a tornado had been blowing in his head.
He could not tell whence these two had come, with what object, or how much they knew. They might have been only messengers from Rio Medio to Havana. They generally went in couples. If Manuel had escaped alive out of the sea, everything was known in Rio Medio. From where he sat he beheld the empty, open sea over the dunes, but the edge of the upland, cleft by many ravines (of which the one we had ascended was the deepest), concealed from him the little basin and the inlet. He was certain these men had not come up that way. They had approached him over the plain. But there was more than one way by which the upland could be reached from below. The thoughts rushed round and round his head. He remembered that our boat must be floating or lying stranded in the little bay, and resolved, in case of necessity, to say that we two were dead, that we had been drowned.
It was El Rubio who put the very question to him, in an insolent tone, and sitting on the ground out of his reach, with his gun across his knees. His long knife ready in his hand, squinting José remained standing over Castro. Those two men nodded to each other significantly at the intelligence. He perceived that they were more than half disposed to credit his story.

===Chinese===

——小姐往后要用得着他的每一分气力。他要让我们一直睡到他打泉水回来；趁着清晨空气里有一种可喜的清凉，他抓起水壶，光着头就出发了。太阳刚刚升起。但愿他从没见过它才好！他把脸浸进奔流的水里之后，便跪在那儿淘洗、灌水。激流涌得猛，声响很大；他拧好壶盖，正要起身，无意间抬眼一望，看见两个男人拄着他们的火枪（*escopetas*），正一声不响地望着他。他们就站在他头顶上方；他都认得：一个他们唤作埃尔·鲁比奥（El Rubio）；另一个，矮个子，是何塞——斗鸡眼的何塞。他们一言不发；一言也不发。他猛地使出一股大力保持住了自制，装出满不在乎的样子，不但没有起身，反倒换了姿势坐下来，脱掉鞋袜，洗起脚来。可他胸口像被点起了一盆烈火，脑袋里像刮着一场旋风。
他说不上这两个人从哪儿来、来做什么、又知道多少。他们也许只是从里奥梅迪奥前往哈瓦那的信使。他们通常是成双成对走的。倘若曼努埃尔从海里活着逃了出去，那么里奥梅迪奥那边就什么都知道了。从他坐的地方，越过沙丘，他能望见空旷的开阔海面，但高地边缘被许多沟壑割裂（我们爬上来的那条是最深的一条），把那小小的水湾和湾口都遮在了他视线之外。他确信这两个人不是从那条路上来的。他们是越过平原向他走来的。而从下方登上高地，路不止一条。种种念头在他脑子里转来转去。他想起我们那条小船必定还漂着，或是搁浅在小湾里，便打定主意，万一被逼到绝境，就说他和我都死了，说我们都淹死了。
恰恰是埃尔·鲁比奥用一种傲慢无礼的口气向他提出了这个问题；他坐在地上，隔着一段够不着的距离，枪横在膝头。长刀握在手里随时可用，斗鸡眼的何塞一直站在卡斯特罗身旁。听到这个消息，那两个人意味深长地彼此点了点头。他觉察出，他们多半信了他的话。

===Original===

They had nearly been drowned themselves pursuing that accursed heretic of an Englishman. When, from their remarks, he learned that the schooner was in the bay, he began putting on his shoes, though the hope of making a sudden dash for his life down the ravine abandoned him.
The schooner had been run in at night during the gale, and in such distress that they let her take the ground. She was not injured, however, and some of them were preparing to haul her off. Our boat, as I conceived, after bumping along the beach, had drifted within the influence of the current created by the little river, or else by the water forced into the basin by the tempest, seeking to escape, and had been carried out towards the inlet. She was seen at daylight, knocking about amongst the breakers, bottom up, and in such shallow water that three or four men wading out knee-deep managed to turn her over. They had found Mrs. Williams’ woollen shawl and my cap floating underneath. At the same time the broken mast and sail were made out, tossing upon the waves, not very far off to seaward. That the boat had been in the bay at all did not seem to have occurred to them. It had been concluded that she had capsized outside the entrance. It was very possible that we had been drowned under her. Castro hastened to confirm the idea by relating how he had been clinging to the bottom of the boat for a long time. Thus he had saved himself, he declared.
“Manuel will be glad,” observed El Rubio then, with an evil laugh. And for a long time nobody said a word.
El Rubio, cross-legged, was observing him with the eyes of a basilisk, but Castro swore a great oath that, as to himself, he showed no signs of fear. He looked at the water gushing from the rock, bubbling up, sparkling, running away in a succession of tiny leaps and falls. Why should he fear? Was he not old, and tired, and without any hope of peace on earth? What was death? Nothing. It was absolutely nothing. It comes to all. It was rest after much vain trouble﻿—and he trusted that, through his devotion to the Mother of God, his sins would be forgiven after a short time in purgatory. But, as he had made up his mind not to fall into Manuel’s hands, he resolved that presently he would stab himself to the heart, where he sat﻿—over this running water. For it would not be like a suicide.

他们自己追那个该死的异教徒英国佬，也差点淹死。当他从他们的话里得知纵帆船就在湾里，他便开始穿鞋，尽管那个顺着沟壑猛冲逃命的指望已经放弃了。
那条纵帆船是夜里顶着大风驶进来的，情势那样危急，他们只得任它抢滩搁下。不过船没有损坏，有几个人正打算把它拖下来。依我推想，我们那条小船在滩头磕磕撞撞漂了一阵之后，被小河卷起的水流——也可能是风暴灌进湾里的海水在寻路外泄——裹挟着，被带出了湾口。天亮时人们看见它翻着底朝天，在碎浪间颠簸，水又那样浅，三四个男人蹚到齐膝深，就把它翻了过来。他们在船底下发现了威廉斯太太的羊毛披肩和我的便帽。与此同时，断掉的桅杆和帆也在不太远的海面上被认了出来，在浪头间颠簸。他们似乎压根儿没有想到小船曾经进过湾里。大家断定它是在湾口外面倾覆的。我们多半是压在船底下淹死了。卡斯特罗连忙讲他怎样在船底上趴了许久，坐实了这一想法。他声称，他就是这样捡回一条命的。
“曼努埃尔会高兴的。”埃尔·鲁比奥这时说，发出一声恶毒的笑。好一阵子没有人说一句话。
埃尔·鲁比奥盘着腿，用王蜥般的眼光打量他，而卡斯特罗狠狠赌了一个咒：至于他自己，他毫无惧色。他望着从岩石里涌出来的水，汩汩上冒，晶晶发亮，一跳一跌地奔流而去。他有什么可怕的呢？他不是又老、又累、在人世间再没有安宁可盼了吗？死是什么？什么也不是。完完全全什么也不是。人人都有份。那是无穷劳碌之后的一场休息——他相信，凭着他对圣母的虔敬，他的罪过会在炼狱里受罚短短一阵之后得到赦免。不过，既然他已打定主意绝不能落入曼努埃尔的手里，他便决意，过一会儿，就坐在原地——坐在这流淌的水边——把刀子捅进自己的心口。因为那可不算自杀。
